=== 0002e5e0 [PLATE]
Paints a solid square of one palette colour directly into the visible mode-13h VGA screen.

Algorithm:
Computes the top-left destination as 0xa0000 + y * 0x140 + x -- the VGA graphics aperture plus the 320-byte mode-13h scanline pitch -- and keeps it in a local. Then loops i from 0 while i < cell_pitch - 1, calling memset(dst, color, cell_pitch - 1) once per iteration and advancing dst by 0x140 to the next scanline. The square it paints is therefore cell_pitch-1 pixels wide and cell_pitch-1 pixels tall, one pixel short of cell_pitch in each direction. There is no clipping and no bounds check: x, y and cell_pitch are used exactly as given, so a run that passes column 319 spills into the following scanline.

Parameters:
  x -- screen pixel column of the square's left edge, 0..319 for an on-screen result; fdps_battle_map_overview passes 160 + tile_x * cell_pitch - (map_width_in_tiles * cell_pitch) / 2.
  y -- screen pixel row of the square's top edge, 0..199 for an on-screen result; fdps_battle_map_overview passes 100 + tile_y * cell_pitch - (map_height_in_tiles * cell_pitch) / 2.
  color -- VGA palette index, passed straight to memset so only the low byte matters. fdps_battle_map_overview uses a per-side base colour plus a 0..7 pulse counter for unit markers, and 0x82 plus that counter for the cursor marker.
  cell_pitch -- spacing in pixels between adjacent squares; the square drawn is cell_pitch-1 on a side. fdps_battle_map_overview passes its pixels-per-tile zoom step, 4 normally and 3 for maps taller than 0x28 tiles.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library; hard-coded VGA aperture 0xa0000 and mode-13h pitch 0x140, called only from fdps_battle_map_overview and calling only the CRT memset]

Rebuild note:
The side length is cell_pitch-1, not cell_pitch: both the row count and the memset length are the argument minus one, so writing the obvious `for (i = 0; i < size; i++) memset(dst, color, size)` makes every overview marker one pixel wider and taller, closing the one-pixel gaps that separate adjacent map tiles. The routine also writes to 0xa0000 -- the live screen -- after the caller has already presented its offscreen page, so redirecting it to the game's back buffer would make the markers disappear.

=== 0002f240 [PLATE]
Uploads a contiguous run of VGA DAC palette entries from three separate per-channel byte arrays, after waiting for vertical retrace so the change lands during blanking.

Algorithm:
Spins on inp(0x3da) -- the VGA Input Status #1 register -- until bit 3, the vertical-retrace-active flag, reads as set; the wait happens once, before any entry is written, so a call made while retrace is already active proceeds immediately. Then for i from 0 while i < count: writes i + first_index to the DAC write-index port 0x3c8 through outp, then writes red[i], green[i] and blue[i] to the DAC data port 0x3c9 in that order. The index port is rewritten for every entry instead of relying on the DAC's own auto-increment. The channel bytes are passed through unchanged: unlike fdps_set_palette_range there is no per-channel bias and no clamp to 0x3f, and the DAC simply ignores the top two bits of each byte. The loop bound is a signed JL, so a count of zero or less writes nothing and the retrace wait is the call's only effect.

Parameters:
  first_index -- DAC entry the run starts at, 0..255. fdps_cycle_scene_palette passes fixed high indices: 0xf0, 0xf5, 0xf6 and 0xf8.
  red -- pointer to count consecutive red bytes, one per DAC entry.
  green -- pointer to count consecutive green bytes, one per DAC entry.
  blue -- pointer to count consecutive blue bytes, one per DAC entry. The caller aims all three at per-channel ramp arrays it copied onto its own stack, displaced by a rotating phase offset, which is what makes the colours cycle.
  count -- how many consecutive DAC entries to program; the caller passes 5, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 15.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and a body hash unique in the image; the only caller is game code and the only callees are the shared inp/outp port primitives, and no CRT or AIL routine drives the VGA DAC]

Blits a rectangular block of 8bpp pixels between two surfaces of independent pitch, skipping every source byte that is 0 so that palette index 0 reads as transparent.

Algorithm:
Copies src and dst into the stack cursors at [EBP-0x8] and [EBP-0x4], leaving the caller's pointers untouched, then runs the row counter [EBP-0x14] from 0 while it is less than height. For each row it runs the column counter [EBP-0xc] from 0 while it is less than width, loads src_cursor[x] zero-extended into the pixel local at [EBP-0x10], and stores that byte to dst_cursor[x] only when it is non-zero; a zero source byte is the transparency key and leaves the destination pixel as it was. After each row it adds src_stride to the source cursor and dst_stride to the destination cursor, which is what lets the two buffers have different pitches. Both loop tests are signed JL, so a width or height of 0 or less transfers nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check of any kind -- the callers do the clamping, as fdps_draw_gauge_fill does when it refuses to call with coord above 0x7d. Calls nothing and touches no global.

This is the colour-keyed counterpart of fdps_blit_rect at 0x0002f2f0, and the two are not interchangeable in two ways: this one tests every pixel instead of running memmove over the row, and a src_stride of 0 is not a fill mode here -- it simply makes every destination row draw from the same source row.

Parameters:
  src -- pointer to the top-left pixel of the source rectangle, 8 bits per pixel, palette indices with 0 meaning transparent
  src_stride -- source pitch in bytes, added to the source cursor once per row; the full width of the source sheet, which is normally larger than width (0x75 from fdps_draw_gauge_bar, 0x7d from fdps_draw_gauge_fill)
  dst -- pointer to the top-left pixel of the destination rectangle in the surface being composed
  dst_stride -- destination pitch in bytes, added to the destination cursor once per row
  width -- pixels per row to consider, 0 or less transfers nothing
  height -- rows to consider, 0 or less transfers nothing

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; all ten references are direct calls from game code, and nothing in CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387 is a strided colour-keyed pixel copy]

Rebuild note:
The destination is read-modify-write, not overwrite: source bytes equal to 0 are skipped entirely, so the pixels underneath survive. Rewriting this row loop as the obvious memcpy/memmove per row -- which is what its sibling fdps_blit_rect at 0x0002f2f0 does, with the same six-argument signature -- would paint colour 0 over the background and erase whatever the previous blits had put there. The second trap is inherited from that sibling: fdps_blit_rect treats src_stride == 0 as a fill mode where the first argument is a fill byte rather than a pointer, and this function has no such branch, so carrying that special case over while writing the transparent version would dereference a colour value as a pointer.

=== 0002f40f [EOL]
Single-byte 0x90 NOP alignment pad before FUN_0002f410.

=== 0002f410 [PLATE]
Plays the box screen transition between two pictures: a rectangle of the outgoing picture shrinks toward the centre, or a rectangle of the incoming picture grows out of the centre, one delayed frame at a time.

Algorithm:
Allocates two width*height scratch buffers with malloc, neither result checked, and snapshots the rectangle currently sitting on dst into the second one with fdps_blit_rect, so the outgoing picture survives the animation. Both scratch buffers are packed: every blit into or out of them passes width as the stride, whatever dst_pitch is.
style == 0, the outgoing picture closes in. cur_w/cur_h start at width/height and the centring offset at 0. While 2*step_x <= cur_w and 2*step_y <= cur_h, each pass rebuilds the frame from scratch: blit the whole of src into buffer A, blit the cur_w x cur_h rectangle of the snapshot at the current offset over it, present buffer A to dst, then delay(frame_delay). cur_w then drops by 2*step_x, cur_h by 2*step_y, and the offset advances by step_y*width + step_x, so the surviving rectangle of the outgoing picture keeps its centre as it shrinks.
style != 0, the incoming picture opens out. The frame count is min(width / (2*step_x), height / (2*step_y)), with one subtracted from either term that divides evenly, so the animation deliberately stops one step short of covering the whole rectangle. The rectangle starts at offset (steps*step_x, steps*step_y) sized (width - 2*steps*step_x) x (height - 2*steps*step_y). Each pass: memmove the snapshot over buffer A, blit the matching rectangle of src into buffer A at that position, present buffer A to dst, delay(frame_delay); the rectangle then grows by 2*step_x and 2*step_y while its origin walks back by (step_x, step_y), and the counter is decremented.
Both paths finish with one full fdps_blit_rect of src onto dst, which is what actually completes the transition, then free both scratch buffers.

Parameters:
  src -- the incoming picture, an 8bpp image of at least width x height
  src_pitch -- row stride of src in bytes
  dst -- the target surface; it carries the outgoing picture on entry, because the opening blit reads the rectangle back off it
  dst_pitch -- row stride of dst in bytes
  width -- rectangle width in pixels; also the stride of both scratch buffers and, times height, their malloc size
  height -- rectangle height in pixels
  step_x -- how far each vertical edge of the rectangle moves per frame; the rectangle's width changes by twice this. Must not be 0 for style != 0, which divides by 2*step_x. For style 0 a zero step_x alone does not hang -- cur_w simply never shrinks and the loop still ends when cur_h falls below 2*step_y -- but step_x and step_y both 0 loops forever
  step_y -- the same for the horizontal edges. Must not be 0 for style != 0, which divides by 2*step_y. For style 0 a zero step_y alone does not hang -- cur_h simply never shrinks and the loop still ends when cur_w falls below 2*step_x -- but step_x and step_y both 0 loops forever
  frame_delay -- handed straight to the CRT delay() between frames
  style -- 0 shrinks the outgoing picture toward the centre; any other value grows the incoming picture out of the centre

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; calls fdps_blit_rect, a symbol only the game's own code can reference]

Rebuild note:
In the style != 0 path the frame count subtracts one whenever the extent divides evenly by twice the step, so the animation stops one step short and the trailing full blit is what finishes it. Writing the obvious steps = width / (2*step_x) adds a frame that paints the complete incoming picture plus an extra delay(), and the closing blit then repeats that same picture.

=== 0002f6c7 [EOL]

=== 0002f6d0 [PLATE]
Plays one of eight sliding screen transitions from a source image to a destination rectangle: four directions, each available either as the new image sliding in over the old picture or as the old picture sliding away to uncover the new one.

Algorithm:
Allocates two width*height scratch buffers with malloc and never checks either for NULL: a compose buffer for the frame being assembled, and a snapshot buffer that immediately receives a copy of the destination rectangle through fdps_blit_rect, i.e. the picture that was on screen when the transition started. Both are packed at pitch = width. Both are allocated and the snapshot is taken even for the four styles that never read them.
Dispatches on style; the compare is unsigned against 7, so any other value (a negative one included) skips every branch and drops straight to the final blit. Each branch runs i = step, 2*step, ... while i is below height (styles 0-3) or below width (styles 4-7), draws one frame with fdps_blit_rect, then calls delay(frame_delay). The last partial step is never drawn.
  style 0 -- rows 0..i of dst take the bottom i rows of src: the new image descends into view from the top edge while the old picture stays put underneath.
  style 1 -- the compose buffer takes the snapshot shifted up by i rows plus the bottom i rows of src left where they belong, then goes to dst whole: the old picture slides off the top edge and uncovers the new one.
  style 2 -- rows height-i..height of dst take the top i rows of src: the new image rises into view from the bottom edge.
  style 3 -- the compose buffer takes the top i rows of src in place plus the snapshot shifted down by i rows: the old picture slides off the bottom edge.
  style 4 -- columns 0..i of dst take the rightmost i columns of src: the new image slides in from the left edge.
  style 5 -- the compose buffer takes the snapshot shifted left by i columns plus the rightmost i columns of src in place: the old picture slides off the left edge.
  style 6 -- the horizontal counterpart of style 2, the new image arriving from the right edge, but the destination it anchors on is dst + (height - i) where every other horizontal branch works in columns of width. See the rebuild note.
  style 7 -- the compose buffer takes the leftmost i columns of src in place plus the snapshot shifted right by i columns: the old picture slides off the right edge.
Ends every path with one full-rectangle blit of src over dst, so the destination always holds the complete new image whatever the style was, then frees the compose and snapshot buffers.

Parameters:
  src -- the incoming 8bpp image, read with src_pitch as its row stride
  src_pitch -- byte stride of one row of src
  dst -- the destination surface, holding the outgoing picture on entry and the whole of src on return; written with dst_pitch as its row stride, and read once at the start to take the snapshot
  dst_pitch -- byte stride of one row of dst
  width -- width in bytes/pixels of the rectangle being transitioned; also the packed pitch of both scratch buffers, and the loop bound of styles 4-7
  height -- height in rows of the rectangle; the loop bound of styles 0-3
  step -- pixels or rows advanced per frame; also the position of the first frame drawn
  frame_delay -- milliseconds handed to the CRT delay() after each frame
  style -- which of the eight effects to run, 0-7; anything else does the final blit with no animation

Returns:
  nothing.

Pool: fdps  [game presentation code: draws only through fdps_blit_rect, which library objects cannot reference, and merely consumes malloc/free/delay; no Function ID hit and a unique hash in the image]

Rebuild note:
Style 6 anchors its destination at dst + (height - i) while its loop counts i up to width. Writing the obvious dst + (width - i) draws a different picture on any rectangle that is not square, and it also removes an out-of-bounds write the original has: on a 320x200 rectangle i runs past 200, so the original starts writing in front of dst. Keep height here, and do not add a bounds guard.

=== 0002fb80 [PLATE]
Mosaic screen transition: shuffles a table of every cell of a grid_cols x grid_rows phase grid and, one shuffled cell at a time, blits every block belonging to that phase from src to dst, pausing with delay() after each cell so the image appears in random patches.
Pool: fdps  [called by game code, calls fdps_blit_rect; no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ail set]
Evidence: Both callers are game-side screen code (fdps_load_game_screen, fdps_save_game_screen) and it calls the game's fdps_blit_rect at 0002f2f0, which library objects cannot do; malloc/free/rand/delay are its only vendor calls, the application usage pattern. full_hash a78787bdeb7cc69f is unique in the image and absent from ailv3.lib, and 689 bytes of parameterised nested loops rule out a linker or compiler product.
Name: no library symbol identified; fdps_ + snake_case describing the effect the code produces.
Boundary: 0002fb80-0002fe30, Watcom prologue at the entry and the matching epilogue RET at 0002fe30; the 15 bytes after it are LEA-form alignment padding before FUN_0002fe40.
Signature: __cdecl, eleven 32-bit stack arguments at [EBP+0x14]..[EBP+0x3c] (src_or_fill, src_pitch, dst, dst_pitch, width, height, grid_cols, grid_rows, block_w, block_h, frame_delay), returns void, bare RET so the caller cleans.
Details: allocates grid_cols*grid_rows four-byte entries (int16 col, int16 row) and fills them row-major. The shuffle is NOT Fisher-Yates: for each index i it draws two independent rand() values and swaps entry i with entry j = grid_cols*(rand()%grid_rows) + rand()%grid_cols, so an entry can be revisited and the permutation is not uniform. Per-phase block counts are blocks_x = ceil((width/block_w)/grid_cols) and blocks_y = ceil((height/block_h)/grid_rows). For shuffled cell (bx,by) it walks x = bx + i*grid_cols and pixel row y = block_h*(j*grid_cols + by), drawing only when x < width and y < height; the source argument is the [EBP+0x14]/[EBP+0x18] pair, built as src_or_fill + (src_pitch ? x*block_w : 0) + y*src_pitch, and the destination is the [EBP+0x1c]/[EBP+0x20] pair, built as dst + x*block_w + y*dst_pitch with no conditional; size block_w by block_h. The zero-stride case is fdps_blit_rect's fill mode: with src_pitch 0 the first argument is a palette index that has to arrive unchanged, which is why the block offset is dropped from it. delay() is called once per shuffled cell, after all of that cell's blocks, not per block row. The horizontal bound test compares a block-column index against the pixel width while the vertical one compares a pixel row against the pixel height, so the horizontal test is far looser; the real horizontal bound is the blocks_x loop count. The table is freed before returning.

=== 0002fe31 [EOL]
Watcom 16-byte alignment padding between fdps_transition_random_blocks and FUN_0002fe40

=== 0002fe40 [PLATE]
Draws a rectangular region from one 8bpp surface into another as a mosaic: each block_w x block_h cell of the region becomes one flat colour, taken from the source pixel at the middle of that cell.

Algorithm:
Divides the region into ceil(width/block_w) columns by ceil(height/block_h) rows of cells, each count computed as a signed divide plus one when the remainder is non-zero. Walks the cell rows outermost: for each row it forms the source sample row pointer src + sample_row*src_stride (sample_row starts at block_h/2 and grows by block_h), resets the sample column to block_w/2 and the destination x to 0, and shortens the band height to height - dest_y when a full block_h would overrun the region. Inside it walks the cell columns, shortening the run width to width - dest_x when a full block_w would overrun, then fills the cell by calling memset once per destination row: memset(band_row + dest_x, src_sample_byte, run_width), stepping band_row by dst_stride. After each cell the destination x advances by the run width and the sample column by block_w; if the sample column has reached width it is snapped back to width - width%block_w, the start of the trailing partial column, and the run width is set to that remainder. The same snap is applied to the sample row and the band height against height at the end of each cell row, while the destination band pointer advances by dst_stride*block_h. Nothing is read from the destination and nothing is written to the source, so src and dst may be the same surface only if the mosaic is not meant to feed back into itself.

Parameters:
  src -- base of the 8bpp surface sampled; the region's top-left pixel, not the surface's
  src_stride -- bytes between two source rows; 0x140 (320) from the only caller
  dst -- base of the 8bpp surface written; the region's top-left pixel. The only caller passes 0xa3b58, the VGA framebuffer at 0xa0000 plus 47*320+152
  dst_stride -- bytes between two destination rows; 0x140 (320) from the only caller
  width -- region width in pixels; 0x97 (151) from the only caller
  height -- region height in pixels; 0x95 (149) from the only caller
  block_w -- mosaic cell width in pixels, 1 or more
  block_h -- mosaic cell height in pixels, 1 or more. The only caller always passes block_w == block_h

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; its only caller is game code (fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window) and its only callee is the CRT memset, which is the normal direction]

Rebuild note:
The source sample position is a running accumulator that is snapped to width - width%block_w (the first pixel of the trailing partial cell) once it passes the region, not clamped to width-1; the same snap applies to rows against height. Writing the obvious src[min(row*block_h + block_h/2, height-1)*src_stride + min(col*block_w + block_w/2, width-1)] agrees everywhere except the trailing partial row or column, and only when the remainder is 2 or more but no larger than half the block: with the caller's height 149 and block_h 7, the original fills the last two-pixel band from source row 147 while the clamped form uses row 148. The same accumulator makes width%block_w == 0 leave a run width of 0 and a sample column of width on its final update; that value is never used only because the cell loop ends on that iteration, so a rewrite that keeps looping would read one pixel past the region.

=== 00030010 [PLATE]
Alpha-blends a single constant palette colour over an 8bpp source rectangle, resolving each blended colour back to a palette index through an inverse-palette table.
Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit on either library set; hash unique in the image; called only from named game code]
Evidence: fid.watcom and fid.ail are both empty with zero candidates, and full_hash aa05da20779be6da has same_hash_in_image 1 and same_hash_in_ail_lib 0, so these bytes match nothing in CLIB3S/MATH387S/EMU387 or ailv3.lib. The only references are three static calls from fdps_play_vfs_animation and fdps_show_game_over - no function-pointer table slot, so no other module decides the pool. It calls nothing and touches no globals, no AIL state and no DOS state. The arithmetic is game-specific 8bpp palette compositing against the game's own weighted blend table and inverse-palette LUT, which is no C runtime service, and at 262 bytes with a full frame and two nested loops it is far larger than anything the linker or compiler emits, so not binary_artifact.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code; no vendor symbol to collide with, and the unique hash rules out a shape collision.
Boundary: 00030010-00030115, entry on the Watcom prologue 53 56 57 55 89 e5 / sub esp,0x1c whose four pushes explain the first argument sitting at [EBP+0x14], end on the RET closing the matching epilogue; the 10 bytes after it are LEA-form NOP padding aligning the next function to 00030120.
Signature: __cdecl, confirmed by the assembly - all ten arguments are read from [EBP+0x14] through [EBP+0x38], EAX/EDX/EBX/ECX are written before ever being read so nothing arrives in registers, and the plain RET leaves the caller to clean up. Returns nothing.

Algorithm:
shade_ramp is a [18][256] array of dwords holding each palette entry pre-scaled by a weight, with the three colour channels packed one per byte as 0x000R0G0B - blue in byte 0, green in byte 1, red in byte 2, each channel's nibble sitting at bits 8n+4..8n+7 before the shift below. Rows 0..8 hold weights 0..8; rows 9..17 (dword offset 0x900 = 9*256) hold the complementary weights. To keep the row index inside 0..8 the function folds alpha: for alpha <= 8 the constant colour reads row alpha and the source pixels read row 9+alpha; for alpha > 8 alpha is replaced by 16-alpha, the constant colour reads row 9+alpha' and the source pixels read row alpha'. Either way the constant colour ends up weighted by the caller's alpha and the source pixel by 16-alpha.
The scaled constant colour is fetched once before the loops. For each pixel the scaled source colour is added to it, the sum is shifted right by 4 (dividing out the /16 of the weights) and masked with 0x000F0F0F, leaving 4 bits per channel: blue at bits 0..3, green at bits 8..11 and red at bits 16..19. Those are folded into a 12-bit index by (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12), giving green in bits 8..11, red in bits 4..7 and blue in bits 0..3. That index selects a palette byte from the 4096-entry inverse-palette table inverse_palette_cube, which is stored to the destination.
Rows advance by src_stride and dst_stride; no clipping, no transparency test, every pixel in the rectangle is written.

Parameters:
src                  - source 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
src_stride           - bytes to add to src per row
dst                  - destination 8bpp pixels, top-left of the rectangle
dst_stride           - bytes to add to dst per row
width                - pixels per row
height               - number of rows
shade_ramp           - base of the [18][256] dword weighted-colour table
inverse_palette_cube - base of the 4096-entry packed-RGB to palette-index table
tint_color           - palette index of the constant colour being blended in
alpha                - blend weight of tint_color, 0..16 (0 = source only, 16 = tint only)

Returns:
Nothing.

=== 00030116 [EOL]

=== 00030120 [PLATE]
Blits an 8bpp source rectangle into a destination surface with one constant palette colour blended over it, skipping every source pixel of palette index 0 so it reads as transparent; the colour-keyed counterpart of fdps_blit_tint_rect at 0x00030010.

Algorithm:
shade_ramp is an [18][256] array of dwords, the table fdps_build_palette_tables builds at DAT_000653f0: every palette entry pre-scaled by a weight, with the three channels held one per byte (red in bits 16-19, green in 8-11, blue in 0-3 of the packed word). Rows 0..8 carry weights 0..8 and rows 9..17 (dword offset 0x900 = 9*256) the complementary weights, so the row index is kept inside 0..8 by folding alpha: for alpha <= 8 the constant colour reads row alpha and the source pixels row 9+alpha; for alpha > 8 alpha is replaced by 16-alpha, the constant colour reads row 9+alpha' and the source pixels row alpha'. Either way tint_color ends up weighted by alpha and the source pixel by 16-alpha. The row base is shade_ramp + alpha*0x100 dwords (SHL 0xa, 0x400 bytes per row) and is computed once, after the fold.
The scaled constant colour shade_ramp[alpha][tint_color] is fetched once before the loops. Then height rows of width pixels each: a source byte of 0 is skipped and the destination pixel keeps what it had; any other byte has its own scaled colour added to the constant, the sum shifted right by 4 to divide out the weights, masked with 0x000F0F0F and folded into a 12-bit value by (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12), which lands green in bits 8-11, red in bits 4-7 and blue in bits 0-3 -- the order fdps_build_palette_tables fills the 4096-entry cube at DAT_000643f0 in. That value indexes inverse_palette_cube and the palette byte it holds is stored to the destination.
At the end of each row src_stride is added to src and dst_stride to dst, both in the caller's own argument slots. Both loop tests are signed, so a width or height of 0 or less draws nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check; the function calls nothing and touches no global.

Parameters:
  src -- top-left pixel of the source rectangle, 8bpp palette indices with 0 meaning transparent. fdps_draw_unit_gauge passes a record of the 0x2b-by-6 gauge-bar table at DAT_000643b4.
  src_stride -- bytes added to src once per row; 0x2b from fdps_draw_unit_gauge, the full width of one gauge-bar record.
  dst -- top-left pixel of the destination rectangle in the surface being composed.
  dst_stride -- bytes added to dst once per row, the destination pitch, independent of src_stride.
  width -- pixels per row to draw; 0 or less draws nothing.
  height -- rows to draw; 0 or less draws nothing.
  shade_ramp -- base of the [18][256] dword weighted-colour table; DAT_000653f0 from fdps_draw_unit_gauge.
  inverse_palette_cube -- base of the 4096-entry inverse-palette cube indexed green:red:blue, 4 bits per channel; DAT_000643f0 from fdps_draw_unit_gauge.
  tint_color -- palette index of the constant colour blended in, 0..255. fdps_draw_unit_gauge forwards its own blit_mode argument, which reaches here whenever it is neither 0 nor 1.
  alpha -- weight of tint_color, 0..16 (0 = source only, 16 = tint only); values above 8 are mirrored onto the low half of the table.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image; no CRT, AIL or DOS idiom, no callees, and the arithmetic is game-specific 8bpp palette compositing over the game's own blend table and inverse-palette cube]

Rebuild note:
The 12-bit index into the inverse-palette cube is green:red:blue, not red:green:blue: the fold (v & 0xFFFF) | (v >> 12) at 000301ee-000301ff puts green in bits 8-11, red in 4-7 and blue in 0-3, which is the order fdps_build_palette_tables fills DAT_000643f0 in (its outer 0..15 loop is the green argument of fdps_palette_find_nearest_color, the middle loop the red one). Writing the obvious (r << 8) | (g << 4) | b here while leaving the table builder faithful swaps red and green in every blended pixel.

=== 0003022c [EOL]
4-byte alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0x0] (8d 44 20 00)

=== 00030230 [PLATE]
Alpha-blends two 8bpp source rectangles into a destination rectangle, resolving every blended colour back to a palette index through the game's inverse-palette cube. The untransparent twin of fdps_blit_blend_transparent_rect at 0x00030360, which is this same algorithm plus an index-0 mask test.

Algorithm:
When alpha is greater than 8 the two source pointers and their strides are swapped and alpha becomes 0x10 - alpha. That yields the same blend and keeps the table row index inside 0..8, which is what the two lookups below require.
blend_table is the [18][256] dword array that fdps_build_palette_tables fills at DAT_000653f0. Each entry holds one palette colour with its three 4-bit channels packed as red at bits 16-19, green at bits 8-11 and blue at bits 0-3, pre-multiplied by that row's weight; the coefficients at DAT_0002ae40 are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,16,15,14,13,12,11,10,9,8, so row alpha and row alpha+9 always sum to a weight of 16. The row base is computed once as blend_table + (alpha << 10) and the second lookup adds 0x2400, the byte offset of nine further rows.
For each of height rows and width columns it reads one byte from each source span, looks the fg byte up in row alpha and the bg byte up in row alpha+9, adds the two packed values, arithmetic-shifts the sum right by 4 to divide by the weight total and masks it with 0x0f0f0f to drop the bits that bled between channels. It then folds the three surviving nibbles into a 12-bit key as green<<8 | red<<4 | blue -- green major, which is the order fdps_build_palette_tables walks when it fills the cube -- and stores rgb444_lut[key] into the destination span. After each row fg, bg and dst each advance by their own stride.
Both loop tests are signed, so a width or height of 0 or less draws nothing. There is no clipping and no bounds check; the function calls nothing and touches no global.

Parameters:
  fg -- pointer to the top-left byte of the foreground rectangle, the source whose weight is alpha; 8bpp palette indices. Callers pass a rendered CEL panel or window image.
  fg_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of fg; 0x97 or 0x12e in the callers, i.e. the panel's own packed pitch.
  bg -- pointer to the top-left byte of the background rectangle, the source whose weight is 16 - alpha. fdps_message_window_open and fdps_message_window_close pass the same address they pass as dst, blending in place.
  bg_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of bg; 0x140 (320) in all three callers.
  dst -- pointer to the top-left byte of the destination rectangle; either VGA memory (0xa3b58 from fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window) or an offscreen 320-wide page.
  dst_stride -- byte distance between successive rows of dst; 0x140 (320) in all three callers.
  width -- pixels blended per row; 0 or less blends nothing.
  height -- rows blended; 0 or less blends nothing. fdps_message_window_open clamps it to 0x49 so the sliding panel never runs off the bottom of the screen.
  blend_table -- base of the 18 x 256 dword weighted-palette table; always DAT_000653f0.
  rgb444_lut -- base of the 16x16x16 inverse-palette cube indexed green<<8 | red<<4 | blue; always DAT_000643f0.
  alpha -- weight of fg out of 16, 0..16. 0 copies bg, 16 copies fg. The callers ramp it (1,3,..,15 and 5,7,..,15) to fade a panel in or out.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; hash unique in the image, and all three callers are game code, one of them fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window]

Rebuild note:
The 12-bit key this routine builds is green-major -- green<<8 | red<<4 | blue -- not the r<<8|g<<4|b an RGB444 lookup is usually written as. It is not a bug: fdps_build_palette_tables fills DAT_000643f0 with green as the outer loop, so the cube and the key agree. Writing the obvious RGB ordering in either place alone swaps red and green in every blended pixel.

=== 00030353 [EOL]
Alignment padding: lea eax,[eax+0] / lea edx,[edx+0] / nop, 13 bytes to 16-byte boundary.

=== 00030360 [PLATE]
Blends one 8bpp source rectangle over a background rectangle with index-0 transparency and writes the resulting palette indices into a destination rectangle.

Algorithm:
1. Saves src and src_pitch in locals; that saved pointer is the transparency mask for the whole run and is never swapped.
2. When alpha > 8, swaps (src, src_pitch) with (back, back_pitch) and replaces alpha with 16 - alpha, so the weight taken from the first table row is always 0..8.
3. Selects the two blend rows out of blend_tables (DAT_000653f0 at both call sites): row alpha at blend_tables + alpha*0x400, and row alpha+9 at a further +0x2400. fdps_build_palette_tables fills those rows: row L holds, for each of the 256 palette indices, the entry's colour packed as red nibble in bits 16-19, green in bits 8-11, blue in bits 0-3, multiplied by the coefficient table at 0002ae40 whose 18 entries are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,16,15,14,13,12,11,10,9,8. Pairing row alpha with row alpha+9 therefore gives weights alpha and 16-alpha, which sum to 16.
4. For each row y < height, for each column x < width: leaves dst[x] untouched when the mask byte at that column is 0; otherwise adds the row-alpha entry for src[x] to the row-alpha+9 entry for back[x], shifts the sum right by 4 and masks 0x0f0f0f, which leaves the three blended 4-bit channels one per byte with no carry between them, folds them into the 12-bit key green<<8 | red<<4 | blue, and stores inverse_palette[key] into dst[x].
5. At the end of each row advances src, back and dst by their own pitches, and the mask pointer by the original src pitch.

This is the index-0-transparent member of the blend pair; fdps_blit_blend_rect at 00030230 is the same blend with no mask test.

Both callers, fdps_draw_unit_gauge and fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up, pass the same pointer for back and for dst, so the visible effect is a translucent sprite drawn onto the surface it reads through.

Parameters:
  src -- top 8bpp span, the sprite or foreground; also the transparency mask, whose zero bytes suppress the write. fdps_draw_unit_gauge passes a gauge-bar graphic of stride 0x2b, fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up a 0x28-wide sprite.
  src_pitch -- byte stride between rows of src.
  back -- 8bpp span blended underneath src; both callers pass the destination itself.
  back_pitch -- byte stride between rows of back.
  dst -- 8bpp destination span receiving the blended indices.
  dst_pitch -- byte stride between rows of dst.
  width -- columns per row.
  height -- rows.
  blend_tables -- base of the 18 x 256 dword weighted packed-colour table built by fdps_build_palette_tables; DAT_000653f0 at both call sites.
  inverse_palette -- the 16x16x16 nearest-palette-index cube built by fdps_build_palette_tables, indexed green<<8 | red<<4 | blue; DAT_000643f0 at both call sites.
  alpha -- weight of src out of 16, 0..16. 0 leaves back showing, 16 leaves src showing. Values above 8 are handled by the swap in step 2, so both halves of the range are served by table rows 0..8.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either library set and the hash is unique in the image; both callers are game bodies and nothing in the Watcom CRT or Miles AIL does paletted blending]

Rebuild note:
The index-0 transparency test reads the ORIGINAL first source, saved to [EBP-0x4] and [EBP-0x10] at 00030372 and 0003036c before the alpha > 8 swap, not the post-swap src. Writing the obvious C -- swap the two operands, then test src[x] != 0 -- masks against the background instead of the sprite for every alpha above 8, and the sprite's transparent pixels come out painted. That path is live: fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up feeds alpha = (n / 3) + 8, which crosses 8 as the floating experience number ramps up.

Algorithm:
Returns -1 at once unless both audio gates are open: the digital-driver-present flag at 0x00069d71, which fdps_audio_init sets only when AIL_install_DIG_INI succeeded, and the sound-effects-enabled flag at 0x00069d70, which fdps_audio_init sets to 1 and fdps_options_menu toggles. This is the barest of the game's three sample-starting routines. The other two, fdps_sfx_play@000142d0 and fdps_audio_start_wav@00030a00, claim a voice by the identical eight-slot scan and then call both AIL_set_sample_type and AIL_set_sample_volume; this one calls neither, so the block plays in whatever format and at whatever volume AIL_init_sample leaves behind. Returns:
The index 0..7 of the sample voice the sound was started on, or -1 when the digital driver is absent, when sound effects are switched off, or when all eight voices are already playing.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the ailv3 set; it consumes public AIL entry points and owns the game-side audio globals 0x00069d30, 0x00069d5c, 0x00069d70 and 0x00069d71, which vendor code would not own]

=== 00030829 [EOL]
alignment filler after the ret: 8d 80 00 00 00 00 + 90, aligns next function entry 00030830 to 16

=== 00030830 [PLATE]
Parses an in-memory RIFF/WAVE image and fills a caller-supplied 14-byte packed descriptor with the sample format and the location of the PCM data.

Algorithm:
Checks the four bytes at wav_data for 'R','I','F','F' (0x52/0x49/0x46/0x46) and the four at wav_data+8 for 'W','A','V','E' (0x57/0x41/0x56/0x45); either mismatch returns -1 without touching info_out. Otherwise it sets a cursor to wav_data+0xc, the first chunk header, clears its two chunk pointers and walks the chunk list: each pass compares the cursor's four id bytes against 'fmt ' (0x66/0x6d/0x74/0x20) and against 'data' (0x64/0x61/0x74/0x61), remembering the cursor in the matching slot, and stops as soon as both slots are non-NULL. When neither test has completed the pair it advances the cursor by the chunk's 32-bit payload size at +4 plus the 8-byte chunk header and repeats; there is no end-of-buffer test and no pad-to-even-boundary step. On the break it writes, in this order: byte fmt+0xa (WAVEFORMAT payload+2, the low byte of nChannels) to info_out+0; byte fmt+0x16 (payload+0xe, wBitsPerSample) to info_out+1; dword fmt+0xc (payload+4, nSamplesPerSec) to info_out+2; dword data+4 (the data chunk's payload size) to info_out+6; and data+8 (the address of the PCM bytes) to info_out+0xa. Returns 0. The dwords sit at unaligned offsets 2, 6 and 0xa, so the descriptor is byte-packed, not naturally aligned.

Parameters:
  wav_data -- pointer to a whole .WAV file already read into memory; in practice a MISC.VFS/IconAni.vfs entry such as Levup.wav loaded by the caller. Never NULL-checked.
  info_out -- pointer to a 14-byte packed descriptor the caller owns (fdps_audio_start_wav passes a stack local): channels (byte), bits per sample (byte), sample rate (dword at +2), PCM byte count (dword at +6), PCM data pointer (dword at +0xa). Written only on success.

Returns:
  0 when both the RIFF/WAVE tags matched and the descriptor was filled; -1 when either tag check failed, in which case info_out is left untouched. The sole caller, fdps_audio_start_wav, discards the value and reads the descriptor's channel byte immediately.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID candidate in either the Watcom or the ailv3 set; sole caller is game code that drives AIL through its public entry points and reads this descriptor at exactly these packed offsets]

Rebuild note:
The chunk walk advances by exactly payload_size + 8 with no RIFF pad-to-even-boundary and no end-of-buffer guard, and it only stops once BOTH 'fmt ' and 'data' have been seen. Writing the correct RIFF loop -- rounding odd chunk sizes up to an even stride, or bounding the walk by the RIFF size and bailing out -- diverges from the original: the original desynchronises on an odd-sized chunk and runs off the end of a WAV that is missing either chunk, where the careful version would stop cleanly.

=== 000309fc [EOL]
Alignment padding: 4-byte Watcom NOP form lea eax,[eax+0x0] before FUN_00030a00.

=== 00030a00 [PLATE]
Starts one in-memory .WAV sound playing on the first of the game's eight AIL digital sample voices that is not busy, and hands the caller back the voice it used.

Algorithm:
Returns -1 immediately unless both audio flags are set: the digital-driver-present flag at 00069d71, which fdps_audio_init sets only when AIL_install_DIG_INI succeeded, and the sound-on option flag at 00069d70, which fdps_options_menu toggles with XOR 1 and the save code restores. Then it scans the eight-entry AIL sample handle table at 00069d30 from slot 0 upward, stopping at the first slot whose AIL_sample_status is not 4 (playing); if all eight are playing it returns -1 without touching anything. With a free slot in hand it calls fdps_wav_parse_header on wav_data, filling a 14-byte packed descriptor on its own stack -- channels at +0, bits per sample at +1, sample rate at +2, PCM byte count at +6, PCM data pointer at +0xa -- and turns the (channels, bits) pair into an AIL format code: (1,8) gives 0, (1,16) gives 1, (2,8) gives 2, and anything else, (2,16) included, gives 3, i.e. DIG_F_MONO_8, DIG_F_MONO_16, DIG_F_STEREO_8, DIG_F_STEREO_16. A playback_rate of -1 is replaced here by the descriptor's sample rate. It then configures the voice in this order: AIL_init_sample, AIL_set_sample_address with the descriptor's PCM pointer and byte count, AIL_set_sample_type with the format code and the fixed flags word 2, AIL_set_sample_loop_count, AIL_set_sample_playback_rate, and AIL_start_sample. Volume is set last, after the sound is already running: AIL_set_sample_volume with the caller's volume, or with 0x3c (60) when the caller passed -1. The voice index is the return value.

Parameters:
  wav_data -- pointer to a whole .WAV file image already read into memory, in practice a VFS entry such as Levup.wav. Not NULL-checked and not validated; see the rebuild note.
  loop_count -- passed straight to AIL_set_sample_loop_count. Every caller passes 1, one playthrough.
  playback_rate -- sample rate in Hz to play at, or -1 to use the rate in the .WAV header. Every caller passes -1.
  volume -- AIL sample volume, or -1 to use the game's default of 0x3c (60). Every caller passes -1.

Returns:
  The index 0..7 of the sample voice the sound was started on, which the caller can hand to fdps_audio_sample_is_playing or fdps_audio_stop_sample; -1 when sound is off, when the digital driver is absent, or when all eight voices are already playing.

Pool: fdps  [calls the public Miles AIL entry points and game code; no Function ID hit in either the Watcom or the AIL set]

Rebuild note:
The return value of fdps_wav_parse_header is discarded. On a buffer that is not RIFF/WAVE the parser leaves the 14-byte descriptor untouched, and this function goes on to hand AIL whatever uninitialised stack bytes are sitting there as the PCM address, length and format. Adding the obvious guard -- return -1 when the parse fails -- makes the rebuild behave differently from the original, so do not add it. The same applies to the format ladder's final else: it is reached by any (channels, bits) pair the first three tests missed, not only by (2,16), and it must stay a plain else rather than becoming an error path.

=== 00030be4 [EOL]
Alignment padding: two 6-byte NOP forms (lea eax,[eax+0]; lea edx,[edx+0]) aligning FUN_00030bf0 to 16 bytes.

=== 00030bf0 [PLATE]
Sets the CD background music: records which music track the game wants playing and makes the CD-ROM drive match, stopping playback instead when music is switched off or the caller asks for silence.

Algorithm:
Copies the requested music index into the working slot, and when the music-enabled setting at DAT_00060008 is 0 forces that slot to -1, so a music-off setting discards whatever the caller asked for. Publishes the result in the current-music global DAT_00069d54, which fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll reads to restart the track when it runs out. If that value is -1 it calls fdps_cd_stop_audio and returns; otherwise (the music-enabled setting is retested, and is always non-zero on this path) it calls fdps_cd_play_track with DAT_00069d54 + 1 -- the CD track number is one more than the music index the game uses.

Parameters:
  music_index -- 0-based background-music index, or -1 to stop the music. fdps_title_screen and fdps_play_ending_credit_roll pass 1, fdps_run_village_phase passes 2 on entering the village and -1 on leaving it, and fdps_icon_script_run passes the byte operand of an IconAni script opcode, mapping the operand 0xff to -1.

Returns:
  Nothing.

Pool: fdps  [game state and game-only call graph; no library match -- calls only fdps_cd_stop_audio and fdps_cd_play_track and drives the game globals DAT_00060008 and DAT_00069d54]

Rebuild note:
When the music-enabled setting DAT_00060008 is 0 this routine does not just skip playing -- it overwrites the current-music global DAT_00069d54 with -1 and calls fdps_cd_stop_audio, discarding the index the caller asked for. Writing the obvious early-out (if (!music_enabled) return;) leaves the previous selection in DAT_00069d54, so the CD keeps playing and fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll goes on restarting the stale track after the player turns music off.

=== 00030c50 [PLATE]
Per-tick CD background-music keep-alive: once the live timer tick advances it bumps a counter, and every 0x4b ticks it restarts the selected CD track if the drive has gone idle.
Pool: fdps  [no library match; calls only fdps CD helpers, called only by game loops]
Evidence: fid.watcom and fid.ail are both empty, so no Watcom or ailv3 module owns these bytes. Its two callees are the classified game helpers fdps_cd_audio_is_idle (0003c6e8) and fdps_cd_play_track (0003c85b), and its eight callers are all game loops (battle player phase, map cursor select, palette cycling, village signboard menu and four unnamed scene loops) - no crt or AIL module reaches it. The body is pure game-state polling over five globals with a game-specific period constant, and at 112 bytes with a full Watcom prologue it is not a linker thunk.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case for game code; no vendor symbol claimed, and the name states what the body does.
Boundary: 00030c50-00030cbf, a single closed flow whose every branch target is internal, ending at the pop ebp/edi/esi/ebx; ret at 00030cbf; gap_after is empty and 00030cc0 starts the next function's own prologue.
Signature: __watcall void(void). No argument register or stack slot is read; sub esp,0 means no locals and the epilogue purges nothing. The callee fdps_cd_play_track takes its argument on the stack with the caller cleaning up - PUSH EAX at 00030c9e and ADD ESP,0x4 at 00030ca4 - which is the -4s stack convention the whole game was built with, not a deviation from it.
Algorithm: return at once when the cached tick at 0x00069d74 equals the live tick at 0x00069d64, so the body runs at most once per tick however often it is polled. On a new tick increment the accumulator at 0x00060170; when it reaches 0x4b (75) and a track is selected (0x00069d54 != -1) and the audio-enable flag at 0x00060008 is non-zero, query fdps_cd_audio_is_idle - a non-zero 16-bit result means playback has stopped, so fdps_cd_play_track is called with (track index + 1), the selected-track global being zero-based while the play routine takes a one-based CD track number. The accumulator is then reset to zero, on every arm of the 0x4b test and not only when a track was played. The cached tick is refreshed from a second read of the live tick at 00030cb1, which is also where the counter's JNZ lands, so every pass that got past the entry test refreshes it whether or not the period was reached.

=== 00030cc0 [PLATE]
Waits until the disc required by the given chapter is inserted, then starts that chapter's CD audio track.
Pool: fdps  [game strings, game globals, five named game callers]
Evidence: References "%s\\Pack.vfs" and the VFS entry "Pass.Dat", the game path global at 000643e8 and the draw context at 000643c4; writes the current-track global at 00069d54 that fdps_cd_play_track / fdps_cd_stop_audio use. No Function ID hit in either library set and the body hash is unique in the image, so not crt; no Miles state or AIL caller, so not ail; a full Watcom frame with real control flow, so not binary_artifact.
Name: fdps_ + snake_case describing the behaviour; no vendor symbol involved.
Boundary: 00030cc0-00030f31, ends at the epilogue MOV ESP,EBP / POP EBP,EDI,ESI,EBX / RET; the 14 bytes after it are Watcom alignment padding before the next function at 00030f40.
Signature: __cdecl void (int chapter, int slot) - both arguments read as dwords from [EBP+0x14] and [EBP+0x18], bare RET so the caller cleans; confirmed by the assembly, not a guess.

Algorithm:
1. Copy the 60-byte constant table at 000304a0 onto the stack (15 dwords). It is 30 chapter rows of 2 bytes; the row is the chapter, the column is the slot, and the byte is a zero-based CD audio track index, read unsigned.
2. Stop any playing CD audio (fdps_cd_stop_audio).
3. Loop until the inserted disc is acceptable:
   - Release the keyboard ISR (fdps_uninstall_keyboard_isr) and drain pending input (kbhit / getch).
   - Format "%s\\Pack.vfs" from the game path global at 000643e8 with sprintf and probe it with access(path, 0). A non-zero result means no usable disc.
   - When the probe succeeds, load the "Pass.Dat" entry through fdps_vfs_load_entry and take its first byte minus '0' as the disc number (1 or 2).
   - Chapters 0..17 live on disc 1, chapters 18 (0x12) and above on disc 2. If the probe failed, or the disc number does not match the chapter, draw the matching prompt through fdps_draw_text with the draw context at 000643c4 (message 0x223 for "insert disc 2", 0x222 for "insert disc 1"), wait for a keypress with getch, draw message 0x22a, delay(0x4e20), tear the prompt down (fdps_message_window_close) and retry from the top of step 3.
   - Otherwise set the done flag and leave the loop.
4. Reinstall the keyboard ISR (fdps_install_keyboard_isr).
5. If the CD audio enable flag at 00060008 is clear, store -1 into the current-track global at 00069d54 and stop CD audio. Otherwise take table[chapter * 2 + slot], store it at 00069d54, and then start playback of that value + 1; the -1 test on that arm can never fire, because the byte is zero-extended (fdps_cd_play_track).

Parameters:
  chapter - chapter index; also selects the required disc (>= 18 means disc 2).
  slot    - which of the chapter's two track entries to use, 0 or 1.

Returns:
  Nothing. Does not return until an acceptable disc is present.

=== 00031040 [PLATE]
Compiler-emitted initialiser image for the 9-entry int array that gives the screen zoom transition its magnification on each step.

fdps_transition_zoom copies these 36 bytes with REP MOVSD into its local array at EBP-0x3c on every call, then runs nine steps. Its fourth argument selects the direction: non-zero walks the index 0..8 (zoom in from a point), zero walks it 8..0 and follows the last step with a full-screen memset and a black palette (zoom out to black). On every step but the last the element is passed as the third argument of fdps_blit_rotated_scaled, which computes 2000 minus it as the source step per output pixel -- so a larger entry is a more magnified image -- while the blit centre is interpolated linearly from the caller's focus point (arguments 2 and 3) to the screen centre 159,99 and the palette is dimmed by 3 units per remaining step. Step 8 does not use the table at all: it takes the 1:1 path, memmove of 0xfa00 bytes from the source buffer to 0xa0000, which leaves element [8] = 1500 dead.

The sequence is 50, 200, 500, 800, 1000, 1200, 1300, 1400, 1500 -- deltas 150, 300, 300, 200, 200, 100, 100, 100, an eased ramp that opens fast and settles slowly.

Pool: binary_artifact  [read-only initialiser image the compiler emitted for a local array and block-copies into the stack frame; nothing indexes it where it lies]

Rebuild note:
The step positions are interpolated linearly in the code but the scale is not: the table's deltas are 150, 300, 300, 200, 200, 100, 100, 100. Computing the scale with the same linear formula the centre uses, or as an even ramp between 50 and 1500, compiles and looks plausible but changes the pacing of every zoom transition in the game.

=== 00031064 [PLATE]
Red-component template for the pulsing palette of the village signboard menu: nine DAC levels, of which any five consecutive entries are one frame of the cycle.

It is read-only image data, never written at run time. fdps_village_signboard_menu copies it into a 9-byte stack buffer at [EBP-0x48] on entry (MOVSD/MOVSD/MOVSB from 0x31064), together with the green template at 0x3106d and the blue template at 0x31076 which go to [EBP-0x3c] and [EBP-0x30]. Once per frame, between the two waits on the vertical-retrace bit of port 0x3DA, the loop computes phase = (tick/3) % 5 from the tick counter DAT_00069d64 and reprograms DAC entries 0xF0..0xF4: for slot i in 0..4 it writes i+0xF0 to port 0x3C8 and then red[phase+i], green[phase+i], blue[phase+i] to port 0x3C9. Those five palette entries are the ones the CanBan.cel cursor sprites are drawn in, so the effect is a colour wave travelling along the highlighted signboard option.

Values are 60,55,49,51,55,60,55,49,51 - VGA 6-bit levels. The array is a 5-entry cycle written out with its first four entries repeated, so the sliding window phase..phase+4 never has to wrap; green (60,57,51,54,57,...) and blue (60,60,58,59,60,...) have the same shape, and all three peak at 60 on the entry the phase currently points at.

Pool: binary_artifact  [not a source-level global: it is the initialiser image Watcom emits for a local `uchar[9]`, copied into the frame with an inline MOVSD/MOVSD/MOVSB and referenced from nowhere else]

=== 000310c0 [PLATE]
The secret-shop entry codes, one 8-byte row of keyboard scancodes per chapter: the key sequence that unlocks the hidden sixth entry of the village signboard menu.

Read-only image data, never written at run time. fdps_check_secret_code_key copies all 192 bytes into its stack frame on entry (MOV ESI,0x310c0 / MOV ECX,0x30 / REP MOVSD to [EBP-0xc4]) and then reads one byte per call: row = chapter index at DAT_00069cf4 minus 1, column = DAT_000601c0, the running match position. On a match the function advances DAT_000601c0 and reports success when the next row byte is 0 or the position reaches 8; on a mismatch it resets to 0. The caller is fdps_village_signboard_menu, which feeds it one make code from fdps_read_keyboard_queue and, on success, selects entry 5 for fdps_run_village_phase to dispatch to fdps_run_secret_menu.

Values are set-1 make codes, NUL-terminated when the code is shorter than 8; the longest here is 7. By the chapter number the player sees: ch2 Right Down Right A; ch3 Right Left Down Right A; ch4 Up Left Down Right Up; ch5 SOAR; ch6 SECRET; ch7 12211; ch8 . . . . ; ch9 BARNADO; ch10 ENTER; ch11 Up Left Down Right; ch12 Left Down Right; ch13 20-40; ch14 NIGHT; ch15 15; ch16 LOTORIA; ch19 12; ch20 1324; ch21 HERO; ch24 Down Down Down Down; ch25 WEST. Pool: binary_artifact  [not a source-level global: it is the initialiser image Watcom emits for an auto uchar[24][8], copied into the frame with REP MOVSD at function entry and reached from nowhere else]

Rebuild note:
The row is codes[chapter_index - 1], with the -1 folded into the addressing and no bounds check anywhere: chapter index 0, or 25 and up, reads outside the table. Writing the obvious codes[chapter_index][pos], prepending an empty row for chapter index 0, or clamping the index all change what those chapters do. Also, the four all-zero rows mean 'no code' only because fdps_village_signboard_menu filters the keyboard queue down to 0x01..0x7e before calling -- let a 0 through and those chapters' codes complete on the first keystroke.

=== 00031700 [PLATE]
Collects the item ids one village shop is stocking this chapter into a caller-supplied array, and returns how many there are.

Algorithm:
Walks all twelve bytes of row shop_index of the 12-byte-per-row table pointed to by DAT_00069d80 -- the chapter's "Shop%02d.dat" image that fdps_load_field_chapter_resources loads out of "Field.vfs" and fdps_run_village_phase frees. The row base is DAT_00069d80 + shop_index * 0xc; each byte is read zero-extended. 0xff marks an empty slot and is skipped wherever it appears, including between two stocked entries, so the scan never stops early; every other byte is stored as an int in the next free element of out_item_ids and the write counter is bumped. That counter is the return value. The loop is a fixed twelve iterations with no bounds check on shop_index, and out_item_ids must therefore have room for twelve ints. The shipped SHOP%02d.DAT members are 36 bytes, i.e. exactly three rows: 0 the item shop, 1 the weapon shop, 2 the secret shop.

Parameters:
  shop_index -- which shop's row to read; 0 item shop, 1 weapon shop, 2 secret shop. Comes down unchanged from the second argument of the shop transaction loop at 0x00033b80, which fdps_village_item_menu, fdps_run_weapon_shop and fdps_run_secret_menu set to 0, 1 and 2 respectively.
  out_item_ids -- caller's array, one int per stocked slot, receiving item ids in the item table's numbering (the ids fdps_get_item_record takes). The shop item picker at 0x00032710 passes a twelve-int stack array.

Returns:
  The number of ids written, 0 to 12. 0 means the shop stocks nothing this chapter; the picker at 0x00032710 uses the count to clamp its highlight and scroll window.

Pool: fdps  [no Function ID hit in either library set; its one data reference is the game's shop stock table and its only caller is game menu code]

Rebuild note:
The 0xff byte marks an empty slot, not the end of the row: shipped data such as SHOP01.DAT's weapon row (02 71 FF FF 72 73 FF ...) and SHOP05.DAT's (03 04 FF 1F 20 30 31 65 FF 74 75 83) stock items after empty slots, so the obvious `for (i = 0; i < 12 && row[i] != 0xff; i++)` truncates most shops' stock. The row must also be typed unsigned char: as signed char the 0xff compares as -1, the skip never fires, and empty slots are sold as item id 255.
