That function draws the corner panel showing the tile under the map cursor -- terrain cel, the AP and DEF modifiers of the tile's attribute class, and, when a unit stands there, the unit's 24x24 sprite and current HP. Before drawing, it converts the cursor's world pixel position into on-screen tile coordinates (cursor minus camera origin, divided by 0x18) and re-latches this column so the panel does not sit under the cursor: row > 4 and column < 2 stores 0x124, row > 4 and column > 10 stores 0x19. Any other cursor position leaves the previous value standing, so the column is sticky and changes only when the cursor actually reaches one of the two lower corners.

Every blit in the panel is placed from this value: it is the x argument of fdps_cel_blit_sprite for the backdrop cel at y 0xa0 and, plus 9, for the terrain cel at y 0xaf, and it is added to the destination pointer for the two fdps_draw_number calls that print the AP and DEF modifiers (rows 164 and 203), for the unit sprite blitted through fdps_blit_dispatch (row 175) and for the HP figure (row 190). The surface is 8bpp with pitch 0x168, so the x coordinate and the byte offset are the same number. Only these two values are ever stored, and the image initialises the variable to 0x19, so the panel starts in the left corner.

Pool: fdps  [its only referencing function is the game's own HUD renderer; referencing_pools is fdps alone]

Rebuild note:
The two stores are a latch, not a choice: the source is if (row > 4 && col < 2) x = 0x124; else if (row > 4 && col > 10) x = 0x19; with no final else, and the variable is initialised to 0x19 in the data image rather than living in _BSS. Adding the else that the shape invites, or leaving the definition uninitialised, moves the panel on cursor positions where the original leaves it alone.

=== 00060170 [PLATE]
Timer ticks elapsed since the last CD background-music keep-alive check, counting 0..0x4b (75).

Written only by fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll (00030c50), which the game loops call every frame: when the live tick at 00069d64 differs from the cached tick at 00069d74 it increments this counter, so it advances at most once per tick however often the poll runs. On reaching 0x4b it performs the keep-alive -- if a track is selected (00069d54 != -1) and data_fdps_audio_bgm_enabled_flag (00060008) is set, it asks fdps_cd_audio_is_idle (0003c6e8) whether playback has stopped and if so restarts it via fdps_cd_play_track (0003c85b) with (selected track + 1) -- and then resets this counter to 0. Nothing else reads or writes it, and no other function resets it, so it is a free-running 75-tick divider for the CD repeat check.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll, a game function with no library match, touches it]

=== 00060174 [PLATE]
Screen x column of each of the six village-map signboard destinations, in pixels.

Read-only initialiser data, never written. Indexed by the signboard menu selection 0..5; the parallel y table is data_fdps_village_signboard_destination_y_table at 0006018c. fdps_village_signboard_menu reads the pair to blit the 24x24 destination marker at page + y * 0x140 + x; fdps_village_animate_walk_to_destination reads it for both the departing and arriving selection, picks the marker's facing from the dominant axis of the delta, and interpolates x_from - (x_from - x_to) * i / 5 over its six frames; fdps_run_village_phase pushes the x and y of a selection into the village destination handler at 00031780. Values are 138, 214, 253, 46, 54, 4 -- all inside a 320-pixel row. Entries 0..4 are the destinations the menu cycles through with (sel+1) % 5; entry 5 is only ever selected by fdps_village_signboard_menu writing *selection = 5 when the secret-shop key code has been entered.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it: the three village-phase functions and nothing else]

Rebuild note:
The table has six entries even though the menu wraps modulo 5. Sizing it by the visible menu (five entries), which is the obvious reading of the wrap arithmetic, makes the secret-shop destination read the first element of the y table instead of its own column.

=== 0006018c [PLATE]
Screen y coordinate, in pixels, of each of the six village signboard destinations on the 320x200 town screen.

Read-only initialiser data; nothing writes it. Indexed by the village menu selection, which is the same 0..5 value fdps_run_village_phase dispatches on: 0 leave the village, 1 bar, 2 church, 3 item menu, 4 weapon shop, 5 secret shop (reachable only after the secret code). Values are 0, 74, 151, 135, 49, 160. It is always used together with data_fdps_village_destination_marker_x_table at 00060174, which holds the matching x: 138, 214, 253, 46, 54, 4.

fdps_run_village_phase passes the pair to fdps_transition_zoom to draw and then erase the highlight over the current selection. fdps_village_signboard_menu turns the pair into a destination address as page + y * 0x140 + x for the 24x24 marker. fdps_village_animate_walk_to_destination reads both entries for the outgoing and incoming selections, picks the marker's facing from the dominant axis of the delta, and interpolates the marker across six frames.

Pool: fdps  [only village-screen game code reaches it; no library object references it]

Rebuild note:
Entry 0 is zero and sits immediately after the six-dword x table, so it reads as alignment padding at the end of that table. It is not: it is the y of destination 0. Dropping it and starting the array at 00060190 shifts every destination by one entry.

=== 000601a4 [PLATE]
Index of the party-roster member whose walking sprite is drawn as the marker on the village map screen.

Written only by fdps_village_signboard_menu: on entry it is reset to 0 if it has grown stale (>= DAT_00064114, the roster member count), and scancode 0x0f (Tab) advances it as (value + 1) % DAT_00064114, so the player cycles the on-map figure through the party. It is read as a slot index into data_fdps_cel_sprite_cache_ptr, one CEL group of 0x30 bytes per roster member in roster order (fdps_load_field_chapter_resources caches them in that order): the menu reads slot * 0x30 + cell * 4 for the idle animation cell, and fdps_village_animate_walk_to_destination reads slot * 0x30 + facing * 0xc while sliding the marker from one signboard destination to the next. The range is 0 .. DAT_00064114 - 1; the value survives between village visits, which is why the entry guard exists.

Pool: fdps  [only pool_fdps code reaches it -- the two village screen routines at 00031bc0 and 00031f60]

=== 000601a8 [PLATE]
Index of the first shop stock entry shown in the buy list's six-cell window.

Private to fdps_shop_select_item; no other function in the program references it. The picker shows six entries at a time, two columns by three rows, so cell i displays stock entry (this + i) and this always moves in steps of 2, one row at a time: forward when the highlight data at 000601ac reaches this + 6, back when the highlight drops below this. It survives between calls, so reopening a shop restores the previous view; both it and the highlight are reset to 0 on entry only when the saved highlight is past the end of the current shop's stock. It also drives the blinking scroll arrows: the up arrow (Command.cel sprites 0x44/0x45) is drawn only while this is non-zero, the down arrow (sprites 0x46/0x47) only while this + 6 is still short of the stock count. Range is 0 to stock count rounded down to an even value; 0 means the list is scrolled to the top.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_shop_select_item, a game-logic function]

Rebuild note:
This is a file-static that deliberately keeps its value between calls, and it is reset only when the saved highlight is out of range for the new shop's stock. Making it a function local, or zeroing it on entry, loses the "shop reopens where you left it" behaviour.

=== 000601ac [PLATE]
Index of the highlighted entry in the village shop's buy list.

Written and read only by fdps_shop_select_item, which owns it as a function-scope static together with the window top at 000601a8; nothing else in the program touches either. It indexes the twelve-slot stock array that fdps_shop_collect_stock_items filled on that function's stack, so it runs 0 .. stock_count-1; the selected slot is read out at the end of the picker and its item id is what the function returns. The picker's grid is two columns by three rows, so scancode 0x4d (right) adds 1 while the index is below stock_count-1, 0x4b (left) subtracts 1 while it is above 0, 0x50 (down) adds 2 while it is below stock_count-2, and 0x48 (up) subtracts 2 while it is above 1; each accepted move plays Beep.wav and drags the window top at 000601a8 by two whenever the index leaves the visible range top .. top+5. It survives between calls, so the picker reopens on the entry chosen last time; it is forced back to 0, along with the window top, only on entry when the saved index is at or past this shop's stock count.

Pool: fdps  [every reference is inside fdps_shop_select_item, a pool_fdps function, and the value is a game UI selection index]

Rebuild note:
The highlight is a static that persists across calls and across the three shops (item, weapon, secret), and it is reset only when the saved value is past the new stock count. Writing it as a local initialised to 0 each call, or resetting it unconditionally on entry, makes the picker always open on the first entry and loses the original's behaviour of reopening where the player left off - including the cross-shop carry-over, where opening the weapon shop after the item shop starts on whatever row the item shop ended on.

=== 000601b0 [PLATE]
Roster index of the first entry shown on the visible row of the village shop's buy-target picker, i.e. the list's scroll position. Always the cursor index rounded down to a multiple of three, because the picker shows one row of three members at a time.

Written and read only by fdps_shop_select_buy_target (00032c40); no other function in the program references it. The four arrow keys keep it in lockstep with the cursor at 000601b4: right (scancode 0x4d) adds 3 once the cursor has passed the last visible entry, left (0x4b) subtracts 3 once the cursor has moved above the visible row, up (0x48) and down (0x50) move both this and the cursor by 3 together. Each of those moves first plays a seven-frame slide, calling fdps_render_roster_select_frame with the source row stepped in eighths of the 0x43-pixel row height. Read to place the list: (value / 3) * 0x43 is the pixel row of the visible entries, and the raw value is passed as the fourth argument of fdps_render_roster_select_frame. Values run over the roster, 0 to DAT_00064114 - 1 rounded down to a multiple of 3; there is no sentinel and no reset -- nothing initialises it on entry to the picker, so it keeps whatever the previous visit left and the screen reopens where the player last was.

Pool: fdps  [reached only from fdps_shop_select_buy_target, a game-logic function with no library match]

Rebuild note:
This and the cursor at 000601b4 are module statics that survive between calls and are never clamped on entry. Writing them as locals of the picker, or zeroing or clamping them at the top of the function, changes behaviour twice over: the picker would stop reopening on the member chosen last time, and it would lose the original's unchecked case where a roster that has shrunk since the previous visit leaves the cursor and this scroll position pointing past the end.

=== 000601b4 [PLATE]
Cursor index of the highlighted roster member in the village shop's buy-target picker, 0 to DAT_00064114 - 1.

Written and read only by fdps_shop_select_buy_target, which is the sole function in the program that touches it. Its modal loop moves the cursor on the arrow scancodes: 0x4d adds 1 while the value is below DAT_00064114 - 1, 0x4b subtracts 1 while it is above 0, 0x50 adds 3 while it is below DAT_00064114 - 3, and 0x48 subtracts 3 while it is above 2 -- the steps of 3 are one row, because the roster is drawn three entries to a row. The value drives the drawing directly: (value % 3) * 0x65 + 5 is the column passed to fdps_render_roster_select_frame, and (value / 3) picks the row, kept on screen by the scroll top at 000601b0 which the same code steps by 3 whenever the cursor crosses a row boundary. It is also read once as a value rather than a position: at 000330b8, when the loop ends on a confirm, it is copied out as the function's return value, the roster index the caller buys the item for. One extra reader is the confirm path at 00032cd0, which drops the confirm when the value is exactly 3 and DAT_00069cf4 (chapter index) is 0x17 or higher -- roster slot 3 is the fourth member to join, out of the party from chapter 24 on.

Nothing resets it. It lives in initialised data with an initial value of 0, so the picker starts on the first member the first time and reopens on whatever the player last left it on for the rest of the run.

Pool: fdps  [the only referencing function is fdps_shop_select_buy_target, a game-logic function; no library reaches it]

Rebuild note:
This is a file-static that survives between calls, not a local. Declaring it inside fdps_shop_select_buy_target, or resetting it on entry, makes the picker always open on the first roster member instead of on the member chosen last time. It is also never re-clamped on entry, only on movement, so a value left over from a larger party stays out of range until the player presses a key; adding an entry-time clamp changes which entry is highlighted on the first frame after the roster shrinks.

=== 000601b8 [PLATE]
Roster index of the top-left cell of the village party-member picker's 3x2 icon grid, i.e. the first roster entry currently visible.

Read and written only by fdps_village_select_member. The draw loop shows the six entries scroll_offset..scroll_offset+5, cell i at x = (i % 3) * 0x65 + 0xb, y = (i / 3) * 0x1b + 9, skipping any cell whose entry has reached the roster member count in data_fdps_map_unit_count's village counterpart at 0x00064114. It only ever moves a whole row at a time: +3 when a right (0x4d) or down (0x50) keypress pushes the cursor at 0x000601bc to scroll_offset + 6 or beyond, -3 when a left (0x4b) or up (0x48) keypress drops the cursor below it, so the value is always a multiple of 3 and always <= the cursor. Two blinking scroll arrows are keyed off it: Command.cel sprite 0x44 + b at (150,5) when it is not 0 (entries exist above the window) and 0x46 + b at (150,64) when scroll_offset + 6 is still under the roster count (entries exist below). It is a file-scope static that nothing resets on entry, so it keeps the window position from the previous visit -- including a visit made from a different village screen.

Pool: fdps  [the only code that touches it is fdps_village_select_member, game-logic pool]

Rebuild note:
This is a file-scope static that survives between calls and is never reset on entry; declaring it as a local seeded to 0 (the obvious rewrite, since the picker looks self-contained) makes the grid always reopen on the first row instead of where the player left it, and it also desynchronises it from the cursor static at 0x000601bc, which persists the same way.

=== 000601bc [PLATE]
Cursor position of the village party-member picker: the roster index of the entry the highlight sits on.

Owned by fdps_village_select_member, which is the only function in the program that touches it, and by the scroll top data_fdps_village_member_select_scroll_top at 000601b8 that follows it. The arrow keys move it: scancode 0x4d one entry right while it is below DAT_00064114 - 1, 0x4b one entry left while it is above 0, 0x50 three entries (one row) down while it is below DAT_00064114 - 3, 0x48 three entries up while it is above 2 -- the grid is three cells wide and two rows tall. After each move the scroll top is dragged along in steps of 3: up by 3 when the cursor falls below it, down by 3 when the cursor reaches scroll top + 6. It is read while composing the frame, at 000338e9, to pick the one cell of the six that gets the selection-bar highlight, and read at 00033b5c to become the function's return value once the player confirms; a cancel returns -1 instead and leaves this untouched. Valid range is 0 to DAT_00064114 - 1, the roster member count. The value 3 is special from chapter index 0x17 (chapter 24) onward: a confirm on slot 3 is dropped silently, because that roster slot is the member who has left the party by then.

Nothing resets it on entry, and it is not reset anywhere else either -- it starts at 0 from the initialised image and afterwards always holds the last entry the player stood on, so the picker reopens where it was left, across screens and across visits.

Pool: fdps  [the sole referencing function is game village-screen logic; no library reaches it]

Rebuild note:
The cursor and the scroll top are file-scope statics that survive between calls and that nothing resets or clamps on entry. Declaring them as locals seeded to 0, or adding an entry-time clamp against the current roster count, both change observable behaviour: the grid would stop reopening on the last-picked member, and the case where the roster has shrunk since the previous visit -- where the retained cursor can still sit past the new end and be returned as-is -- would stop happening.

=== 000601c0 [PLATE]
Running match position inside the current chapter's secret-shop unlock code: how many consecutive expected scancodes the player has entered so far, 0..8.

Written and read only by fdps_check_secret_code_key, which is called once per keystroke from fdps_village_signboard_menu. That function copies the 24-row, 8-byte-per-row scancode table at 000310c0 to the stack and compares the incoming scancode with row byte [chapter_index * 8 + this]. On a match it increments this counter and reports success when the next row byte is 0 (the code's terminator) or the counter has reached 8 (the row is full). On a mismatch it clears the counter to 0, then sets it back to 1 when the offending keystroke happens to be the row's own first byte, so a fresh attempt starts on the same key that broke the previous one. Value 0 means no progress; 8 is the maximum a full row can reach. The row is selected as chapter index DAT_00069cf4 - 1, so the codes cover chapter indices 1..24.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_check_secret_code_key, a game-logic function; pure game state, no library reaches it]

Rebuild note:
Nothing outside fdps_check_secret_code_key ever clears this counter -- not chapter change, not entering or leaving the village, not a completed code. Partial progress therefore survives across villages and chapters and is only ever broken by a mismatching keystroke. A rewrite that makes it a static inside the signboard menu, or that resets it when the menu opens or the chapter changes, would reject sequences the original accepts.

=== 000601c4 [PLATE]
Link-time table of the 50 scripted chapter-event handlers the battle code dispatches through by event index.

Read-only and never written at run time: each slot holds the address of one fdps_chapter_NN_event_* function, from slot 0 fdps_chapter_03_event_deploy_wave_for_turn (00036bb0) to slot 49 fdps_chapter_30_event_deploy_wave_3 (000398c0). Every entry is void __cdecl f(int) and is reached only by CALL through this table. Three dispatch sites supply the index, and none of them bounds-checks it: fdps_battle_run_turn_events takes it from byte [1] of a 3-byte turn-event record in the loaded chapter script image (data_fdps_tile_event_data_table_ptr) and calls the slot with a literal 0; fdps_run_death_scripts calls the slot named by the operand of a death-script record whose opcode is 2, passing the acting unit's index; fdps_battle_search_cell_at_cursor calls the slot named by a searchable cell record's payload word when its kind byte is 2 or more, passing the searching unit's index. fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase, fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase, fdps_battle_unit_turn and the status-effect tick dispatch through it too, each time immediately followed by a call into the per-chapter post-action table at 0006028c.

Slot numbers are global over the whole game, not per chapter: handlers for chapter 3, chapter 16 and chapter 30 sit next to each other in one run, and how many slots a chapter owns varies from none to four.

Pool: fdps  [only game functions reach it, and every slot holds the address of a named game chapter-event handler]

Rebuild note:
The chapter data files store raw slot numbers into this table and no dispatch site range-checks them, so the 50 entries must be emitted in exactly this order. Grouping the handlers per chapter for readability, or dropping a slot no chapter appears to use, silently reassigns every later event to the wrong handler.

=== 0006028c [PLATE]
Per-chapter post-action handler table: 30 code pointers, one per chapter, holding the win/lose and scripted-event test the battle loop runs after a unit has acted.

Read-only, laid out at link time in CONST/_DATA; nothing writes it at run time. Indexed by the 0-based chapter id in DAT_00069cf4 (0..29, shown to the player as chapters 1..30), scaled by 4 and called with no arguments and no stack cleanup: void __cdecl f(void). Slot 0 is fdps_chapter_01_post_action, slot 29 is fdps_chapter_30_post_action. The dispatch sites are fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase (twice, at 00012a48 and 00012aff), fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase (00012beb), fdps_battle_unit_turn (0001584e) and fdps_battle_tick_status_effects (0001fb50); each of the phase loops compares DAT_00069da0 against 0 on the instruction after the call, because a handler reports its verdict there -- 0 battle continues, 1 defeat, 2 chapter cleared. Most handlers begin by calling fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions and then add the chapter's own extra defeat clauses. The index is never bounds-checked at the call sites, but it cannot run off the end: fdps_chapter_30_end leaves DAT_00069cf4 at 29 and raises the quit flag DAT_000643eb instead of advancing it.

The adjacent table at 00060304 is the separate per-chapter chapter-end handler table, dispatched from main on the same index; the two sets of handler bodies alternate in code order because each chapter's pair is defined together in the source.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it, and every slot is a game chapter handler that touches game globals no vendor object could name]

=== 00060304 [PLATE]
Per-chapter end-of-chapter handler table: 30 function pointers, one for each chapter, indexed by the 0-based current chapter index at 00069cf4.

Read-only, built by the linker from the addresses of fdps_chapter_01_end (0003a410) through fdps_chapter_30_end (0003ba80); nothing writes it at runtime. The single reader is main at 000293a1: when fdps_battle_player_phase_loop returns with request code 2 in 00069da0 (the chapter was cleared), main calls the slot selected by 00069cf4 and then runs fdps_run_village_phase. Slot n holds the handler for the chapter the player calls n+1, so the index runs 0..29 while the player sees 1..30. The selected handler is what plays the chapter's win scene and advances 00069cf4 to the next chapter, so the index must be read for the outgoing chapter before the handler runs. There is no bounds check and no terminator; only the 30 defined slots are ever reachable because 00069cf4 never leaves 0..29.

The adjacent 30-slot table at 0006028c has the same shape and the same index but a different purpose (the per-chapter post-action handlers called from fdps_battle_unit_turn, fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase, fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase and fdps_battle_tick_status_effects); the two must not be confused.

Pool: fdps  [only main reaches it, and every entry is a named game-logic chapter routine]

=== 0006037c [PLATE]
Status code of the most recent AIL file operation; 0 means the operation succeeded.

Cleared to 0 at the top of every AIL file entry point (AIL_internal_filesize_path, AIL_internal_load_file_to_memory, AIL_internal_write_buffer_to_file_create, AIL_internal_write_buffer_to_file_truncate) and overwritten with a failure code on each error exit of those functions; the failing call also returns 0 or -1 to its caller. AIL_get_last_error_code is the only reader and simply returns this dword, so the value is meaningful only until the next AIL file call begins.

The codes observed, matching the Miles Sound System file-error enumeration: 0 no error; 2 out of memory, stored by AIL_internal_load_file_to_memory when the allocation for the file image comes back null; 3 file not found, stored when the open in AIL_internal_filesize_path, AIL_internal_load_file_to_memory or AIL_internal_write_buffer_to_file_truncate returns -1; 4 cannot write file, stored when the create/open for writing fails or the write call returns -1; 5 cannot read file, stored when the seek/size query or the read comes back short or -1; 6 disk full, stored when a write returns fewer bytes than requested. Value 1 (I/O error) is never stored by this build.

Pool: ail  [only the sound library's file-I/O routines reference it; no game or CRT code touches it]

=== 00060380 [PLATE]
Replaceable memory-allocation hook of the Miles AIL sound library: the address of the routine AIL calls whenever it needs a block.

Holds 0003d375 (the CRT's malloc) from its .data initialiser, and forms a pair with the free slot at 00060384, which defaults to 0003d478 (free). FUN_0003c9db is the accessor over this slot - it returns the previous value in EAX and stores the new one from [ESP+4]; its twin at 0003c9eb does the same for the free slot. Nothing in FDPS calls either accessor, so both slots keep their default CRT routines for the whole run. Callers push the byte count, CALL dword ptr [0x00060380], and clear the argument themselves; the return value is the block or zero, and every caller tests it: AIL_internal_alloc_and_commit at 0003c9fb (which then page-locks the block through DPMI 0x600 so it is safe for DMA and interrupt-time use), AIL_internal_load_file_to_memory at 0003d1d2 when the caller supplied no buffer of its own, AIL_internal_mdi_driver_setup_full at 000497f0 for its 0x6d4-bytes-per-voice state block, and FUN_0003ccf8 for a driver image buffer.

Pool: ail  [every reader and the only writer are AIL code; the CRT's malloc is what the slot points at, not what owns it]

Rebuild note:
This slot is initialised data, not BSS - it already contains malloc before any startup code runs, and no code in FDPS ever assigns it. Emitting it as a plain uninitialised pointer, or leaving the assignment to a startup hook the way FD2's game main did, leaves it zero and the first AIL allocation calls through a null pointer. The pointee must also be callable with one pushed argument that the caller pops (cdecl); a register-convention allocator would read garbage as its size.

=== 00060384 [PLATE]
Function pointer AIL calls to release a memory block; the free half of AIL's replaceable {alloc, free} hook pair, whose alloc half is the adjacent slot at 00060380.

Initialised in the image to 0003d478, the CRT's free, and never rewritten in this build: the only writer is the get-old/set-new accessor FUN_0003c9eb (an unused library API entry the linker pulled in, zero callers), so at runtime the slot always holds free. Called with one pushed pointer and cleaned up with ADD ESP,0x4, return value never used -- void (*)(void *), cdecl. Readers: AIL_internal_decommit_and_free (0003ca3e) releases a locked block after unlocking it; AIL_internal_load_file_to_memory frees its partial buffer on a seek failure (0003d241) and on a short read (0003d25c, which then sets the AIL error code at 0006037c to 5); AIL_internal_install_DIG_driver_file_inner (00047044) and AIL_internal_install_MDI_driver_file_inner (00049ee4) release the driver-image buffer after AIL_install_driver has copied what it needs, unconditionally, whether the install succeeded or not. No call site checks the slot for NULL.

Pool: ail  [only AIL internals reference it; the CRT is what the pointer points at, not what owns it, and no game code touches it]

Rebuild note:
The slot lives in initialised data and holds free from image load; nothing at runtime installs it. Declaring it as a plain uninitialised global (or leaving the initialiser to a startup hook that the game never calls) makes the first AIL release call through NULL, because no caller null-checks it. Write it as an initialised definition: void (*data_ail_free_fnptr)(void *) = free;

=== 00060388 [PLATE]
Head of the Watcom near-heap mini-heap list: pointer to the lowest-addressed mini heap descriptor, NULL while no near heap exists yet.

Written in two places only: 0004409a in FUN_00044070, which inserts a freshly created mini heap into the address-ordered list and takes the head slot when the new block sorts below every existing one, and 00043ec4 in FUN_00043e9f, which unlinks a mini heap and promotes its +0x08 successor when the released block was the head. Read by _nmalloc, _nfree, _nexpand via __HeapManager_expand, __ExpandDGROUP, __FreeDPMIBlocks, __ReAllocDPMIBlock and __LastFree; each walks the list from here through the +0x08 forward link (+0x04 is the back link, +0x20 the mini heap's own circular free-list head, +0x24 a free-list pointer __LastFree and __FreeDPMIBlocks dereference) to find the mini heap that owns a given pointer or has room for a request. _nmalloc starts its scan here only when the rover __MiniHeapRover (0006038c) is NULL, and in that case also zeroes __LargestSizeB4MiniHeapRover (00060390). NULL means the near heap has not been created yet and every reader tests for it before walking: 00043ee9, 000440eb, 0004407a onwards.

Pool: crt  [reached only by the Watcom heap modules nmalloc/nfree/nexpand/grownear; __nheapbeg is a PUBDEF in the 10.0a CLIB3 objects and the game never touches it]

=== 0006038c [PLATE]
Rover of the Watcom near heap: the mini-heap that _nmalloc tries first, or NULL to start from the head of the chain.

The near heap is a chain of mini-heaps whose head is __nheapbeg (00060388); each mini-heap carries its own free list, and __LargestSizeB4MiniHeapRover (00060390) caches the largest free block available in the heaps that precede this rover. _nmalloc (0003d383) consults the pair on entry (0003d3c0-0003d3d8): when the rounded request exceeds the cached largest size it resumes the walk at this rover, and only when the rover is NULL does it zero the cached size and restart at __nheapbeg; the path that has settled on a heap stores it back here at 0003d3f7, immediately before calling __MemAllocator (00043cec) with that heap in EBX and the size in EAX. _nfree (0003d486) reads it at 0003d4bd to decide whether the heap that owned the block it just released may raise the cached largest size - the heap only counts when it is not the rover itself, because the rover's own free space is by definition not "before the rover". FUN_00043e9f, which takes a mini-heap out of the chain, advances this cell to the removed block's successor (field +0x08) at 00043eb1 when the heap being unlinked is the current rover, and does the same for __nheapbeg just below.

Values: NULL means no rover is set and the walk starts at __nheapbeg; anything else is a pointer to a mini-heap header, of which +0x08 is the next heap in the chain and +0x14 is that heap's largest free block. The cell starts at zero from the image, so the first allocation of the run always walks from the head.

Pool: crt  [Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S nmalloc.obj publishes __nheapbeg, __MiniHeapRover and __LargestSizeB4MiniHeapRover at _DATA offsets 0, 4 and 8; the three land at 00060388, 0006038c and 00060390, and only CRT heap code reads or writes them]

Rebuild note:
This dword belongs to the Watcom library, not to the program: nmalloc.obj of CLIB3S defines __MiniHeapRover together with __nheapbeg and __LargestSizeB4MiniHeapRover in its own _DATA contribution (offsets 0, 4, 8 of a 12-byte segment). Because it is initialised data holding zero, an emit stage driven by the image will see an ordinary zero-initialised dword in the .data region and declare it; writing void *__MiniHeapRover = 0; in src/ duplicates the library's PUBDEF as soon as anything calls malloc, and moving it to BSS does not help. The three near-heap globals must have no definition in our translation units at all and must come in with CLIB3S.

=== 00060390 [PLATE]
Near-heap allocator cache: the largest free block size known to exist in the mini heaps that lie before the rover in the mini-heap list.

Written and read only by _nmalloc (0003d383) and _nfree (0003d486). _nmalloc uses it to decide where to start scanning: if the (already clamped to >= 0xc) request is larger than this value, no mini heap before the rover can satisfy it, so the scan resumes at __MiniHeapRover (0006038c); otherwise -- and also when the rover is still NULL -- the scan restarts at the list head __nheapbeg (00060388) and this cache is reset to 0. As the scan walks the list (next pointer at mini_heap+8), each mini heap whose allocation attempt fails raises this value to that heap's largest-free-block field (mini_heap+0x14), so it always holds the maximum over the heaps already passed. _nfree raises it the same way after returning a block to a mini heap that is not the current rover, so a later request small enough to fit that block restarts the scan from the head instead of skipping it.

A pure optimisation: the value is a size in bytes, never an address; 0 means "nothing is known to be free before the rover", which forces a full scan and is always safe. Zero at image load, and the CRT never needs to seed it.

Pool: crt  [reached only by _nmalloc and _nfree, both FID-matched to CLIB3S objects; the symbol is a public name in the linked 10.0a library]

=== 00060394 [PLATE]
Watcom CRT: the 80x87 coprocessor type the runtime will use. 0 = none, 2 = 80287, 3 = 80387 or an installed 387 emulator.

Zero-initialised by CLIB3S module _8087386, which also registers __chk8087 in the startup XI initialiser table. __chk8087 (00044749) reads this first and returns immediately if it is already non-zero; otherwise it clears __real87 (00060395), runs FNINIT/FNSTCW and, when a coprocessor answers (control-word high byte 3), calls __init_8087 (00044710) which reloads the control word from __8087cw (00061448) and calls __init_80x87 (00051b7e); that routine returns 2 for a 287 and 3 for a 387 from the signed-infinity comparison. The result is written to both __8087 and __real87 unless __no87 (0006044c) is non-zero, in which case both stay 0 and no 80x87 is used. The 387-emulator installer FUN_000444d4 stores 3 here directly and leaves __real87 alone, so a non-zero __8087 means 387 instructions may be issued, not that hardware is present -- __real87 is the one that records real hardware, and it is what __init_8087 and _fpreset (0004473f) test before installing or invoking the real FSAVE/FRSTOR paths (__Save8087 at 0006144c, __Rest8087 at 00061450).

Pool: crt  [defined in CLIB3S/_8087386.obj and referenced only by chk8087 and the 387-emulator installer; the game never touches it]

=== 00060395 [PLATE]
Watcom CRT flag: the type of real floating-point hardware detected, 0 when there is none.

Written only by __chk8087: it first stores 0 here ('assume no coprocessor') and then, after the FNINIT/FNSTCW probe and only when __no87 (0006044c) is clear, stores the detected coprocessor code - the same value it puts in __8087 (00060394). Read as a gate by __init_8087, which skips the FNINIT/FLDCW/FRSTOR sequence when it is 0, and by _fpreset, which falls through to a bare RET when it is 0 and otherwise jumps into __init_8087. Distinct from __8087: __8087 says 'x87 instructions may be issued' and is also set to 3 by the 387 emulator installer at 000444d4, whereas __real87 says 'real silicon is present' and stays 0 under the emulator.

Pool: crt  [only __chk8087, __init_8087 and _fpreset reach it; it is a PUBDEF of the CLIB module _8087.obj, alongside __8087, __chk8087 and __no87]

Rebuild note:
Do not collapse __real87 and __8087 into one 'FPU present' flag. They hold the same value on a machine with a real coprocessor, but this build ships the 387 emulator, which sets __8087 = 3 while __real87 stays 0; a rewrite that gates _fpreset on __8087 would execute real FNINIT/FRSTOR on a machine that has no FPU.

=== 00060398 [PLATE]
Non-zero while the main AIL code region and its interrupt-time statics are DPMI page-locked; zero when they are not. Initial image value is 0.

Set to 1 by AIL_internal_init_globals_once (0003d566), the one-shot lock guard for this region: if the flag is already non-zero it returns immediately, otherwise it calls fdps_dpmi_lock_region(0x0003d566, 0x000423fd) to lock its own code range and fdps_dpmi_lock_size on the eight 4-byte statics at 00069e64/68/70/74/78/7c/80/84, then stores 1. Its only caller is AIL_startup (0003d718). Cleared back to 0 by AIL_internal_dpmi_unlock_main_3c6d3 (000423fd), which skips its body when the flag is already 0 and otherwise calls fdps_dpmi_unlock_region for the same address pair before storing 0. The two functions are the region markers themselves: the locked range runs from the lock guard's own entry to the unlock guard's entry and contains AIL_startup and the 100 Hz timer callback AIL_internal_log_timer_tick (0003d60a), i.e. code that runs at interrupt time and must not be paged out.

Only 0 and 1 are ever stored, and no other code reads the cell. It is one of three independent per-region guards of the same shape: the voc dispatcher's (lock guard 000477f4, unlock 00047e0a) and the wave synth's (lock guard 0004b370, flag 00061138) are separate variables covering separate ranges.

Pool: ail  [both referencing functions are library bodies present in ailv3.lib; the DPMI primitives they call are game-side helpers reached across the EXTDEF seam, which does not make the flag the game's]

=== 0006039c [PLATE]
The Watcom C library's pseudo-random seed: the 32-bit LCG state that rand() advances, `next` in CLIB3S.LIB's rand.obj, initialised to 1 in the image.

Only the six-byte accessor L$1_rand_seed_ptr (00042cf2) names this address; it returns the address and both rand() (00042cf8) and srand() (00042d1a) reach the cell through it. rand() computes seed = seed * 0x41c64e6d + 0x3039, stores it back and returns (seed >> 16) & 0x7fff, so the full 32-bit state lives here but only bits 16..30 are ever handed out -- the value is never a count or an index and means nothing on its own. srand() would overwrite it with the caller's seed, but nothing in FDPS calls srand: the cell starts at 1 from the initialised image, so every run of the game replays the same sequence of rand() values, and each battle's hit, critical, double-strike and ailment rolls (fdps_combat_compute_hit_outcome, fdps_unit_resolve_attack_hit, fdps_unit_inflict_random_ailments and the other game-side callers of rand) are determined by how many rand() calls came before them.

Pool: crt  [rand.obj from Watcom LIB386\DOS\CLIB3S.LIB -- that module's whole _DATA contribution is these four bytes, and no game or AIL code touches the address]

Rebuild note:
The initial value 1 is load-bearing and the program never seeds the generator. Adding srand(time(NULL)) at startup, or letting the cell land in BSS as zero, keeps the generator working but shifts the entire stream, so every roll of every battle differs from the original. In a rebuild the cell arrives with the real rand.obj when CLIB3S.LIB is linked; defining a seed of your own in src/ would add a second copy rather than replace the library's.

=== 000603a0 [PLATE]
The Watcom C library's at-exit hook: the function pointer exit() calls before it does anything else, which is where the handlers registered with atexit() would run.

exit (00042e0f) calls through this cell first, then through __int23_exit (000603a4), then tail-calls _exit (00042e29), which in turn calls __int23_exit and __FPE_handler_exit (000603a8) before jumping to __exit (00043527), the DOS terminate path in CSTRT386. Only two values are meaningful. The image ships it holding 00042e0e, exit.obj's own `_null_exit_rtn` -- a bare RET one byte before exit's entry -- and CLIB3S.LIB's atexit.obj is the only thing that ever overwrites it, storing `_Full_at_exit_rtn` so the walk over _ExitList/_ExitCount happens. Nothing in FDPS writes this address: atexit.obj was never linked, no exit handler is ever registered, and the call at 00042e0f lands on the RET stub on every quit. The three slots 000603a0-000603ab are the whole of exit.obj's _DATA contribution.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __atexit at offset 0 of exit.obj's _DATA in Watcom 10.0a LIB386\DOS\CLIB3S.LIB; the sole reader is the library's own exit()]

Rebuild note:
The slot is initialised data holding a live pointer to a do-nothing RET, and exit() calls it with no null test. Writing it as a zero-initialised pointer -- or letting it fall into BSS -- makes the game jump to address 0 the moment it quits. It arrives correctly with exit.obj when CLIB3S.LIB is linked; a definition in src/ would duplicate the library's, not replace it.

=== 000603a4 [PLATE]
Function pointer holding the routine that terminates the runtime's INT 23h (Ctrl-Break) hook; in this link it holds the do-nothing stub __null_int23_exit at 0x00042e0e (a bare RET).

Its value comes from the initialised image, not from any runtime store: no instruction in FDPS.LE writes this address. The linker resolved the initialiser of the 'exit' module's _DATA+4 slot to __null_int23_exit, which is what the slot holds whenever nothing that installs an INT 23h handler is linked in -- and nothing here does. Read by exactly two call sites, both indirect: exit (00042e0f) calls it at 00042e15 as its second step, after __atexit at 0x000603a0 and before handing the status to _exit; _exit (00042e29) calls it at 00042e29 as its first step, before __FPE_handler_exit at 0x000603a8 and the tail jump to __exit (00043527). On the exit() path it therefore runs twice, which is harmless only because the target is the empty stub. The three slots 0x000603a0 / 0x000603a4 / 0x000603a8 are the whole _DATA segment of the CLIB 'exit' module, in that order, and all three currently point at the same one-byte RET.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __int23_exit at _DATA+4 of the OMF module 'exit' in WATCOM 10.0a LIB386/DOS/CLIB3S.LIB; only exit and _exit reach it]

Rebuild note:
Declaring this as a null-initialised pointer -- void (*__int23_exit)(void) = NULL; -- crashes at exit: exit() and _exit() call through it unconditionally with no null test. The original initialises it to an empty RET stub, and that stub is why no test is needed.

=== 000603a8 [PLATE]
Hook called on the way out of the process to shut down the floating-point exception (SIGFPE) trap handler.

One of three exit hooks CLIB3S's exit module publishes as consecutive dwords: __atexit (000603a0), __int23_exit (000603a4) and this one. exit (00042e0f) calls [__atexit] then [__int23_exit] and then calls _exit; _exit (00042e29) calls [__int23_exit] again and then [__FPE_handler_exit], and tails into __exit (00043527), which ends the program through INT 21h AH=4Ch. So this hook runs on every exit path, normal or _exit, and always last.

The value is fixed at link time, not at run time. exit.obj's own initialised image sets the slot to _null_exit_rtn, the bare RET at 00042e0e, and the only thing that ever overwrites it is __GrabFP87, which stores __Fini_FPE_handler here when the FP signal machinery is pulled in. FDPS links neither -- no instruction in the image writes this address, and no __GrabFP87 / __Fini_FPE_handler / __FPE_handler body exists among its functions -- so the slot holds 00042e0e for the whole run and the call at 00042e2f is a deliberate no-op. Same for its sibling __atexit at 000603a0: this program registers no atexit handlers.

Pool: crt  [public data symbol of CLIB3S exit.obj; the only reader is _exit]

Rebuild note:
The slot has to be defined with an initialiser that points at a real do-nothing function, and it has to stay in initialised data. _exit calls through it with no null check, so declaring it the obvious way -- void (*__FPE_handler_exit)(void) = NULL; -- or letting it fall into _BSS, which the CRT zeroes at startup, turns program exit into a call to address 0.

=== 000603ac [PLATE]
Pointer to the Intel Code Builder Global Data Area, the extender kernel structure whose address is handed to the program in EDX at entry.

Written once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 00043398, on the startup branch taken only when the extender signature in AX is 0x4243 ('CB', Intel Code Builder); that same branch reads the caller's stack limit from GDA+0x1c, the PSP address from GDA+0x10 and the environment selector from PSP+0x2c, and ends by setting _Extender to 9. Read by FUN_000444d4 (the 387-emulator init) at 00044567 and by __sys_fini_387_emulator at 00044659, in both cases only after the guard CMP AL,0x9 on _Extender: they load the GDA pointer into ECX and CALL dword ptr [ECX + 0x30], the extender's service entry, with EAX = 0x0e02 and EBX = 4 to hook the 387 emulator, EBX = 0 to unhook it. FDPS runs under DOS/4GW, whose signature fails the 0x4243 test, so this pointer is never written and stays NULL for the whole run; the two call sites that dereference it are unreachable in this binary.

Pool: crt  [defined by the Watcom startup module that publishes _cstart_, imported by the math library's dosinite module; no game or AIL code refers to it]

Rebuild note:
Do not simplify the 387-emulator hook by dropping the _Extender == 9 test around the two call sites: under DOS/4GW this pointer is always NULL, so an unconditional CALL through GDA+0x30 dereferences null. Equally, do not delete the symbol for looking permanently zero -- dosinite imports it and the link needs the definition.

=== 000603b0 [PLATE]
Selector of the Rational DOS/16M-family information segment (the DOS/4G extender's own data area), as the loader leaves it in GS at program entry.

Written once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body during host detection. On the DPMI/DOS-4G branch -- the one taken when INT 21h AX=FF00h, DX=78h answers -- it stores GS here at 000433e3, but only when GS is non-zero (000433dd CMP AX,0x0 / JZ), so a host that starts the program with GS = 0 leaves the built-in default 0x0020 standing. Nothing writes it after startup. It is read only on the 80x87 emulator hook path: FUN_000444d4 at 0004457b and __sys_fini_387_emulator at 00044678 load it into DX with EAX = 0 and call __hook387 (00051a56) / __unhook387 (00051b27), whose contract is EAX = offset into the extender data area, DX = the selector for it; __unhook387 moves DX into ES and addresses the area from there. Both reads are gated on the host-type byte _Extender at 0006044e being 1, the Rational extender; the other host kinds hook the emulator through INT 21h AX=2507h, INT 21h AH=F3h, or the service vtable reached through __GDAptr at 000603ac instead, and never look at this word.

Pool: crt  [cstrt386.obj _DATA+0x4 in Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S.LIB, published as __D16Infoseg; the object's whole _DATA image is __GDAptr dd 0, __D16Infoseg dw 20h, __x386_zero_base_selector dw 0, matching 000603ac / 000603b0 / 000603b2 exactly]

Rebuild note:
The initial value is 0x0020, not zero. Declaring this as a plain uninitialised global -- or letting it land in BSS, which is what its runtime-scratch role suggests -- hands selector 0 to __hook387 on any host that starts the program with GS = 0, and the emulator hook is installed against a null selector.

=== 000603b2 [PLATE]
Selector with linear base 0, used by the 387-emulator hook to reach absolute linear addresses.

Defined in the Watcom startup module (cstrt386) alongside __GDAptr at 000603ac and __D16Infoseg at 000603b0, and initialised to 0. Nothing in FDPS.LE writes it: the only reference in the whole image is the read at 00044511, in the tail of __sys_init_387_emulator that Ghidra still carries as FUN_000444d4, where it is loaded into ES so the emulator's INT 7 gate can be stored straight into the IDT -- EBX comes from SIDT plus 0x38 (vector 7 x 8 bytes) and the two dwords in EDX:ECX are the gate descriptor. That store is gated on the byte at 00060450 (__X32VM) being non-zero; that byte is likewise only ever read in this image, so the path is not taken and the emulator is hooked through the DOS INT 21h AX=2507h branch at 00044526 instead. The value, when a host does set it, is a selector index+RPL; 0 means no zero-base selector is available.

Pool: crt  [Watcom CLIB3S cstrt386.obj PUBDEF, referenced only by MATH387S dosinite.obj code; the game never touches it.]

Rebuild note:
The variable must stay defined and zero even though no code assigns it: MATH387S's dosinite module needs the external, and both this word and the __X32VM gate at 00060450 being zero is what keeps the direct-IDT branch dead in the original.

=== 000603b4 [PLATE]
Watcom CRT _argc: the process argument count, the public copy the C library exposes to user code through <stdlib.h>.

Written twice by __Init_Argv during startup and read nowhere in this image. __Init_Argv walks the command-line copy at _LpCmdLine, mallocs the argv vector, fills it, then stores the count here (0004e0d4, from EBP) and the vector base in _argv at 000603b8; when the allocation fails it stores 0 into both instead (0004e0e7 and 0004e0e2, EAX = 0). Immediately afterwards the same count and vector are mirrored into ___Argc at 0006a3b4 and ___Argv at 0006a3b8 (0004e0f1, 0004e0f7), and it is that _BSS pair -- not this one -- that __CMain hands to main at 0004df88. So _argc is the user-visible alias of the count; nothing in FDPS reads it, because the game accepts no command-line options.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF _argc at offset 0 of the 8-byte _DATA segment of CLIB3S argcv386.obj, with _argv at +4 landing on 000603b8; the only referencing function is the CRT's __Init_Argv]

Rebuild note:
_argc, _argv and the initialiser record that schedules __Init_Argv all live in one CLIB3S module (argcv386.obj: the 8-byte _DATA segment plus a 6-byte XI segment). Declare these in src/ as extern only. Emitting a definition of your own -- `int _argc;` -- either collides with the library symbol or displaces that module, and displacing it takes the XI entry with it, so __Init_Argv never runs and main receives argc = 0, argv = NULL with no diagnostic.

=== 000603b8 [PLATE]
Pointer to the CRT's argument vector: _argv[0] is the program name, _argv[1..] the parsed command-line words, _argv[_argc] is NULL.

Written only by __Init_Argv (0004e040), which the C startup runs from the XI auto-init list before main -- __CMain calls __InitRtns at 0004df7c, and argcv386.obj registers __Init_Argv in XI. __Init_Argv parses _LpCmdLine (00060424) once to count the words and measure the text, allocates a single block holding a copy of the command-line text followed by (argc+1) pointer slots, and points _argv at the start of that slot area (buf + text_len). It then stores _LpPgmName (00060428) into _argv[0], parses the copied text a second time to fill _argv[1..], writes NULL into _argv[argc], and sets _argc (000603b4) to the word count. If the allocation fails, the 0004e0e2 path sets both _argv and _argc to 0.

Nothing in FDPS reads _argv. At its tail __Init_Argv copies the pair into ___Argc (0006a3b4) and ___Argv (0006a3b8), in _BSS, and those are what __CMain pushes into main at 0004df8f. _argv exists because argcv386.obj publishes it for user code that wants the vector outside main.

Pool: crt  [only __Init_Argv touches it; it is a PUBDEF of Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S argcv386.obj, so it keeps the library's own symbol]

Rebuild note:
_argv/_argc and ___Argv/___Argc are two separate pairs, not one variable seen twice. Collapsing them loses the allocation-failure asymmetry: on failure _argv and _argc go to 0, but ___Argc is still assigned the parsed word count while ___Argv is NULL, so main can be entered with argc > 0 and argv == NULL.

=== 000603bc [PLATE]
Saved SS selector for the Watcom stack-overflow check -- the stack segment the stk386 module records for itself, and the value __STK compares the live SS against before it is willing to declare an overflow.

Written only by FUN_00043612 (MOV word ptr [0x603bc],SS / RET), the unnamed file-static helper at offset 0 of the linked clib3s stk386 module; that helper is an orphan block with no caller anywhere in FDPS.LE, so this word keeps its link-time value of 0 for the whole run. Read only by __STK (0x4362d): after a probe finds that the requested frame would drop ESP to or below _STACKLOW (0x60430), __STK does MOV AX,SS / CMP AX,[0x603bc] and falls through to __STKOVERFLOW (0x4364b, which passes the "Stack Overflow!" text at 0x603be to __fatal_runtime_error) only when the two selectors are equal; otherwise it returns and the caller proceeds. A non-zero value would be the flat DGROUP stack selector, i.e. "this is the stack the check was armed for"; 0 means no stack was ever recorded, which is the state the shipped image is in. Only the 17 library functions that kept their prologue probes call __CHK/__STK at all -- the game modules are compiled with -s.

Pool: crt  [2-byte file-static at offset 0 of stk386.obj's _DATA, immediately ahead of that module's "Stack Overflow!" string; reached only by stk386's own code]

Rebuild note:
The "Stack Overflow!" abort is unreachable in FDPS.LE because this word is never armed: the only writer, the offset-0 helper at 0x43612, has no caller, so __STK's SS comparison against 0 never matches. Reimplementing __STK as the obvious if (new_esp <= _STACKLOW) fatal("Stack Overflow!"), or adding a startup call that captures SS, turns a silent no-op into a program abort for the library modules that kept their probes -- FD2 hit exactly that failure when AIL's ISR called a probed thunk on AIL's own low private stack. Link stk386 from the vendor lib and leave the offset-0 helper uncalled.

=== 000603d0 [PLATE]
64-byte system-state block that the 387-emulator installer hands to the DOS extender's INT 21h AX=2535h fetch/store service; of it, only the dword at offset 0 -- the host's copy of CR0 -- is ever touched by this program.

FUN_000444d4, the body of __sys_init_387_emulator, takes this route when the extender flag at 0x60450 is non-zero: it locates the IDT with SIDT, writes a 386 interrupt gate for INT 7 pointing at the emulator entry 0x4ec18 (descriptor built by FUN_0004459f, type byte 0x8e), then calls FUN_00044609. FUN_00044609 calls the service with EBX=0 to fetch the block into this buffer, sets bit 2 (CR0.EM) and clears bit 1 (CR0.MP) in the dword at offset 0, and calls it again with EBX=1 to store it back -- that is what makes x87 opcodes trap to the INT 7 emulator. __sys_fini_387_emulator undoes it through FUN_000446de: fetch the block the same way, overwrite offset 0 with the zero-extended startup machine status word saved at 0x60416 (SMSW & 6, the original MP and EM bits), store it back. The remaining 60 bytes are never read or written by the program; the fetch fills them and the store hands them straight back. The image holds all 64 bytes as zero.

Pool: crt  [only the Watcom dosinite module reaches it -- __sys_init_387_emulator, __sys_fini_387_emulator and their two helpers, and nothing else]

Rebuild note:
The store must always be preceded by its matching fetch. Only four of these 64 bytes are set by the CRT and the other 60 come back from the fetch, so a rewrite that fills a fresh local block and issues only the store hands the extender 60 bytes of garbage system state. Note also that the fini path assigns the whole dword (offset 0 = saved MSW & 6) rather than masking and OR-ing, unlike the ring-0 path at 0x446ca; writing the obvious read-modify-write there changes what is stored back.

=== 00060410 [PLATE]
Offset half of the protected-mode INT 7 handler that was installed before the Watcom 387 emulator hooked the vector; the matching selector is at 00060414.

Written once by FUN_000445bc, the install helper reached from FUN_000444d4 at 00044599 on the __sys_init_387_emulator (000444a4) path: it issues INT 21h AX=2502h with CL=7 (DOS/4G get protected-mode interrupt vector), which returns the current handler in ES:EBX, stores EBX here and ES at 00060414, then installs the emulator's own INT 7 handler with AX=2504h -- 0004eba8 when the extender type byte at 0006044e is below 3, 0004ec18 otherwise. Read once by FUN_000446a3, called from __sys_fini_387_emulator at 00044693 during shutdown: it loads this dword into EDX and 00060414 into DS and issues AX=2504h on CL=7, putting the original handler back. Vector 7 is #NM (device not available), the trap the emulator uses to catch x87 instructions when no coprocessor is present. Zero here means no vector has been saved yet, which on this path only holds before __sys_init_387_emulator runs.

Pool: crt  [reached only by crt code; it is a file-static of math387s.lib(dosinite), whose extent 000444a4-0004470f matches the reference link map offsets exactly]

Rebuild note:
This is the offset half of a 48-bit far pointer, not a flat handler address. Re-declaring the saved vector as one void * and restoring only it hands INT 21h AX=2504h whatever selector DS happens to hold, installing the old handler in the wrong segment; the selector at 00060414 must be loaded into DS with it.

=== 00060414 [PLATE]
Selector half of the protected-mode INT 7 handler that was installed before the Watcom 387 emulator took the vector over.

Written once by FUN_000445bc, which asks the DOS extender for the current handler of vector 7 (INT 21h AX=2502h, CL=7) and files the returned ES:EBX far pointer away as offset at 00060410 and selector here. Read once by FUN_000446a3, which reloads DS:EDX from that pair and hands it back with INT 21h AX=2504h, CL=7, restoring the previous owner of the vector. FUN_000446a3 runs from __sys_fini_387_emulator, and only when the install flag at 00060418 is 1, so the restore never fires unless FUN_000444d4 actually installed the emulator. Vector 7 is coprocessor-not-available: with CR0.EM set (FUN_000444d4 records the original MP/EM bits at 00060416) every ESC instruction traps there and the emulator interprets it. Zero here means nothing was saved yet; the image ships both halves as zero.

This word and the dword at 00060410 are one 48-bit far pointer split across two objects because the type vocabulary has no far-pointer spelling.

Pool: crt  [only FUN_000445bc and FUN_000446a3 touch it, both Watcom 387-emulator startup code; the game never sees it]

=== 00060416 [PLATE]
The CR0.MP and CR0.EM bits as they stood before the Watcom 80x87 emulator hooked the FPU, saved so the pair can be put back at shutdown.

Written once, by the emulator installer FUN_000444d4: SMSW stores CR0's low 16 bits here and the following AND masks the word with 0x6, leaving only bit 1 (MP, monitor coprocessor) and bit 2 (EM, emulation). Any of four values can result -- 0, 2, 4 or 6 -- and each simply mirrors how the host had CR0 set on entry. The install path then sets EM and clears MP so that every x87 opcode raises exception 7 into the emulator's handler.

Read only on the teardown paths, each of which restores the saved pair by a different route depending on privilege level and extender type: FUN_000446a3 reads CR0, clears MP and EM with AND 0xfffffff9, ORs this word back in and writes CR0 directly; FUN_000446de writes it into the extender's CR0 image at 000603d0 and commits it with INT 21h AX=2535h, EBX=1, the ring-3 route where MOV CR0 is not available; __sys_fini_387_emulator at 00044668 loads it into AL and issues INT 21h AH=0xF3h. Only the low byte ever reaches those services, because the masked value never exceeds 6.

The companion state of the same module sits either side: 00060410/00060414 hold the previous INT 7 handler far pointer, 00060418 is the byte flag __sys_fini_387_emulator tests to know the emulator was installed, and 00060394 (__8087) is set to 3 by the same installer.

Pool: crt  [only the Watcom 387-emulator install/teardown cluster 000444d4-000446fe touches it; no game or AIL code reads or writes CR0 state]

Rebuild note:
Read this back with SMSW, not with MOV from CR0. SMSW stays legal at CPL 3, while MOV EAX,CR0 is privileged and general-protection-faults under DOS/4GW at ring 3 -- which is exactly why the teardown has a second path (FUN_000446de) that goes through the extender's INT 21h AX=2535h service instead of writing CR0 itself.

=== 00060418 [PLATE]
Watcom CRT: set once the 387 emulator has been hooked into the machine, so the shutdown path knows there is something to unhook. Only 0 and 1 are ever stored.

Written by FUN_000444d4, the emulator installer, which stores 1 here as its second act, right after setting __8087 (00060394) to 3 and before it saves CR0's MP/EM bits into 00060416, reads the IDT base with SIDT to reach gate 7, and calls __hook387 -- so the value means "installation was begun", not "installation succeeded". __sys_init_387_emulator (000444a4) reaches that installer only when its own FNINIT/FNSTCW probe found no real coprocessor (control-word high byte not 3), so on a machine with a 387 this byte stays 0 for the life of the program.

__sys_fini_387_emulator (00044629) is the only reader. It returns immediately unless the byte is exactly 1; otherwise it undoes the install along whichever arm _Extender (0006044e) selects -- FUN_000446de puts the CR0 MP/EM bits saved at 00060416 back through the extender's CR0 get/set service (INT 21h AX=2535h, EBX 0 = read, 1 = write), FUN_000446a3 first restores the protected-mode INT 7 vector saved at 00060410 (offset) and 00060414 (selector) via INT 21h AX=2504h -- and stores 0 here on the way out, which makes a second call a no-op.

Pool: crt  [file-static in the private _DATA of MATH387S module dosinite, offset 0x48 of 0x49; reached only by that module's own routines, never by the game]

=== 0006041c [PLATE]
End of the runtime's dynamic area: the DGROUP address one past the last byte startup handed out, which on this target is the stack pointer as it stood when initialisation finished.

Written exactly once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 000434c6 (MOV dword ptr [_dynend],EBX with EBX taken from ESP), in the same store group that records the no-x87 flag at __no87 (0006044c) and sets _STACKLOW (00060430) from the first free byte past the copied program name. Nothing in this image reads it. The 32-bit flat runtime tracks the heap through _curbrk (00060420, moved by sbrk/__brk/__ExpandDGROUP) and the stack through _STACKLOW and _STACKTOP (00060430/00060434, read by __STK, stackavail and __brk); _dynend is the near-heap-model bound that crwd386 still defines and startup still fills in. The value is always a DGROUP linear address near the top of the stack region and is never zero once startup has run.

Pool: crt  [offset 0x00 of the 65-byte _DATA segment of crwd386.obj in CLIB3S.LIB, the vendor object that defines the whole low-globals block at 0006041c-0006045c; only CRT code touches it]

=== 00060420 [PLATE]
Current program break: the linear address of the first byte past the end of the near heap, i.e. the top of DGROUP as the C runtime currently sees it.

Seeded twice during startup by L$1_cstrt386_start_body -- first with the startup ESP at 0004331c as a provisional value, then at 00043376 with the extender's memory top from ES:[0x5c] rounded up to a 4K page. After that __brk is the only function that stores an arbitrary value: it returns the old break and writes its argument (0004e81e/0004e823), which is how sbrk moves the break (sbrk computes increment + _curbrk and calls __brk). The three near-heap growers do not trust the stored value: sbrk (0004e755), __ExpandDGROUP (0004434d) and __LastFree (0004411a) each recompute it as the DS selector limit plus one (LSL EAX,EAX; INC EAX) and store that back before using it, because under DOS/4GW the flat data segment can have grown since the last update. __LastFree then tests whether the last free block ends exactly at the break; __ExpandDGROUP adds the requested amount and rejects the result if it wraps. The value 0xfffffffe is a latched sentinel meaning DGROUP can no longer be grown -- it is what __ExpandDGROUP's overflow path at 00044362 hands to __brk -- and both __ExpandDGROUP (0004430e) and FUN_00044201 (00044215) test for it and give up before attempting any further expansion.

Pool: crt  [reached only by cstrt386's startup body and the sbrk386/grownear heap modules; _curbrk is a library symbol in all three of those 10.0a objects and the game never touches it]

Rebuild note:
sbrk, __ExpandDGROUP and __LastFree recompute _curbrk from the DS selector limit immediately before each use and overwrite whatever was stored; only __brk carries a value forward. A rewrite that treats it as an ordinary variable maintained solely by brk/sbrk uses a stale break under DOS/4GW. The magic 0xfffffffe is a sentinel meaning "DGROUP is maxed out", not an address, so the equality tests against it must survive whatever type the declaration is given.

=== 00060424 [PLATE]
Pointer to the DOS command-line tail that the startup code copied just past the end of _BSS.

L$1_cstrt386_start_body (00043310) writes it once during startup, at 0004350b: it takes _end (0x0006a3bc), rounds it up to the next 16-byte boundary (ADD 0xf / AND AL,0xf0) and stores the resulting 0x0006a3c0 here, which is where the startup has copied the PSP command-line tail. The value is a NUL-terminated string pointer and never changes afterwards. __Init_Argv (0004e040) is the only reader: it calls _SplitParms (0004e104) with this pointer twice -- once with a NULL vector to count the arguments and measure the buffer, once to fill argv[1..argc-1] -- and also uses it as the base when computing the length of the copied parameter text. argv[0] does not come from here; it comes from _LpPgmName at 00060428. A NUL first byte means the program was started with no arguments and argc comes back as 1.

Pool: crt  [Only the Watcom startup and __Init_Argv touch it; _LpCmdLine is a PUBDEF in cstrt386.obj and an EXTDEF in initargv.obj of WATCOM 10.0a CLIB3S.]

=== 00060428 [PLATE]
Pointer to the program's own name, the NUL-terminated pathname the C runtime hands to main as argv[0].

Written once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body (00043310) at 00043510, before any C code runs. The startup copies the PSP command tail to the 16-byte-aligned buffer just past the end of _BSS (0006a3bc rounded up to 0006a3c0) and points _LpCmdLine (00060424) at it, then walks the environment strings, skips the terminating double NUL and the word count that follows, and copies the program name to the end of that same buffer; _LpPgmName is set to the first byte after the command line's NUL, so the two strings sit back to back in one block. _STACKLOW (00060430) is then set one byte past the program name's NUL, which is why the near heap and stack start above these strings rather than overwriting them. On the DPMI/DOS-4G path the name comes from the extender's environment block; the value is never a static string in the image.

Read once, by __Init_Argv (0004e040) at 0004e0b4, which stores it into slot 0 of the freshly allocated vector at _argv (000603b8) and then fills _argv[1..] by parsing a copy of _LpCmdLine. Nothing in FDPS reads it; the game's main never inspects argv.

Pool: crt  [only the Watcom startup and __Init_Argv touch it; it is a PUBDEF of Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S, sitting in the _curbrk/_LpCmdLine/_LpPgmName/_psp/_STACKLOW/_STACKTOP run, so it keeps the library's own symbol]

=== 0006042c [PLATE]
The PSP (Program Segment Prefix) selector for this process: the Watcom C runtime's _psp.

Written three times by L$1_cstrt386_start_body during startup. It is preloaded with 0x24, Phar Lap 386|DOS-Extender's fixed PSP selector, before the host probe; the Intel Code Builder path then overwrites it with DS and the DPMI / DOS-4G path with ES, so it ends up holding whichever selector the detected extender supplies for the PSP. The startup reads it straight back into ES to reach PSP fields through it -- the memory-block end at PSP:5Ch when shrinking the DOS block down to the 4K-rounded break stored at 00060420, and the environment selector at PSP:2Ch. getpid at 0004c162 returns it, and its only caller __MkTmpFile formats the low four hex digits of that return value into the temporary file name tXXXX_YY.tmp. Declared unsigned (4 bytes) by Watcom's stdlib.h, but only the low 16 bits are ever written, each write being a 16-bit segment-register store; the high 16 bits stay zero from the image's initialised data, which is why getpid's 32-bit load yields a clean selector.

Pool: crt  [defined by cstrt386.obj of CLIB3S.LIB and imported by EXTDEF _psp in the same library's gtpid module; only CRT startup code and getpid reach it]

Rebuild note:
_psp occupies all four bytes 0006042c-0006042f even though every store into it is 16-bit, because getpid reads it with MOV EAX,[_psp]. Typing it as a word and giving 0006042e-0006042f to a neighbouring variable would put that neighbour in getpid's high half.

=== 00060430 [PLATE]
Watcom C runtime stack-low limit: the lowest linear address the stack is allowed to grow down to.

Written once at startup by L$1_cstrt386_start_body (MOV dword ptr [0x00060430],EDI at 000434c0), which sets it to the first free byte past the command line and program name it has just copied into the space above the end of BSS; everything above this address is stack and near heap, everything below it is that copy, which must not be overwritten. Read by __STK at 00043635, the per-function stack probe: __STK receives the requested frame size in EAX, forms the prospective new ESP, and falls through to __STKOVERFLOW when that address is at or below this value (unsigned CMP/JBE) or when SS no longer matches L$N_stk386_saved_ss. Read by stackavail at 0004e694, whose whole body is MOV EAX,ESP / SUB EAX,[0x00060430] / RET, so the value it returns is the number of stack bytes still free; its CRT callers (__CMain, spawnve, write) size on-stack scratch buffers from that count. The value is an address used only in comparisons and subtractions, never dereferenced. crwd386 publishes a second PUBDEF, __x386_stacklow, at the same segment offset; every object linked into this image reaches the variable through _STACKLOW.

Pool: crt  [_DATA offset 0x14 of module crwd386 in Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S.LIB; all three referencing functions are CRT]

=== 00060434 [PLATE]
Lowest address the program break is allowed to take: the initial ESP, which is the top of the stack and therefore the base of the near heap.

Written exactly once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 00043316, right after ESP is aligned down to a dword boundary; the same value goes to _curbrk at 0006041c+4 (00060420) two instructions later, so the near heap starts empty at the top of DGROUP and grows upward from here. Nothing writes it again for the life of the process. __brk reads it as its first act: the requested break in [ESP+0x18] is compared against it unsigned and any value below it is rejected out of hand, which is what keeps sbrk from handing out memory that overlaps the stack. sbrk reaches this variable only through __brk. The value is always a flat linear address; zero is not a legal value and only appears before startup runs.

Pool: crt  [defined by the Watcom 10.0a startup module cstrt386 and read by sbrk386's __brk; no game or AIL code refers to it]

=== 00060438 [PLATE]
Byte size of the alternate stack that the Watcom C startup carves off the main stack; it is 0 in this build, so no alternate stack is ever taken.

Nothing in the image writes it. It is a library variable defined by CLIB3S.LIB module crwd386.obj, which supplies the whole Watcom low-globals block _dynend.._osminor at 0006041c-00060458, and its image initialiser is zero. It is read twice, both times in __CMain (0004df4c): the value is rounded up to a multiple of four (ADD EBX,3 / AND BL,0FCh) and compared unsigned against stackavail (0004e692). When it is strictly smaller than the free stack, that many bytes are subtracted from ESP and __ASTACKPTR (0006043c) is set to base + size, the top of the carved block; when it is not, the base is NULL and __ASTACKPTR is set to the size alone. Because the value is zero the subtraction is a no-op, __ASTACKPTR ends up holding __CMain's own ESP, and no code in this program reads __ASTACKPTR at all -- the alternate-stack feature is linked in but dormant.

Pool: crt  [an EXTDEF of cmain386.obj resolved by crwd386.obj, both CLIB3S.LIB; the only referencing function is the CRT's __CMain, no game or AIL code reaches it]

Rebuild note:
__ASTACKSIZ belongs to CLIB3S.LIB (crwd386.obj), not to the game. Emitting a definition for it in rebuilt source -- the obvious response to a zero-initialised dword that no code writes -- gives a duplicate symbol at link time, and giving it a non-zero value silently moves ESP for the entire program, because __CMain subtracts it from the stack before calling main.

=== 0006043c [PLATE]
Watcom C runtime auxiliary-stack pointer: the high end of the stack block __CMain reserves at startup, whose size comes from __ASTACKSIZ (00060438).

Written exactly once and never read. __CMain (0004df4c), before it calls __CommonInit (00054dbc) and main, loads __ASTACKSIZ, rounds it up to a multiple of 4 (ADD EBX,3 / AND BL,0xfc) and compares it with stackavail() (0004e692, which returns ESP - _STACKLOW at 00060430). If the rounded request is below the space available, it subtracts it from ESP and takes the new ESP as the block base; if it does not fit, the base is taken as 0 instead. __ASTACKPTR then receives base + __ASTACKSIZ -- note the unrounded size is re-loaded for this addition, so the recorded top can sit up to 3 bytes below the original ESP. In the failure path the stored value is __ASTACKSIZ itself rather than an address. In FDPS.LE __ASTACKSIZ is zero (a C-only program never sets it), so nothing is reserved and __ASTACKPTR ends up holding ESP as it stood inside __CMain's prologue. Nothing else in the image reads it, and within CLIB3S.LIB itself the only module that references it is cmain386.

One member of the crwd386 runtime data block, which runs from _dynend (0006041c) through _curbrk, _LpCmdLine, _LpPgmName, _psp, _STACKLOW, _STACKTOP, __ASTACKSIZ, __ASTACKPTR, _cbyte (00060440) and on to _Extender, __no87 and __FPE_handler.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __ASTACKPTR at +0x20 of module crwd386's _DATA in CLIB3S.LIB; its sole referencing function is the byte-exact cmain386 __CMain, and the game never touches it]

=== 00060440 [PLATE]
Console pushback slot: the character a previous ungetch() stored, or 0 when nothing is pending.

Read by kbhit (00043570), which reports a keystroke is waiting whenever the slot is non-zero without going to the BIOS; read and immediately cleared to 0 by getch (00043587) and getche (000549bf), each of which returns the pending character as-is when it is non-zero and otherwise falls through to INT 21h (AH=8 for getch, AH=1 for getche). 0 is the sentinel for "nothing pushed back", which is also why ungetch cannot push a NUL. FDPS.LE links getch, getche and kbhit but not ungetch, so nothing in this image ever stores a non-zero value here and all three pushback branches are unreachable at runtime; the slot stays at its initial 0 for the life of the process.

Pool: crt  [Watcom CLIB3S internal state: EXTDEF _cbyte in getch.obj, gtche.obj and kbhit.obj, defined by crwd386.obj at _DATA+0x24 -- the same runtime data module that supplies _dynend, _curbrk, _LpCmdLine, _LpPgmName and _psp at 0006041c..0006042c. No game code touches it.]

=== 00060448 [PLATE]
Watcom CLIB3S runtime flag: non-zero while a child process launched through the spawn/exec family is executing.

Written only by __dospawn, and only around the DOS EXEC call: set to 1 at 0005625e, immediately after the AH=0Bh check and just before MOV AH,4Bh / INT 21h, and cleared to 0 at 00056284 once control returns and SS, ESP and DS have been restored from the spawn386 save slots at 0006154c, 00061548 and 0006154e. The only path that reaches it is L$2_spve_build_cmdline_and_spawn -> __dospawn. The values are a boolean: 1 means the DOS EXEC is in flight, 0 means it is not. No code in FDPS.LE reads it.

It is a public of CLIB3S module crwd386, which holds the C runtime's writable scalars; its _DATA block starts at 0006041c, which is why _psp, _STACKLOW, __ASTACKSIZ, _cbyte and __no87 sit either side of this address.

Pool: crt  [defined by CLIB3S crwd386 at _DATA+44 and referenced by an EXTDEF in the byte-identical spawn386 module; no game or AIL code touches it]

=== 0006044c [PLATE]
Nonzero when the NO87 environment variable was present at program start, telling the math library to ignore whatever coprocessor the machine has.

Written once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 000434b9, from the counter EBP accumulates while walking the DOS environment: for each entry the startup case-folds the first four characters and compares them against "no87", checks that the fifth is '=', and increments EBP on a match. The store is a 16-bit MOV even though every reader tests one byte, so the symbol owns the two bytes 0006044c-0006044d and the high byte is always zero. Normal values are 0 (no NO87 in the environment) and 1 (present).

Read by __chk8087 at 00044772, and only there. When it is zero, __chk8087 publishes the coprocessor type it just detected into __8087 (00060394) and __real87 (00060395); when it is nonzero it leaves both at their linked-in values, so the program runs on the 387 emulator no matter what hardware is present.

Slot +0x30 of the crwd386 runtime-data block that begins at 0006041c (_dynend); _Extender follows at +0x32 (0006044e).

Pool: crt  [only the Watcom startup and __chk8087 reach it, and __no87 is the library's own PUBDEF, spelled identically in CLIB3S and CLIB3R.]

Rebuild note:
__no87 owns two bytes although every reader reads one. cstrt386 declares it EXTRN :BYTE and __chk8087 tests `byte ptr`, so declaring it `char` in a hand-written CRT equivalent looks right; it lets the linker pack _Extender at 0006044d, and the startup's 16-bit store at 000434b9 then zeroes the extender type that was set earlier in the same routine at 00043425. Every later near-heap path (__ExpandDGROUP, __LastFree, __brk, all of which branch on _Extender being 1, 2..8 or 9) would take the unknown-extender branch. Keep the slot two bytes wide.

=== 0006044e [PLATE]
Watcom C runtime host-type byte: which DOS extender or DPMI host the program was found to be running under. Decided once during startup and read-only for the rest of the run.

Written only by L$1_cstrt386_start_body (00043310) at 00043425, together with _ExtenderSubtype at 0006044f, from the host probe that INT 21h AH=30h opens with EBX='PHAR'. The four values it can take, one per branch of that probe:
  0  no host answered. The fallback path at 0004340e (fixed selectors: PSP 0x24, environment 0x2c, flat data 0x17) sets AL=0, AH=0.
  1  a DPMI host answered INT 21h AX=FF00h with DX=78h (000433cc-000433fd). This is the DOS/4G path this game actually runs on. _ExtenderSubtype is set to 0 when the DS segment base returned by INT 31h AX=0006h is zero and to 1 when it is not, so the pair (1,0) means 'DPMI with a zero-based flat DS'.
  2..8  Phar Lap 386|DOS-Extender: INT 21h AH=30h returned 'DX' in the high half of EAX, and the value stored is the major-version digit, BL - '0' (00043354-00043359). _ExtenderSubtype is 0.
  9  Intel Code Builder: the probe returned 'CB' and the info block pointer in EDX was saved to __GDAptr (000603ac); AL=9, AH=0 at 000433c6.

Everything after startup only reads it, to pick a host-specific mechanism:
  - L$1_cstrt386_start_body itself (000434da): when the value is 1, the BSS clear from 00063930 to 0006a3bc is clamped to 0x1000 bytes, because the DOS/4G loader has already zeroed the rest.
