  - sbrk (0004e6ab) and _nexpand (0004d1ae), FUN_0004442b, FUN_00044201, __ExpandDGROUP (000442d0), _nrealloc (000430a1): (1 with subtype 0) or 9 means the heap can ask the host directly - DPMI INT 31h AX=0501h for value 1, INT 21h EAX=80004800h otherwise; 2..8 means the break has to be derived from the DS selector limit with LSL and grown through __brk instead.
  - __brk (0004e76d): 0 selects paragraph granularity (round up by 0xf, shift right 4), anything else page granularity (round up by 0xfff, shift right 0xc), with an extra shift when _ExtenderSubtype agrees.
  - _dos_setvect (00054f51) and FUN_000444d4: 2..8 installs vectors with the Phar Lap form INT 21h AX=2504h (CL = vector), 0 uses INT 21h AX=2507h, 9 goes through __GDAptr+0x30, 1 goes through the D16 entry with __D16Infoseg (000603b0) in DX.
  - FUN_000445bc / FUN_000446a3 (387-emulator INT 7 hook and unhook): a value of 3 or more means Phar Lap 3.x or later, which runs the program at privilege level 3, so CR0 cannot be written directly and the extender-mediated path is used instead.
  - FUN_00055fb0 / FUN_00055fd3 (DTA save and restore): only value 9 needs the DTA copied.

Pool: crt  [_Extender is a PUBDEF of crwd386.obj in the linked CLIB3S.LIB, in the same publics block and the same data cluster as _curbrk, _dynend, _psp and _LpCmdLine; only CRT code references it]

Rebuild note:
Because this byte is 1 under DOS/4G, the startup code zeroes only the first 0x1000 bytes of _BSS and trusts the LE loader to have zeroed 00064930 upward. A rebuild that keeps the same source but is launched some other way - a different extender, a hand-written start-up, an image whose BSS pages are not loader-zeroed - leaves every global above 00064930 holding whatever was in memory.

=== 0006044f [PLATE]
DOS extender subtype: 1 when the flat DS the extender handed the program has a non-zero linear base, 0 when it is zero-based.

Written once, next to _Extender, by the CRT startup L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 0004342a, from AH of the host-detection result; 00043425 stores AL into _Extender in the same breath. Only the DOS/4G branch can make it non-zero: after INT 21h AX=FF00h/DX=0078h answers with a Rational host (_Extender = 1) the startup asks INT 31h AX=0006h for the segment base of DS and sets AH to 1 only when CX:DX is not zero (000433f6), so the ordinary zero-based DOS/4GW image this game runs under leaves it 0. The Phar Lap branch (_Extender = 0x22), the Intel Code Builder branch (_Extender = 9) and the no-extender branch (_Extender = 0) all reach 00043425 with AH = 0.

Read only by the near-heap and program-break code, and always together with _Extender. __ExpandDGROUP (000442dd), FUN_0004442b (0004444b), _nexpand (0004d1f1) and sbrk (0004e6bb) take their direct path on (_Extender == 1 && _ExtenderSubtype == 0) || _Extender == 9 -- the hosts where an offset is already a linear address. __brk takes the other side: at 0004e809 it compares the subtype against _Extender's own value 1 and, when they match, shifts the segment-limit figure it is about to hand to DPMI left by 8 before issuing the call.

Pool: crt  [only CRT startup and heap code reaches it, and _ExtenderSubtype is a public symbol of Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S.LIB]

=== 00060450 [PLATE]
Non-zero when the program is hosted by the FlashTek X-32VM DOS extender; zero under every other host, including this build's DOS/4G.

Nothing in FDPS.LE ever writes it. It is initialised data whose only writer would be the X-32VM-specific startup module, which is not linked into this image, so it reads 0 for the whole run and every branch guarded by it is dead code here. __LastFree (000440e4) and __ExpandDGROUP (000442d0) both require _Extender (0006044e) to be in 2..8 AND this flag to be clear before they will trust LSL on DS as the DGROUP selector limit when growing the near heap -- under X-32VM's virtual memory that limit does not bound the heap, so the test forces the slow path. The 387 emulator installer FUN_000444d4 patches IDT vector 7 (SIDT base + 0x38) directly through __x386_zero_base_selector (000603b2) only when this flag is set, and jumps past that code when it is clear. __sys_fini_387_emulator (00044629) likewise takes the X-32VM teardown at 000446de when the flag is set, instead of dispatching on _Extender.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __X32VM at +0x34 of crwd386.obj in CLIB3S.LIB; the run from _dynend at 0006041c to __FPE_handler at 00060459 reproduces that object's symbol offsets exactly, and only CRT code reads it]

Rebuild note:
The byte holds 0 and sits between _ExtenderSubtype (0006044f) and _Envptr (00060451), which is itself 4-byte-unaligned, so the whole crwd386 block looks like it has stray filler in it and has none. Treating this zero as alignment padding, or letting a rebuilt version of that module align _Envptr, shifts every crwd386 global after it. It is supplied by the vendor CLIB3S.LIB and must not be declared in project source.

=== 00060451 [PLATE]
Offset half of the far address of the DOS environment block: the 32-bit offset within the real-mode environment segment whose selector sits in _Envseg at +4.

Written once during startup by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 0004343a (MOV dword ptr [_Envptr],ESI, immediately followed by MOV word ptr [_Envseg],CX), which derives the environment block's address from the PSP while it is also recording _Extender / _ExtenderSubtype at 0006044e. Read only by __setenvp at 00054fa6, which loads the selector into FS, copies it into ES, loads this offset into EBP and walks the block byte by byte (CMP DL,byte ptr ES:[EAX]) to find the terminating NUL of each string, measuring each string's length as a pointer difference before allocating and copying it into environ. The block is the usual DOS layout: a sequence of NUL-terminated "NAME=value" strings ended by an empty string. Zero until startup fills it in.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF _Envptr at +0x35 of crwd386.obj in CLIB3S 10.0a, in the same run of run-time work-data symbols that places _dynend, _curbrk, _LpCmdLine, _LpPgmName and _psp on their already-named addresses; the only two referencing functions are the CRT startup and __setenvp.]

Rebuild note:
This is not a flat pointer. The environment block lives in real-mode memory reached through the selector in _Envseg (_Envptr+4), so dereferencing this dword as an ordinary char * in flat 32-bit C reads the wrong memory. _Envptr and _Envseg must also stay adjacent in that order: setenvp.obj names only _Envptr among its externals and reaches the selector as _Envptr+4, so declaring them as two unrelated C variables lets the linker separate or pad between them and the far load breaks.

=== 00060455 [PLATE]
Selector of the DOS environment block -- the segment half of the far pointer whose offset half is _Envptr at 00060451.

Written once, at 00043440, by the CRT startup L$1_cstrt386_start_body. That routine identifies the DOS extender and four paths converge on a single store of CX here and ESI into _Envptr: Phar Lap and the no-extender fallback use the fixed selector 0x2c with offset 0; the DOS/4G "BC" path stores the flat DS selector and puts the real-mode environment paragraph from PSP:0x2C shifted left 4 into _Envptr; the DPMI path stores the selector read from PSP:0x2C with offset 0. The same startup then reloads it at 00043482 to walk the environment looking for a "NO87=" entry, whose presence is counted into __no87 at 0006044c. __setenvp loads it into FS (and copies it to ES) at 00054f9a, takes the offset from _Envptr, and walks the double-NUL-terminated environment strings to build the environ/envp vectors. The value is a protected-mode selector, not a real-mode paragraph: it is only ever moved into a segment register, and in the DOS/4G case it is just the program's flat data selector while the whole address lives in _Envptr.

Pool: crt  [reached only by L$1_cstrt386_start_body and __setenvp; _Envseg is a data PUBDEF of the Watcom crwd386 object, whose other exports -- _dynend, _curbrk, _LpCmdLine, _LpPgmName, _psp, _Envptr, _osmajor, _osminor, __no87 -- occupy the surrounding addresses]

=== 00060457 [PLATE]
DOS major version number, as the host reported it at program start: 6 for a DOS 6.x host, 3 for DOS 3.x.

Written once by L$1_cstrt386_start_body (00043310) at 00043337, from INT 21h AH=30h issued at 00043335 (EAX cleared first, so AL=0 asks for the plain version): AL, the major number, is stored here and AH, the minor number, in _osminor (00060458). Nothing writes it again, so it is read-only for the rest of the run. Both readers use it for the same test, 'is this DOS 3.0 or later':
  - __set_errno_dos (0004bd4a) at 0004bd68: for a DOS error code below 0x100, the extra remap step that turns DOS error 0x50 into 0x0e is applied only when the major version is 3 or more; a major version under 3 jumps straight to 0004bd8a and the plain mapping stands, because DOS 2.x does not produce the later error numbers.
  - spawnve (000556a9) at 000557f3: the DOS 3-or-later path is entered only when the split program name has an empty drive component (*[EBP+0x42] == 0) and an empty directory component (*[EBP+0x48] == 0), i.e. the caller passed a bare filename.
No FDPS game code and no AIL code reads it. Under DOS/4G the value is the version of the real DOS underneath, not a version number of the extender - the extender identity lives in _Extender (0006044e) instead.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF _osmajor at +0x3b of crwd386.obj in the linked CLIB3S.LIB, whose base in this image is 0006041c; the whole run from _dynend at 0006041c to __FPE_handler at 00060459 reproduces that object's symbol offsets, and only CRT code touches it]

=== 00060458 [PLATE]
Minor half of the DOS version the program started under -- the 22 of "DOS 6.22", as a plain binary number, not BCD.

Written exactly once, by L$1_cstrt386_start_body at 0004333c, from AH after INT 21h with AH=30h (DOS Get Version); the same instruction pair stores AL into _osmajor at 00060457 on the line before. Nothing else in FDPS touches it: this build reads only the major half, in __set_errno_dos at 0004bd68 and spawnve at 000557f3, both of which test _osmajor against 3 to decide whether DOS 3.x facilities are available. So _osminor is set up for library and application code that may ask for it and is never consulted here. Its value before startup runs is zero, and it is zero on any DOS that fails the call.

Slot +0x3c of the crwd386 run-time work-data block that begins at 0006041c (_dynend); _osmajor is +0x3b (00060457) and the next symbol follows at +0x3d (00060459).

Pool: crt  [only the Watcom startup reaches it, and _osminor is the library's own symbol, EXTRN __osminor in the vendor startup object and a public in the linked C libraries.]

=== 00060459 [PLATE]
Installable handler for floating-point exceptions: the address the C runtime calls when an FP fault has to be reported.

Part of the Watcom CLIB3S data module crwd386, which the image loads at 0006041c; this slot is the module's offset 0x3d, immediately after _osmajor at 00060457 and _osminor at 00060458. The image ships it non-zero, initialised to 0x00044789, the library's do-nothing stub __null_FPE_rtn (a single RET at FUN_00044789); nothing in the game or the CRT startup path writes it, so unless a program installs its own handler the FP-exception path calls that stub and returns. Two places read it, both by calling through it with one int argument pushed cdecl-style: __FPE_exception_ at 0004be0c (CLIB3S seterrno), which is the generic 'raise an FP exception' entry and forwards the code it was given in EAX; and FUN_0004ee4c in the EMU387 emu387 module, the 80387 emulator's exception raiser, which first copies the 108-byte 387 state block with REP MOVSD and then passes the exception subcode taken from the high byte of the status word, MOVZX EAX,AH. The argument is that exception code, not a pointer.

Pool: crt  [published by CLIB3S module crwd386 as __FPE_handler / ___FPE_handler; both readers are CRT, the game never touches it]

Rebuild note:
This slot belongs to CLIB3S and must not be declared as a definition in src/. Writing the obvious 'void (*__FPE_handler)(int);' in the rebuilt source creates a second, zero-initialised object: the linker then either reports a duplicate against crwd386 or the emulator ends up calling through NULL on the first FP fault, because the original's value is the __null_FPE_rtn stub, not zero. Declare it extern only if it is referenced at all.

=== 00060460 [PLATE]
Callback function pointer for each of AIL's 16 software timer slots.

Written by AIL_internal_register_timer_inner, which stores its caller's callback into the slot it just allocated and sets that slot's state word at 0x604a0 to 1 (allocated, not yet started); a slot is never cleared here, the state word at 0x604a0 is what says whether the slot is live (0 = free, 1 = allocated, 2 = running). Read only by AIL_internal_timer_isr: the tick pass walks all 16 slots, adds the elapsed microseconds to each running slot's accumulator at 0x604e0 and, each time the accumulator reaches that slot's period at 0x60520, increments the slot's pending-call count at 0x60560. The dispatch pass that follows then, for every slot with a non-zero pending count, decrements the count, pushes the slot's user value from 0x605a0 and CALLs through this table, so a callback here is entered with one dword argument and may run more than once per tick. Slot index is the array index; the code carries it as a byte offset (index * 4) throughout, and 0xffffffff is the no-slot sentinel the timer API returns and checks (see AIL_internal_set_timer_user_inner).

The whole bank lies inside the 0x60460..0x61010 data range that AIL_internal_register_state_globals hands to the DPMI page-lock helper at 0x0003cb01 at startup, together with the ISR code range 0x4478c..0x4515e.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_ functions reference it; it is the timer service's own slot bank]

Rebuild note:
This table and its five sibling banks are touched from a hardware interrupt handler and are page-locked as one fixed address span 0x60460..0x61010, not variable by variable. Declaring them as six ordinary statics and letting the compiler place them lets them drift out of that span (or leaves unrelated data inside it), and the lock then covers the wrong pages -- the ISR can fault on swapped-out memory. Their contiguity and order are load-bearing, and the lock range must be derived from the block rather than kept as the original literals.

=== 00060464 [EOL]
interior of the object at 00060460

=== 000604a0 [PLATE]
Allocation and run state of each of AIL's 16 software timer slots: 0 = free, 1 = allocated but stopped, 2 = running.

Zeroed at startup by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults (REP STOSD of 16 dwords) together with its sibling banks at 0x604e0, 0x60520 and 0x60560. AIL_internal_register_timer_inner allocates by scanning this bank for a zero entry and writing 1 into the first one it finds, then storing the caller's callback in the matching slot of data_ail_timer_callback_table; AIL_internal_release_timer_handle_inner writes 0 to free the slot. AIL_internal_start_timer_inner promotes 1 to 2 and AIL_internal_stop_timer_inner demotes 2 to 1, so start and stop are no-ops on a slot that is not in the expected state. AIL_internal_timer_isr reads this bank first on every tick and only accumulates elapsed microseconds into 0x604e0 for slots reading 2; AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor treats any non-zero entry as live and takes the minimum of those slots' periods at 0x60520 to pick the PIT rate, so a merely allocated (state 1) timer still constrains the interrupt rate even while it is stopped.

The slot number is carried throughout as a byte offset (index * 4), never as a plain index: the timer handle the API hands out and takes back is that byte offset, and 0xffffffff is the no-slot sentinel returned when the scan finds nothing free and checked on entry to release, start and stop.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_ functions reference it; it is the timer service's own slot bank]

Rebuild note:
The allocator scans only the first 15 slots -- its loop bound is CMP EAX,0x3c after ADD EAX,0x4, so offset 0x3c (slot 15) is cleared and walked by the ISR but can never be handed out. Writing the obvious loop over all 16 entries gives the rebuild one more usable timer than the original, and this bank must also stay contiguous with its five sibling banks, which are DPMI page-locked as the single fixed span 0x60460..0x61010.

=== 000604dc [EOL]

=== 000604e0 [PLATE]
Per-timer accumulated elapsed time for the 16 AIL timer slots: how much time has piled up on each timer since it last fired.

Zeroed wholesale by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults and AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor (both do REP STOSD of 0x10 dwords from 0x604e0), and zeroed for one slot by AIL_internal_set_timer_period_inner whenever that slot's period at data_ail_timer_period[] (0x60520) is set, so a period change restarts the slot's phase. AIL_internal_timer_isr is the only reader: it walks slot index 0..15 (EDI 0..0x3c step 4), and for every slot whose state word at 0x604a0 equals 2 it adds the per-interrupt interval held at 0x605ee, compares the sum unsigned against that slot's period at 0x60520, and on reaching the period subtracts the period once and increments the slot's pending-trigger count at 0x60560; the sum is stored back here either way. Element index runs 0..15 in parallel with data_ail_timer_callback_table (0x60460), the state array at 0x604a0, the period array at 0x60520 and the pending-count array at 0x60560. Units are whatever 0x605ee and the period array carry (the value passed to AIL_internal_set_timer_period_inner); a slot's value is always strictly below its own period after the ISR has processed it.

Pool: ail  [every reference comes from AIL timer-service code; no game or CRT function touches it]

Rebuild note:
The ISR subtracts the period at most once per interrupt (an if, not a while), so a timer whose period is shorter than the interrupt interval falls behind instead of firing repeatedly; writing the accumulator drain as a while loop changes the tick rate. Setting a timer's period must also zero its accumulator, as AIL_internal_set_timer_period_inner does.

=== 00060520 [PLATE]
Programmed period of each of AIL's 16 software timer slots, in the same units as the current PIT interval at 0x605ee (microseconds by the Miles AIL_set_timer_period contract).

Written only by AIL_internal_set_timer_period_inner, which stores its second argument into the slot named by its first ('MOV dword ptr [EBX + 0x60520],EAX' at 000450c1, EBX being the slot index already scaled to a byte offset), then clears that slot's elapsed accumulator at [EBX + 0x604e0] and calls AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor. AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults zeroes the whole bank at startup with 'MOV EDI,0x60520 / MOV ECX,0x10 / REP STOSD', so a slot that has been registered but never given a period holds 0. Two readers: AIL_internal_timer_isr adds the current PIT interval to each running slot's accumulator and, while the accumulator has reached this slot's period, subtracts the period and increments the slot's pending-call count at [EDI + 0x60560] (unsigned compare, 'CMP EAX,dword ptr [EDI + 0x60520] / JC' at 00044807); and AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor takes the minimum period over every slot whose state word at 0x604a0 is non-zero, starting from 0xffffffff, and reprograms the PIT with it through 0x000448fc when that minimum differs from the interval currently in 0x605ee.

Index is the slot number 0..15, carried through the code as index * 4; the bank is one of six parallel per-slot dword banks 0x40 bytes apart (0x60460 callback, 0x604a0 state, 0x604e0 elapsed accumulator, 0x60520 period, 0x60560 pending-call count, 0x605a0 user value).

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_ timer functions reach it; it is the timer service's own per-slot bank]

Rebuild note:
AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor selects the minimum over slots whose state word is merely non-zero, so a slot that has been registered (state 1) but never given a period contributes its zeroed 0 and drives the PIT programming call with 0. Rewriting the scan as 'for each running timer' (state == 2, the predicate the ISR uses) or skipping zero periods as obviously bogus changes which rate the PIT is programmed at.

=== 00060524 [EOL]
interior of the object at 00060520

=== 00060560 [PLATE]
Pending-expiry count for each of the 16 AIL timer slots: how many times that timer's period has elapsed without its callback having been called yet.

All 16 entries are zeroed by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults (MOV EDI,0x60560; ECX=0x10; REP STOSD). AIL_internal_timer_isr makes two passes over the parallel slot arrays. The first pass walks slot offsets 0x00..0x3c and, for every slot whose status word data at 0x604a0 is 2 (running), adds the elapsed microseconds to that slot's accumulator at 0x604e0; when the accumulator reaches the slot's period at 0x60520 it subtracts one period and increments this counter (00044807-0004481b). The second pass runs only when the ISR lock counter at 0x605f6 is not held; it walks slot offsets 0x00..0x38 and for each slot drains this counter to zero, decrementing it once and calling data_ail_timer_callback_table[slot] with that slot's user value from 0x605a0 on each turn (0004483c-0004485c). A value greater than 1 therefore means expiries piled up while the lock was held or while an earlier callback was still running; they are delivered as a catch-up burst of separate callback calls, not coalesced into one. The slot index runs 0..15 in step with the other timer arrays, but AIL_internal_register_timer_inner only ever hands out 0..14.

Pool: ail  [reached only by AIL_internal_timer_isr and AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults; it is part of the Miles timer service's own slot table.]

Rebuild note:
The array holds 16 entries and the startup code zeroes all 16, but only slots 0..14 are usable: AIL_internal_register_timer_inner scans with CMP EAX,0x3c and the ISR's dispatch pass loops with CMP EDI,0x3c, while only the accumulate pass runs to 0x40. Writing the obvious for (i = 0; i < 16; i++) in the allocator would hand out slot 15, whose pending count the accumulate pass would keep incrementing but whose callback the dispatch pass never reaches -- a registered timer that silently never fires.

=== 000605a0 [PLATE]
Per-slot user value for AIL's 16 software timer slots: the dword the timer service hands back to that slot's callback as its one argument.

Written only by AIL_internal_set_timer_user_inner, which takes the timer handle (the slot's byte offset, index * 4) and the new value, rejects the 0xffffffff no-slot sentinel, and XCHGs the new value in so it can return the previous one. Never cleared at startup: AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults REP STOSDs the four banks at 0x604a0, 0x604e0, 0x60520 and 0x60560 but skips this one, which is harmless because it lives in initialised data with a zero image -- a timer whose user value was never set fires with 0.

Read only by AIL_internal_timer_isr, in the dispatch pass that follows the tick pass: for each slot whose pending-call count at 0x60560 is non-zero it decrements the count, loads this slot's value, pushes it and CALLs through data_ail_timer_callback_table (0x60460). That loop runs slot offsets 0x00 to 0x38 only ('CMP EDI,0x3c / JC'), so elements 0..14 are the ones that ever reach a callback; element 15 belongs to the timer slot the library reserves for its own chained 18.2 Hz system tick, whose expiry the ISR handles directly at 0x6059c without a callback, so that element is dead. The values themselves are opaque -- the service stores and returns them without interpreting them.

Pool: ail  [both references are AIL timer-service functions; it is the timer service's own slot bank, and the game never touches it]

Rebuild note:
The ISR delivers the value both ways: it loads it into EAX and also pushes it, then restores ESP from a saved copy instead of adding to it, so the call works whichever convention the callback was compiled with. Writing the obvious call under Watcom's default register convention passes the value in EAX only, and a stack-based vendor callback then reads whatever was on the stack.

=== 000605e0 [PLATE]
Offset half of the INT 8 (IRQ0) interrupt vector that was in place before AIL installed its own timer ISR. The selector half is the word at 000605e4, and the two are always used together.

Written once, by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults: it asks DOS for the current INT 8 handler (INT 21h AH=35h, which returns ES:EBX), files EBX here and ES at 000605e4 (00044a2e-00044a3a), and then installs AIL_internal_timer_isr on INT 8 with INT 21h AX=2508h. Read on the two paths that give the old handler control again. AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr loads this into EDX and the selector into DS and issues INT 21h AX=2508h (00044a96-00044aa9), restoring the vector at AIL shutdown after the PIT has been put back to 18.2 Hz. AIL_internal_timer_isr reads it on the pass-through path: when the slot-15 pass-through count at 0006059c is non-zero the ISR decrements it, drops the reentrancy count at 000605f2, restores the interrupted SS:ESP from 00061008 / 0006100c, then XCHGs this value into the interrupt frame's return-EIP slot at [EBP+0x28] and the selector at 000605e4 into the CS slot at [EBP+0x2c] (00044887-0004489c), so the ISR's return enters the previous INT 8 handler instead of the interrupted code -- that is how the BIOS timer tick keeps running at 18.2 Hz while the PIT is clocked faster.

The value is a 32-bit offset within the selector at 000605e4, not an address in this program's data or code selector, and under DOS/4G the handler it names normally belongs to the extender. Zero -- the initial value in the image -- means no vector has been saved yet, which is only true before AIL startup runs; nothing ever clears it back to zero.

Pool: ail  [the only three referencing functions, AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults, AIL_internal_timer_isr and AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr, are all pool_ail, and this is part of the 000605e0-000605fc timer state block that AIL startup sets up]

Rebuild note:
The saved vector is an offset plus a selector, not a near pointer. Declaring this dword as a function pointer and restoring the vector with the program's own CS -- the obvious thing in a flat 32-bit rebuild -- points IRQ0 at that offset inside the wrong selector, so the first timer interrupt after AIL shutdown, and every pass-through tick before it, jumps into garbage. The rebuild must carry 000605e4 with it and load it into the segment register, as both AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr and the ISR chain path do.

=== 000605e4 [PLATE]
Selector half of the INT 8 (IRQ0 timer) vector that was installed before the sound library hooked it.

Written once, together with the offset half at 000605e0, by the timer-install path attributed to AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults (00044a2e-00044a34): a DOS get-vector for interrupt 8 returns ES:EBX, the offset goes to 000605e0 and this word takes ES. The store happens immediately before the library installs AIL_internal_timer_isr (00000447a6) as the new interrupt 8 handler via INT 21h/AH=25h at 00044a41.

Read on every tick by AIL_internal_timer_isr (0004488d): the ISR loads 000605e0 into ECX and this word into EAX and XCHGs them into the interrupt frame's saved EIP (EBP+0x28) and saved CS (EBP+0x2c), so the IRET tail-chains into the previous handler instead of returning to the interrupted code. Read again by AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr (00044a9c), which puts it in DS and 000605e0 in EDX and issues INT 21h/AH=25h, AL=8 to put the old vector back.

The value is a 16-bit protected-mode code selector, normally the DOS extender's selector for the previous interrupt 8 owner. Zero means no vector has been saved yet -- the state before the install path has run.

Pool: ail  [only the three Miles timer routines reach it; no game or CRT code refers to it]

=== 000605e6 [PLATE]
Real-mode INT 08h (IRQ0) vector as it stood before the Miles timer ISR was hooked, packed segment-in-high-word, offset-in-low-word.

Written once, by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults at 00044a3b, in the same breath as the protected-mode half of the snapshot: the routine issues DPMI INT 31h AX=0200h with BL=8, gets the real-mode segment in CX and offset in DX, packs them with SHL ECX,0x10 / MOV CX,DX, and stores the pair here while the protected-mode handler goes to data_ail_prev_int8_handler_offset and data_ail_prev_int8_handler_selector. It then installs AIL_internal_timer_isr (000447a6) on INT 08h with INT 21h AH=25h. Zero means the snapshot never ran, which is also the startup value.

Nothing in the image reads this back. AIL_internal_timer_isr chains to the old handler through the protected-mode pair only (it patches the saved CS:EIP on the interrupt frame at EBP+0x28 / EBP+0x2c from 000605e0 and 000605e4), and AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr restores only the protected-mode vector.

Pool: ail  [the sole reference is inside the Miles timer module; no game or CRT code touches it]

Rebuild note:
Write-only in the original. Keep the store, and do not add the symmetric restore that the missing reader invites: AIL never puts the real-mode IRQ0 vector back, and re-writing it at shutdown would step on the vector the DOS extender maintains for its own IRQ0 reflection. Equally, do not let it be folded away as dead -- a rewrite that drops the store should also drop the INT 31h AX=0200h call, and the two belong together.

=== 000605ea [PLATE]
The 8253/8254 channel-0 divisor the sound library last programmed, i.e. the current IRQ0 rate expressed as a divide of the 1.19318 MHz PIT input. Zero means 65536, the power-on 18.2 Hz rate.

Written only by AIL_internal_set_pit_divisor, which stores its argument here in the same breath as programming the chip: CLI, command byte 0x36 to port 0x43 (channel 0, lobyte/hibyte, mode 3, binary), this store, then the low and high halves of the same value out to port 0x40 with the customary JMP $+2 I/O delays. The value therefore always matches what the counter was loaded with. Its callers are 000448fc, which converts a tick period in microseconds into a divisor (period >= 0xd68d us gives 0 = 65536; otherwise divisor = us * 10000 / 8380, 0.838 us being one PIT input tick) and is itself driven by AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor after that routine scans the sixteen timer slots for the shortest requested period and caches it at 000605ee; and AIL_internal_uninstall_timer_isr at 00044a82, which puts the rate back before restoring the previous INT 8 vector from 000605e0 / 000605e4 at shutdown.

Read in one place, AIL_internal_interrupt_divisor_inner, which does nothing but return it. That is the body behind the public API AIL_interrupt_divisor (0003e4d6), the Miles entry point that reports the current timer divisor to the application; on the traced path the returned value is printed as "Result = %u". No game or CRT code reads it.

The value is the divisor as requested, not as truncated by the hardware: only the low 16 bits are clocked into the counter, so a request above 0xffff -- which the conversion in 000448fc can produce for periods in the narrow window just under its 0xd68d threshold -- leaves this variable holding a number the chip is not running at.

Pool: ail  [both referencing functions, AIL_internal_set_pit_divisor and AIL_internal_interrupt_divisor_inner, are pool_ail, and it sits in the 000605e0-000605fc timer block that AIL startup owns]

Rebuild note:
The PIT divisor is a 16-bit quantity, so the obvious declaration is an unsigned short, or a store masked to 0xffff to match what actually reaches port 0x40. Both are wrong: the original stores and returns the full 32-bit argument, and 0 here means 65536, not "unset". Narrowing the variable or normalising the zero changes what AIL_interrupt_divisor reports to the application.

=== 000605ee [PLATE]
Period in microseconds that the 8253 PIT is currently programmed to interrupt at, shared by all 16 AIL timer slots.

AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults sets it to 0xFFFFFFFF at startup, the sentinel for 'no active timer, hardware left at its default rate'. AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor is the only writer afterwards: it scans the 16 slots, takes the unsigned minimum of data_ail_timer_period_us over the slots whose data_ail_timer_state_table entry is non-zero, and when that minimum differs from the value stored here it stores it and calls FUN_000448fc to derive and program a new divisor (the divisor itself lands in data_ail_prev_int8_handler_offset's neighbour at 000605ea). AIL_internal_timer_isr is the reader: it loads this once per interrupt and adds it to data_ail_timer_elapsed_accumulator for every slot in state 2, which is how each slot's own period is honoured at a single hardware rate. Value range is one timer period in microseconds; 0xFFFFFFFF means no slot is allocated.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_timer_isr, AIL_internal_recompute_pit_divisor and AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults touch it; no game or CRT code reaches it]

Rebuild note:
This is unsigned and 0xFFFFFFFF is a sentinel, not -1. Declaring it int and writing the minimum search with a signed comparison makes the seed the smallest value instead of the largest, the minimum never updates, the PIT is never reprogrammed and every AIL timer callback stops firing.

=== 000605f2 [PLATE]
Re-entrancy depth counter for the AIL timer interrupt handler; zero means the handler is not currently running.

AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults clears it to 0 while installing the timer service, alongside the neighbouring 000605ee/000605f6/000605fc scalars. AIL_internal_timer_isr reads it first thing at 000447a6, through CS: because DS is not yet loaded, and if it is above zero it takes the early exit at 000448c5 without touching the timer state at all; otherwise it increments it at 000447ce, right before it saves SS:ESP into 00061008/0006100c and switches to its own stack, and decrements it again on both of its exit paths (00044875 and 000448a9) just before restoring SS:ESP. AIL_internal_get_isr_lock_count_3eeda returns the current value to callers. In practice it only ever holds 0 or 1: nothing outside the handler raises it.

Pool: ail  [only AIL code reaches it; the game never touches the timer service directly]

Rebuild note:
The entry test is a CS-relative read because it happens before the handler loads DS. Plain C reads it through DS and would be testing whatever the interrupted code left in DS, so this test cannot be written as an ordinary access to the global.

=== 000605f6 [PLATE]
Nesting depth of the AIL log/timer lock: how many AIL critical sections are open right now. While it is greater than zero the AIL timer ISR delivers no timer callbacks.

AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults zeroes it at startup (000449ba), together with the rest of the AIL timer state block at 000605ee-000605fc. AIL_internal_log_lock_acquire_3e724 (0004478c) increments it and AIL_internal_log_lock_release_3e731 (00044799) decrements it; those are the bodies behind the five-byte thunks AIL_internal_log_lock_acquire (0003da44) and AIL_internal_log_lock_release (0003da49). Everything in the library that edits timer or handle state brackets itself in that pair -- AIL_set_timer_divisor, the sweeps inside AIL_start_all_timers and AIL_release_all_timers, the timer register/start/stop/release entries, set period / frequency / user, AIL_call_driver, and the sample and sequence handle allocators -- and AIL_internal_log_print_timestamp_prefix takes it around the timestamp it writes to the trace log, which is where the library's name for the lock comes from.

The only reader is AIL_internal_timer_isr. After sending the PIC EOI it tests CMP dword ptr [0x605f6],0 / JG at 0004482e and jumps clear of the whole callback-dispatch pass when the value is positive. Expiries are not lost while it is held: the accumulate pass keeps incrementing data_ail_timer_pending_count, and the first tick after the count returns to zero drains each slot as a catch-up burst of separate callback calls. Zero means no lock held. The value is a depth and legitimately reaches 2 or more, since a bracketed API entry can call another one.

This is not the ISR reentrancy guard. That is the separate dword at 000605f2, which AIL_internal_timer_isr increments on entry and decrements on both exits, and which AIL_internal_get_isr_lock_count_3eeda (00044f42) returns in spite of its name. Nothing outside AIL reaches either counter.

Pool: ail  [all four referencing functions -- AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults, both lock bodies and AIL_internal_timer_isr -- are pool_ail, and this sits inside the ailv3.lib timer state block that AIL startup initialises]

Rebuild note:
It is a nesting counter tested with a signed compare, not a boolean. Writing the lock as a flag that acquire sets and release clears makes the inner release of a nested pair re-enable callback dispatch while the outer critical section is still running, which is the one thing the counter exists to prevent. Declaring it unsigned is the other half of the trap: the ISR's JG lets dispatch proceed when the value is zero or negative, so an unbalanced release leaves a harmless -1, whereas an unsigned count with the obvious `> 0` test turns that same -1 into 0xFFFFFFFF and stalls every AIL timer callback for the rest of the run.

=== 000605fa [PLATE]
The sound library's own data selector, parked where the timer ISR can load it before it has addressability.

Written once by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults at 0004499d (MOV word ptr [0x000605fa],DS), inside the interrupts-disabled block that also zeroes the tick counter at 000605f2, the counter at 000605f6 and sets 000605ee to -1, just before the library installs AIL_internal_timer_isr as the INT 8 (IRQ0) handler. The same routine reads it back into ES at 000449a4 so ES equals DS for the block that follows.

Read twice on every timer tick by AIL_internal_timer_isr (000447be, 000447c6), which loads it into DS and then ES as its first act after saving FS/GS and setting EBP. Both reads use a CS: segment override -- the handler is entered with the interrupted program's DS, so the only selector it can rely on to reach this word is its own CS.

The value is a 16-bit protected-mode data selector supplied by the DOS extender. Zero means the install path has not run yet, in which case the ISR is not hooked either.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults and AIL_internal_timer_isr refer to it; no game or CRT code does]

Rebuild note:
The two ISR reads go through CS:, not DS:, so this word only works because the DOS/4G flat model gives the code and data selectors the same zero base. A rebuilt interrupt handler that reads it as an ordinary C global -- which compiles to a DS-relative access -- would fault or read rubbish on entry, since DS at that point still belongs to the interrupted program. The load has to stay CS-relative (inline assembly or a hand-written handler stub).

=== 000605fc [PLATE]
The IRQ line on which AIL currently has a 16-bit (USE16) interrupt service routine hooked, or -1 when none is hooked.

AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults sets it to -1 at startup (000449ce), in the same run of stores that initialises 000605ee, 000605f2 and 000605f6. AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner, the worker behind public AIL_set_USE16_ISR, tests it first thing at 00044b6f and returns immediately if it is not -1, so only one USE16 ISR can be installed at a time and a second request is skipped silently with no error indication. Once it has allocated the four LDT descriptors and patched the hand-written trampoline at 00044b10, it stores the caller's IRQ number here (00044d3c) and only then saves the previous protected-mode vector into 00060600 (selector) / 00060604 (offset) with INT 31h AX=0204 and installs the stub with AX=0205. AIL_internal_restore_USE16_ISR_inner is the release half: it does nothing unless the IRQ it is given is neither -1 nor different from the value here (00044d85-00044d90), then restores the vector from 00060600/00060604 and writes -1 back (00044db0).

Values are IRQ line numbers 0-15; both halves map them to a vector the same way -- irq+8 for IRQ0-7 on the master 8259, irq+0x68 for IRQ8-15 on the slave. -1 is the only sentinel. The image bytes are zero; the -1 that means "free" is established at runtime by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults, AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner and AIL_internal_restore_USE16_ISR_inner reach it; it is part of the 000605fc/00060600/00060604 state triple those two halves share]

Rebuild note:
The free value is -1 and it is put there at runtime, not by the image, whose bytes here are zero. Declaring the variable without an initialiser and relying on zero -- the obvious thing -- makes AIL_set_USE16_ISR see a value that is not -1, take the early exit and install nothing at all, with no return value to say so: the sound driver's IRQ is simply never hooked. The mirror error is calling AIL_set_USE16_ISR before AIL startup has run, which fails the same silent way.

=== 00060600 [PLATE]
Selector half of the protected-mode interrupt vector that was installed before AIL hooked an IRQ with a USE16 ISR; the offset half is in the next dword.

Written by AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner: after allocating the 16-bit code alias it calls DPMI INT 31h AX=0204 (Get Protected Mode Interrupt Vector) for vector irq+8 (irq+0x68 for IRQ 8 and above) and stores the returned CX here, zero-extended to a dword, and the returned EDX at 00060604. It then installs its own handler with AX=0205. Read once, by AIL_internal_restore_USE16_ISR_inner, which feeds this dword into ECX and 00060604 into EDX for INT 31h AX=0205 (Set Protected Mode Interrupt Vector) to put the original handler back.

The value is a 16-bit protected-mode selector in the low half; the upper half is always zero because the setter masks ECX with 0xffff. There is exactly one of these, so only one USE16 ISR can be hooked at a time: 000605fc holds the hooked IRQ number and acts as the guard, -1 meaning nothing is hooked. The setter refuses to run unless 000605fc is -1, and the restorer refuses unless 000605fc matches the IRQ it was asked to unhook, so this dword is only ever meaningful while 000605fc is not -1. Its zero initial value is never read.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner and AIL_internal_restore_USE16_ISR_inner touch it; it exists solely to save and restore a DPMI vector for the sound library's IRQ hook]

=== 00060604 [PLATE]
Offset half of the protected-mode interrupt vector that was installed on the hooked IRQ before the Miles AIL USE16 ISR stub replaced it; the selector half is in data_ail_prev_use16_isr_handler_selector at 00060600.

AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner writes it once, at the end of its install sequence: it issues INT 31h with EAX=0x204 (DPMI Get Protected Mode Interrupt Vector) on the vector for the requested IRQ, stores the returned CX into 00060600 and the returned EDX here, then installs its own stub with EAX=0x205. AIL_internal_restore_USE16_ISR_inner reads it back, loading ECX from 00060600 and EDX from here into an INT 31h EAX=0x205 call that puts the original handler back, and then marks the hook free by writing -1 to the hooked-IRQ record at 000605fc. Only one IRQ can be hooked at a time: the whole install body is guarded by 000605fc holding -1, and the restore path runs only when the IRQ passed in equals the value recorded there, so this pair always describes that one vector. The value is a segment-relative offset within the selector at 00060600, not a flat address, and nothing in the image dereferences it. Its initial value is zero, which is never read: 000605fc starts as -1 (set by AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults at 000449ce) and only the install path, which writes both halves, can clear that guard.

Pool: ail  [reached only by the two AIL USE16 ISR workers at 00044b65 and 00044d7b, both unique ailv3.lib Function ID matches from ail_code.obj]

=== 00060608 [PLATE]
512-byte private stack the AIL 16-bit (USE16) interrupt service routine stub runs on.

Written only by the stub itself. AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner (00044b65) allocates a fourth LDT descriptor for it with INT 31h AX=0000, sets its base to this address rounded down to a paragraph (0x60600) with AX=0007, its limit to 0xffff with AX=0008 and its access rights from DS with CH=0 so it is a 16-bit data segment (AX=0009), then patches AIL_internal_USE16_ISR_stub_template (00044b10) with that selector as SS (immediate at 00044b24+2) and with 0x208 as SP (immediate at 00044b2b+1) -- the intra-paragraph offset of this array, 8, plus its 512-byte size, so SP starts one past the end and the stack grows down through 00060608..00060807. On each IRQ the stub switches SS:ESP here, builds the synthetic 16-bit IP/CS/FLAGS frame and 16-bit far pointer it RETFs into the driver handler through, and restores the interrupted SS:ESP from BX:ECX before its IRETD. Contents are scratch: no other code reads them, and the array is zero in the image only because it has never been used.

The eight bytes immediately below it are the saved protected-mode vector this hook displaced (00060600 selector, 00060604 offset), and below those the -1/IRQ-index install sentinel at 000605fc that guards the whole install path.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_set_USE16_ISR_inner takes its address, and the only consumer is that routine's own hand-written stub -- a file-static of ail_code.obj]

Rebuild note:
The usable stack is 512 bytes, not the 2552 that the distance to the next referenced address suggests; the 2040 bytes above 00060808 are an inter-object gap nothing touches. Sizing it from that gap and seeding SP at the top of it (as FD2's data audit did, recording the same object as a 2552-byte buffer) would move the initial stack pointer to 00061000 and put the ISR's stack on top of the next AIL object instead of on its own.

=== 00060808 [PLATE]
2,048-byte private stack the AIL 32-bit timer interrupt service routine and the timer callbacks it dispatches run on.

AIL_internal_timer_isr (000447a6) switches onto it on every tick. It saves the interrupted SS into data_ail_timer_isr_saved_ss at 000447d4 and ESP into data_ail_timer_isr_saved_esp at 000447da, loads SS from DS, then does MOV ESP,0x61008 at 000447e6 -- the stack top is the address of data_ail_timer_isr_saved_ss, so the stack grows down through 00061007..00060808. Both exits restore SS:ESP from that pair, at 0004487b and 000448af.

The interrupted register set does not live here: PUSHAD at 000447b4 and PUSH DS/ES/FS/GS at 000447b5..000447b9 happen before the switch, on the interrupted stack. What this array carries is the ISR's own frame and, more importantly, every timer callback it invokes. For each expired timer the dispatch loop pushes the slot's value from data_ail_timer_user_value_table (00044853, landing at 00061004), CALLs through data_ail_timer_callback_table (00044854, whose return address 0x4485a lands at 00061000), then cuts back with MOV ESP,ESI at 0004485a -- so a callback starts with 8 bytes used and the rest of the 2,048 to itself. The two slots the decompiler shows as DAT_00061000 and DAT_00061004 are those two pushes with ESP constant-folded, not globals.

Contents are scratch. Nothing outside the ISR reads them, no instruction anywhere takes this address, and the array is zero in the image only because it has never been used.

The 512-byte stack directly below, data_ail_use16_isr_stack (00060608), is a separate one, belonging to the hand-written USE16 IRQ stub at 00044b10.

Pool: ail  [the only code that touches these bytes is AIL_internal_timer_isr and the callbacks it reaches through the library's own timer table; the whole run 00060608..00061007 is sound-library ISR scratch]

Rebuild note:
The top of this array must be the address of data_ail_timer_isr_saved_ss, because AIL_internal_timer_isr sets its stack pointer with a hard-coded MOV ESP,0x61008. Nothing references the array, its size appears in no instruction, and all 2,048 bytes are zero in the file image, so it reads as dead space or alignment fill and is the obvious thing to drop or shorten. Drop it and the first timer tick pushes over whatever the linker put below that word; shorten it and a timer callback runs off the bottom into data_ail_use16_isr_stack. Declaring the two slots the decompiler shows (DAT_00061000, DAT_00061004) as variables of their own has the same effect.

=== 00061008 [PLATE]
Saved SS of the interrupted context, held across the AIL timer ISR's switch to its own stack.

Written once per interrupt by AIL_internal_timer_isr at 000447d4, in the prologue: it stores SS here and ESP into data_ail_timer_isr_saved_esp (0006100c), then loads SS from DS and sets ESP to 0x61008 so the handler runs on a small private stack that grows downward out of the bytes immediately below this word (the first push, at 00044853, lands on 00061004). Read back by the same function in both exit paths, 0004487b (the path that also decrements the pending-callback count at 0006059c) and 000448af, each doing MOV SS,[0x00061008] followed by MOV ESP,[0x0006100c] to put the interrupted stack back before the IRET-side epilogue. The value is whatever selector the interrupted code was running on; the initial image is zero and it is meaningless until the first timer interrupt. There is exactly one slot, so the handler is not re-entrant with respect to itself -- re-entry is kept out by the in-ISR depth counter at 000605f2 rather than by saving deeper.

Pool: ail  [AIL_internal_timer_isr is the only referencing function and the only pool reaching it is ail.]

Rebuild note:
The ISR's private stack is not a separate named array: the handler sets ESP to the address of this very symbol, so the stack it runs on is the memory directly below it and this word is the stack top. Declaring a stack buffer and a saved-SS word as two independent C objects lets the linker place them apart and the handler then pushes over whatever happens to precede the save slot. This prologue/epilogue has to stay assembly, with the buffer and this word laid out adjacently in that order.

=== 0006100c [PLATE]
Saved ESP of the interrupted context while the AIL timer ISR runs on the library's own stack.

AIL_internal_timer_isr writes it at 000447da, right after storing the interrupted SS into data_ail_timer_isr_saved_ss (00061008) and just before switching SS:ESP to the library's private interrupt stack, whose top is 00061008 (MOV ESP,0x61008 at 000447e6; the first push therefore lands at 00061004 and does not touch the saved SS word). Both exits restore the pair: the chain-to-previous-handler path at 0004487b/00044881 and the plain IRET path at 000448af/000448b5 each reload SS from 00061008 and ESP from here.

The value is a linear stack offset in the interrupted context, meaningful only between entry and exit of one ISR invocation; it is zero until the first timer tick. There is a single slot rather than a stack of them, which is safe only because the ISR's first instruction pair, CMP dword ptr CS:[0x000605f2],0x0 / JA at 000447a6, bails out to the tail before any save when the nesting counter at 000605f2 is non-zero; AIL_internal_init_runtime_defaults clears that counter at 000449b0.

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_timer_isr reaches it, and it exists solely for the sound library's interrupt stack switch]

Rebuild note:
This is a single, unguarded save slot. A rewrite that keeps the SS:ESP save but drops or reorders the re-entrancy test at 000447a6 (or moves the save above it) lets a nested timer interrupt overwrite the outer invocation's saved ESP, and the outer ISR then returns onto a wrong stack. The guard is what makes one slot correct.

=== 00061018 [PLATE]
Pan-position to channel-gain lookup for the digital mixer: 128 unsigned scale factors in 1/128ths, where 0x80 is unity gain.

Static initialised table, never written at run time. AIL_internal_build_sample_volume_tables reads it twice per sample: entry [pan] gives the right-channel scale and entry [0x7f - pan] the left, where pan is the byte-sized position held at sample+0x44 and runs 0..0x7f (0 = hard left, 0x40 = centre, 0x7f = hard right). The two scales are combined with the sample volume (shifted left by 8) to fill the sample's two 0x400-byte per-channel volume tables at sample+0x48 and sample+0x448. Entries 0x00..0x3e hold 2*index (0x00..0x7c); entries 0x3f..0x7f all hold 0x80, so a channel reaches full gain as soon as its index passes the halfway mark and tapers linearly to silence beyond it. AIL_internal_init_clock_globals DPMI-locks this region (address 0x61018, length 0x80) at startup and AIL_internal_dpmi_unlock_dig_mix_416f0 unlocks the same range at shutdown, because the mixer touches it from interrupt context.

Pool: ail  [every reference comes from pool_ail code; no game or CRT code reads it]

Rebuild note:
The table is not 2*index clamped to 0x80. Entry 0x3f holds 0x80 where that formula gives 0x7e, so the centre pan positions 0x3f and 0x40 both yield exactly unity. Emit the 128 bytes literally rather than generating them from a formula.

FUN_00048f90 (00048f90) is entered with an MDI driver and runs one tick of XMIDI playback for every sequence attached to it. === 0006112c [PLATE]
A ready-made XMIDI TIMB chunk describing exactly one timbre, staged for a single AIL_install_timbre request.

The image is "TIMB", a big-endian chunk length of 4, a little-endian entry count of 1, and one timbre entry (patch, bank) whose two bytes start out 0xFF 0xFF. AIL_internal_install_timbre_inner is the only function that touches it: it stores the requested patch at +10 and the requested bank at +11, bumps the pending-request counter at seq+0x14, and then memmoves all 12 bytes into the sequence's timbre-request area at *(seq+8) + 0x100, where the driver picks the request up. Because the block is a single shared scratch template, one request is in flight at a time; each call overwrites the previous patch and bank before the copy. The public entry point is AIL_install_timbre, whose trace line reads "AIL_install_timbre(0x%X,%d,%d)" (handle, bank, patch).

Pool: ail  [only AIL_internal_install_timbre_inner reaches it, and its content is a Miles XMIDI structure]

Rebuild note:
The 4-byte chunk length 00 00 00 04 is big-endian IFF while the entry count 01 00 immediately after it is little-endian; declaring the header as two C integers and assigning 4 and 1 to both produces a different image. The block must also not be declared const -- it lives in the CONST/_DATA image but two of its bytes are written on every install.

=== 00061138 [PLATE]
Non-zero while the AIL wave-synthesizer code range is DPMI page-locked; zero when it is not. Initial image value is 0.

Set to 1 by AIL_internal_dpmi_lock_wave_synth (0004b370), the one-shot lock guard for this region: it returns immediately when the flag is already non-zero, otherwise it calls fdps_dpmi_lock_region(0x0004b370, 0x0004bced) and then stores 1. === 0006113c [PLATE]
The Watcom CRT's 20-entry translation table from DOS error code to C errno value. Element [i] is the errno that DOS error i becomes; 0xff (-1) marks a DOS error with no C equivalent.

Read by exactly one function, __set_errno_dos (0004bd4a), the shared error path of the DOS file primitives. That function first records the raw DOS code through __set_doserrno (0004be05). If its argument is 0x100 or more it takes the high byte as the errno directly and never touches this table. Otherwise, when _osmajor (00060457) is 3 or more, it folds three codes into the table's range before subscripting: 0x50 file-already-exists becomes index 14, anything from 0x22 up becomes index 19, and 0x20/0x21 sharing and lock violations become index 5. Every code is then clamped by CMP BL,0x13 / MOV BL,0x13, so the subscript always lies in 0..19 and index 19 doubles as the catch-all. The value fetched is passed straight to __set_errno (0004bdf9) with no test in between, and __set_errno_dos returns -1.

The 20 entries, against WATCOM 10.0a H/errno.h: [0]=0 EZERO, [1]=9 EINVAL (invalid function), [2]=[3]=1 ENOENT (file/path not found), [4]=11 EMFILE (too many open files), [5]=6 EACCES (access denied, also where sharing and lock violations are folded), [6]=4 EBADF (invalid handle), [7]=[8]=[9]=5 ENOMEM (MCB destroyed, insufficient memory, bad block address), [10]=2 E2BIG (invalid environment), [11]=3 ENOEXEC (invalid format), [12]=[13]=-1 (invalid access code, invalid data), [14]=7 EEXIST (the slot DOS 0x50 is remapped onto), [15]=8 EXDEV (invalid drive), [16]=6 EACCES (attempt to remove current directory), [17]=8 EXDEV (not same device), [18]=1 ENOENT (no more files), [19]=-1 (write-protected disk and the whole >=0x22 catch-all).

The table ends at 0006114f, immediately before the CRT's __iob FILE array at 00061150.

Pool: crt  [its only reader is __set_errno_dos, a body of CLIB3S module dosret; nothing else in the image reaches these bytes]

Rebuild note:
The elements must be signed char. __set_errno_dos loads them with a sign-extending fetch (dword at table-3 followed by SAR EAX,0x18), and indices 12, 13 and 19 hold 0xff meaning -1. Declaring the table unsigned char, or building the module with Watcom's -j default-unsigned-char switch, makes errno come back as 255 instead of -1 for every unmapped DOS error, including the catch-all slot every code from 0x22 up is clamped onto.

=== 00061150 [PLATE]
The CRT's table of 20 FILE records (struct __iobuf, 26 bytes each), 0x61150..0x61358.

Records 0..4 are the DOS standard streams and are statically initialised: _handle at +0x10 is 0,1,2,3,4 (stdin, stdout, stderr, stdaux, stdprn) and _flag at +0x0c is non-zero for each. Records 5..19 start all-zero and are the pool __allocfp hands out. __InitFiles walks the table from the base in steps of 0x1a and stops at the first record whose _flag (+0x0c) is zero, giving every preceding record a buffer and chaining it onto the open-file list at 0006a300; before the walk it rewrites the byte at 00061191, the second byte of record 2's _flag, to set stderr's buffering mode bits. __allocfp scans the same table for a free slot, testing 'byte ptr [rec+0xc] & 3' -- a record with neither the read nor the write bit set is free -- and writes the caller's mode into _flag on claiming one; on finding nothing free it falls back to a heap-allocated FILE. L$N_ioexit_docloseall closes streams at exit by index, computing base + index*26, and skips the first five: it treats anything below 0x611d2 (= record 5) as not closable.

Pool: crt  [only __allocfp, __InitFiles and L$N_ioexit_docloseall reach it; the game never touches it, and the module's EXTDEFs name it __iob]

Rebuild note:
The first twelve bytes read as zeros, but this object is initialised data, not _BSS: records 0..4 carry non-zero _flag and _handle values and __InitFiles' loop terminates on the first zero _flag. Declaring it as a plain zeroed 'FILE __iob[20];' makes that loop exit immediately, so stdin/stdout/stderr get no buffers and no entry on the open-file list.

=== 00061358 [PLATE]
The Watcom CRT's next-temporary-filename character, initialised to 'a'.

One byte of initialised data sitting between __iob (the 20-record stream table at 00061150, 26 bytes per record, ending here) and _fmode at 00061359; the three are the _DATA segment of the library object iob.obj, in that order. Its only consumer in the library is tmpfile(), which reads this byte, stores it into the new stream's FILE._tmpfchar at +0x19, increments it and writes it back, stepping 'a' upward so that successive temporary files get distinct names (stdio.h sets TMP_MAX to 26*26*26). FDPS never calls tmpfile(), and tmpfl.obj is not in the image, so nothing here ever loads or stores this byte: it retains its initial value 0x61 for the whole run.

The one instruction that mentions this address, CMP EBX,0x61358 at 0004be64 in __allocfp, is not an access to it. It is the exclusive upper bound of __allocfp's scan over __iob -- &__iob[20] -- which lands on __tmpfnext only because the linker lays the object's data out in that order.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __tmpfnext in iob.obj of Watcom C/C++ 10.0a CLIB3S; only CRT code is anywhere near it and the game never touches it]

Rebuild note:
The only instruction that names 00061358 is __allocfp's loop bound, and it means &__iob[_NFILES], not &__tmpfnext -- the two addresses coincide only because iob.obj declares __iob, __tmpfnext, _fmode in that order. Transcribing it literally as a comparison against &__tmpfnext works only by that accident and breaks the moment the declaration order or _NFILES changes; the scan has to be written against __iob's own extent. __tmpfnext must still be emitted as an initialised 'a', not a zeroed byte, even though this image never reads it.

=== 00061359 [PLATE]
Default file translation mode used by opens that do not state one: O_TEXT (0x100) or O_BINARY (0x200).

Initialised to O_TEXT (0x100) in the data segment and never written anywhere in this image -- there is no WRITE reference to it, so it holds O_TEXT for the whole run. Read at 000424c5 and 000424fc in __open_flags, on the paths where an fopen mode string carried neither 't' nor 'b', and at 000439d1 in sopen, where the caller's flag word carried neither O_TEXT nor O_BINARY. === 00061364 [PLATE]
Number of entries in the CRT's per-handle I/O mode table.

Initialised to 20 (0x14) in _DATA. Read only by __IOMode (0004e626), which does 'if ((unsigned)handle >= __NFiles) return 0' before indexing the dword table that _iomode (000613b8) points at. That table is the 20-entry static array __init_mode at 00061368, whose first five dwords are 1, 2, 2, 3, 2 -- the open modes of the five DOS standard handles (stdin read, stdout write, stderr write, stdaux read+write, stdprn write); handles 0..5 additionally get an isatty probe that sets bits 0x4000 (mode known) and 0x2000 (is a character device). __SetIOMode (0004e67c) writes entries in the same table but never touches this variable.

The comparison is unsigned, so a negative handle arrives as a huge unsigned value and is rejected by the same test.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF at offset +0 of iomode.obj's _DATA in Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S, alongside __init_mode and _iomode; only CRT code reads it.]

=== 00061368 [PLATE]
Default I/O mode flag word for each of the first 20 file handles, one dword per handle, indexed by handle number.

This is the statically allocated table that _iomode (000613b8) points at when the program starts; __NFiles (00061364) holds its element count, 20. The static initialiser covers the five DOS standard handles -- [0]=1 (read) for stdin, [1]=2 (write) for stdout, [2]=2 for stderr, [3]=3 (read|write) for stdaux, [4]=2 for stdprn -- and the remaining 15 slots start zero and are filled in as handles are opened. __SetIOMode(handle, value) writes an entry, always ORing 0x4000 into the value first; sopen and the other open paths reach the table through it. __IOMode(handle) reads an entry back: it returns 0 for a handle at or above __NFiles, and for handles 0..5 it probes the device once -- if bit 0x4000 is clear it sets it, calls isatty(handle), and ORs bit 0x2000 into the entry when the handle is a character device -- then returns the dword. Low bits 0x0001/0x0002 are the read/write permissions the initialiser uses.

Every access goes indirectly through _iomode, never through this symbol: once more than __NFiles handles are needed the grow-iomode path repoints _iomode at a larger heap block and this array stops being the live table.

Pool: crt  [PUBDEF __init_mode at offset 4 of _DATA in CLIB3S iomode.obj, reached only by __IOMode and __SetIOMode from that same object]

=== 000613b8 [PLATE]
Pointer to the CRT's per-file-handle I/O mode table: element `handle` holds the mode flag word for DOS handle `handle`.

Initialised in .object2 to 00061368, the 20-entry (80-byte) default table that sits between __NFiles at 00061364 and this pointer; the first five entries start out _READ, _WRITE, _WRITE, _READ|_WRITE, _WRITE for stdin/stdout/stderr/stdaux/stdprn and the remaining fifteen start zero. Nothing in this image writes the pointer -- __grow_iomode and __init_mode, which would reallocate the table when a program needs more than __NFiles handles, were not linked in -- so the table stays at 00061368 for the life of the process.

Read by __IOMode (0004e626), which returns _iomode[handle] after range-checking handle against __NFiles, and for handles 0-5 lazily probes the handle with isatty (00045ba9) on first use: if bit 0x4000 of the entry is clear it sets 0x4000 (entry now established) and, when isatty reports a character device, also sets 0x2000 (_ISTTY). Written by __SetIOMode (0004e67c), which stores mode|0x4000 into _iomode[handle]. Flag values are the _flag bits from Watcom's stdio.h: 0x0001 _READ, 0x0002 _WRITE, 0x0040 _BINARY, 0x0080 _APPEND, 0x2000 _ISTTY; 0x4000 marks the entry as explicitly established rather than default.

=== 000613bc [PLATE]
Watcom C library umask: the permission bits that sopen removes when it creates a file.

One dword in the CRT's initialised data, published by a data-only object module in CLIB3S.LIB with an initial value of 0. The only reference in the whole program is a read in sopen (0004381a), on the path taken when the plain INT 21h AH=3Dh open failed with DOS error 2 and O_CREAT (0x20) was requested: sopen fetches the varargs permission argument, substitutes S_IREAD|S_IWRITE (0x180) when it is 0, XORs it with this value, and then tests bit 0x80 (S_IWRITE) of the result to choose the DOS file attribute passed in CL to INT 21h AH=3Ch -- set gives _A_NORMAL (0), clear gives _A_RDONLY (1). Only umask() writes this variable, and umask() is not linked into FDPS.LE, so it holds 0 for the entire run and the XOR is a no-op. The bits are the S_I* permission bits; umask() ANDs its argument with 0x180 before storing, so only S_IREAD (0x100) and S_IWRITE (0x80) can ever be set.

Pool: crt  [reached only by sopen, and both the referencing code bytes and the 4-byte zero-initialised data module carrying the PUBDEF __umaskval are present verbatim in Watcom 10.0a's CLIB3S.LIB]

Rebuild note:
sopen applies the mask with XOR (permission ^ __umaskval), not the POSIX-conventional permission &= ~__umaskval. The two agree only while the mask is a subset of the permission word; writing the conventional form -- which is what anyone reimplementing sopen would write -- silently diverges as soon as a bit is set here that is clear in permission, because XOR sets it instead of leaving it alone. It is unobservable in the original only because umask() is never linked and the value stays 0.

=== 000613c0 [PLATE]
Non-zero while the near heap is allowed to grow; zero once growth has been switched off.

Loaded with 1, so growth is enabled from startup. _heapenable (0004e69b) is the only writer: it reads the current value into EAX, stores its int argument here, and returns the old value, which is the whole body of the function. Both readers sit in the near-heap growth path and treat it as a pure boolean, testing it with CMP dword ptr [0x000613c0],0x0: FUN_00044201 returns 0 immediately when it is clear (it only goes on to consult _curbrk when it is set), and __ExpandDGROUP (000442d0) makes the same test after its call to FUN_00044201 and likewise returns 0. A clear flag therefore makes near-heap allocation fail rather than ask the extender to enlarge DGROUP; no value other than zero/non-zero is distinguished.

Pool: crt  [only CLIB3S near-heap code touches it, and the library that supplies _heapenable publishes __heap_enabled alongside it]

Rebuild note:
The definition must carry the initialiser: int __heap_enabled = 1;. Writing plain `int __heap_enabled;` puts it in BSS at 0, which the readers take as growth-disabled, so every near-heap allocation past the initial DGROUP quietly fails instead of growing.

=== 000613c4 [PLATE]
Watcom C library heap-growth increment: the minimum number of bytes by which the near heap is expanded when it has to grow.

The image initialises it to 16 (the value that ships in the library's amblksiz.obj), and __CommonInit at 00054dbc overwrites it with 0x8000 (32 KB) during startup, so its operative value for the whole run is 32768. FUN_0004442b, the near-heap grow routine, reads it at 00044472: having computed the requested size plus 0x3c bytes of block overhead, it raises that amount to _amblksiz when it is smaller and then clears bit 0 (AND BL,0xfe) to keep the brk request even, so the heap is enlarged in 32 KB steps rather than one allocation at a time. __cenvarg saves the current value at 00056062, forces it to 16 for the duration of the command-line/environment buffer allocation so that buffer is not padded out to 32 KB, and restores the saved value on both the failure path (000560a5) and the success path (000560b7). The value is a plain byte count with no sentinel; only the two writers above ever change it, and the game never touches it.

Pool: crt  [only pool_crt code references it, and it is a PUBDEF of the Watcom library object amblksiz.obj, whose four initial bytes are byte-identical to this anchor's]

Rebuild note:
The initialised bytes here say 16, but startup overwrites them with 0x8000 before any allocation happens. A rebuild that keeps the image's 16 -- for instance by treating __CommonInit at 00054dbc as a do-nothing stub, which is all it is besides this one store -- gets a heap that grows 16 bytes at a time, turning ordinary allocation into a storm of DPMI expand calls.

=== 000613c8 [PLATE]
The emulated 8087 control word -- rounding control, precision control and exception masks of the software FPU -- and the first field of the emulator's state frame that starts at this address.

Written by the FLDCW arm of the emulator dispatcher FUN_0004ec3c (0004f109 stores the instruction's operand word here, then tests bits 8-9 against 0x300 and takes a separate path when precision control is 11b), and wholesale by the FLDENV and FRSTOR arms (0004f0fc, 0004f4e7: REP MOVSD of 7 dwords from the user's memory operand, the 28-byte 32-bit protected-mode environment image). === 000613cc [PLATE]
The emulated x87 status word of the Watcom software FPU: TOP, the condition codes and the exception flags, held as the +4 dword slot of the emulator's 32-bit FSTENV-format state image that begins at 000613c8 with L$N_emu387_control_word.

FUN_0004ec3c, the emulated-instruction interpreter, is the only code that reaches it, and it never forms the address directly -- it loads the image base once with LEA EBP,[0x613c8] (0004eca2, 0004ed2d) and works through DS:[EBP+0x4]. Bits 0x3800 are TOP, the index of the current stack top: read and shifted right by 11 at 0004eca8, 0004ed3a and 0004f4e9, then scaled by ten (LEA EDI,[EDI+EDI*0x4]; ADD EDI,EDI) to address one of the eight 10-byte slots of L$N_emu387_register_stack at 000613e4. Every push or pop rewrites the field with AND word ptr DS:[EBP+0x4],0xc7ff followed by OR of a word taken from L$N_emu387_stack_ring (0004e83a), the table that maps a TOP value and a delta to the next TOP; the same arms then retag the register through L$1_emu387_tag_field_masks at [EBP+0x8]. Bits 0x4000/0x0400/0x0200/0x0100 are the condition codes C3/C2/C1/C0: 0005029f-000502b0 clears exactly those four with AND DX,0xb8ff and ORs in a byte from L$N_emu387_fprem_quotient_cc_bits (0004e8de). FSTSW returns it as a word at 0004f544. The whole image, this slot included, is overwritten wholesale by MOV ECX,0x7 / REP MOVSD from the user's buffer at 0004f0fc and 0004f4e7 (FLDENV/FRSTOR) and copied back out at 0004f150 and 0004f524 (FSTENV/FSAVE, seven dwords of environment then eight registers in TOP order).

Only the low 16 bits are maintained; the high half is the reserved half of the 32-bit environment image and is read only incidentally, by the three dword-wide loads of TOP that mask it away.

=== 000613d0 [PLATE]
The emulated x87 tag word of the Watcom 80387 emulator: two bits per physical register saying whether that stack slot is Valid (00), Zero (01), Special (10) or Empty (11). Third slot of the emulator's 28-byte 386 protected-mode environment image, which starts at 000613c8 with the control word and continues at 000613cc with the status word; only the low 16 bits of each slot are maintained.

Maintained by the push and pop paths of the emulator dispatcher FUN_0004ec3c. Both index L$1_emu387_tag_field_masks (0004e88a) by physical slot number times ten -- the same TOP*10 index that addresses the 10-byte register slots at 000613e4 -- and take the clear mask from entry+0 and the set-Empty mask from entry+8: AND word ptr DS:[EBP+0x8],BX alone marks the slot Valid on a push (0004f0af, 0004f27d, 0004f429, 0004f470, 0004f678, 0004f731, 0004f868, 0004ff14, 0004ff64 and others), AND followed by OR word ptr DS:[EBP+0x8],BX marks it Empty on a pop (0004fb9e, 0004fee8, 0004ff94, 0004ffdf, 0005005b, 000500b3, 000500fe, 00050149, 00050194, 000501fa). FNINIT writes 0xffff here (0004fe3d, all eight registers Empty) beside 0x33f into the control word and 0 into the status word. FLDENV and FRSTOR overwrite it wholesale from the user's memory operand and FSTENV and FSAVE read it back (MOV ECX,0x7 / REP MOVSD at 0004f0e7, 0004f145, 0004f4d2, 0004f519); the SIGFPE shim at 0004ee5b saves the whole 0x6c-byte image.

The slot is 4 bytes wide although only 2 carry meaning: the frame is the hardware's 32-bit environment image, whose fields are dword-spaced. 000613d4..000613e3 are the image's instruction pointer, opcode/selector and operand pointer/selector fields, which this emulator only copies and never inspects.

Pool: crt  [the only code that reaches it is the 80x87 emulator dispatcher at 0004ec3c, matched byte-exact to EMU387.LIB module emu387; no game or AIL reference exists]

=== 000613e4 [PLATE]
The emulated 8087 register stack: eight 80-bit extended-precision registers, ten bytes each, held at offset 0x1c of the emulator state frame that begins at L$N_emu387_control_word (000613c8).

Only FUN_0004ec3c, the Watcom 80x87 emulator's ESC-opcode interpreter, touches it. It loads the frame base once per entry (LEA EBP,[0x613c8] at 0004eca2 and 0004ed2d), takes the stack top from bits 11-13 of the status word at 000613cc (AND 0x3800 / SHR 0xb at 0004ecac and 0004f4ed), multiplies it by ten (LEA EDI,[EDI+EDI*0x4] / ADD EDI,EDI) and addresses ST(0) as EBP + that offset + 0x1c -- so a register number is carried around as a byte offset, and L$N_emu387_stack_ring (0004e83a) is the precomputed ring of the eight offsets 0,10,...,70 that a walk uses to step to the next register and wrap. Within a slot the layout is the 80-bit format: significand low dword at +0, significand high dword at +4, sign and biased exponent word at +8, sign in the top bit of the byte at +9. FLD1 writes 0 / 0x80000000 / 0x3fff (0004fbfe-0004fc0d), FCHS XORs the byte at +9 with 0x80 (0004f8e0) and FABS ANDs it with 0x7f (0004f8ed). FLD and FST of a memory operand move a slot as three dwords at +0, +4 and +6 -- overlapping, ten bytes -- and FXCH exchanges the same three pieces (0004f88c). FSAVE (0004f4d8) writes the 28-byte environment image with REP MOVSD ECX=7 and then eight slots of MOVSD/MOVSD/MOVSW in ST order, stepping through the ring; FRSTOR (0004f519) is its mirror. Every arm that writes a register also updates the tag word at 000613d0 through the masks in L$1_emu387_tag_field_masks (0004e88a), and that tag word, not the bytes here, is what says whether a slot holds a value: the array ships zeroed and FINIT rewrites the control, status and tag words rather than the register bytes. The array runs 000613e4..00061433 and ends exactly where the ten-byte scratch operand L$N_emu387_source_operand (00061434) begins.

Pool: crt  [the only code that reaches it is the 80x87 emulator interpreter at 0004ec3c, an EMU387.LIB module-emu387 file-static; no game or AIL code refers to it]

Rebuild note:
A slot is exactly ten bytes, and the emulator converts a register number into a byte offset by multiplying by ten. Transcribing the +0/+4/+8 accesses as a struct of two dwords and a word -- the obvious reading -- gives a 12-byte record under default alignment, which desynchronises the index arithmetic, the ring table of offsets at 0004e83a and the FSAVE/FRSTOR image the emulator has to reproduce. The element must be ten packed bytes.
