=== 00061e50 [PLATE]
String literal "StBoard.cel": the name of the CEL that holds the title menu's background board, looked up in MISC.VFS every time the attract cycle re-enters the title menu.

Read-only in the C sense but not in the runtime sense, and reached from exactly one call site. fdps_title_screen, at the top of its title-menu loop, does MOV EAX,0x61e50 / PUSH EAX / MOV EAX,0x60128 ("MISC.VFS") / PUSH EAX / CALL fdps_vfs_load_entry at 0002a59d-0002a5a9 and keeps the loaded block in [EBP-0x30]. That block is the board cel: each menu frame clears the 64000-byte offscreen buffer and calls fdps_cel_blit_sprite(board, 0, buffer, 0x140, 0, 0, 0, 0) -- frame 0, full screen at the origin -- before the four selection cels from "StSel.cel" (00061e44) are drawn over it at x=0x77, y=0x48+i*0x11, and the palette comes from "StBoard.pal" (00061e5c). The three literals are loaded together at the top of the loop and the buffers are freed together when the menu loop ends, so the whole cycle repeats on the next attract pass.

The lookup path writes to this literal. fdps_vfs_load_entry passes it to fdps_vfs_load_file, which passes it to fdps_vfs_find_entry, and that function calls strupr(name) on the caller's pointer inside its scan loop (CALL 0x000435f3 at 000399e0) before strcmp against the raw 13-byte name field of each directory record. The image's initial bytes are the mixed-case "StBoard.cel"; after the first title-menu pass these twelve bytes hold "STBOARD.CEL" permanently, which is what makes the comparison against the archive's upper-case entry name succeed.

Extent: 00061e50-00061e5b, eleven characters plus the terminator. Watcom 10.0a 4-aligns each literal in this CONST run, and 12 is already a multiple of 4, so there is no fill after it and next_anchor 00061e5c is the next literal.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a wcc386-pooled literal image in the CONST run of .object2, reached only as an inline argument from pool fdps code -- not a global the game declared]

Rebuild note:
Ghidra's object here is the 14-byte string s_ndStBoard.cel_00061e4e, because the string analyser started two bytes early on the "nd" alignment fill that follows "StSel.cel"; the call decompiles as fdps_vfs_load_entry(s_MISC_VFS_00060128, s_ndStBoard_cel_00061e4e + 2). Copying that text asks the archive for an entry that does not exist and the title menu aborts through fdps_vfs_load_entry's exit(1) path. Separately, this literal must sit in writable storage: fdps_vfs_find_entry upper-cases it in place, so declaring it const char * (or letting a modern toolchain put string literals in a read-only section) either fails to compile or faults on the first title-menu frame.

=== 00061f58 [PLATE]
String literal "Incom.wav": the name of the cash-register sound effect played when a village transaction actually moves money.

=== 00062258 [PLATE]
The pooled string literal "LX", the two-character signature of a 32-bit linear-executable (LX) driver image, plus its NUL terminator.

Nothing writes it; it is read-only literal data at the head of the contiguous Miles AIL literal block in .object2, immediately before the AIL log timestamp format at 0006225c and ahead of "AIL_DEBUG", "AIL_SYS_DEBUG", "3.02" and "AIL_startup()". Both passes of the AIL driver-image loader compare against it, and one pooled copy serves both call sites. AIL_internal_lx_image_size@0003cbc1 (the sizing pass) and FUN_0003ccf8@0003ccf8 (the load-and-relocate pass) each seed a 4-byte stack buffer with the two-space image at 0003c97c / 0003c980, call AIL_internal_read_block@0003c984 to pull the 2-byte magic from the driver file at the header offset stored at file offset 0x3c, and then strcmp that buffer against these bytes. A non-zero result is rejection: the sizing pass returns 0 for required memory and the loading pass returns a null image base, so a file that is not an LX module is refused before its 0xac-byte header, 0x18-byte object-table records and fixup page table are parsed. The pre-seeded spaces mean a read that delivers nothing still compares unequal and the file is refused rather than accepted by accident. Only "LX" is accepted; a plain LE module such as the game's own FDPS.LE would not match.

Pool: binary_artifact  [an image of a source-level string literal that the compiler laid down in the CONST literal pool and that Watcom shared between the two call sites; the source declares no global here, and naming.md forbids giving a string literal a data_ail_ name merely because the code that reads it is AIL's. In the rebuilt source it reappears as the literal written inline in each strcmp call.]

=== 00062277 [PLATE]
The pooled string literal " " -- one space and its terminator -- printed by the Miles AIL debug log to blank out the timestamp column.

Read-only; nothing writes it. Every reference is fprintf(DAT_00069e7c, " "), where DAT_00069e7c is the log stream, and every one sits in the same loop: a counter is zeroed, the loop prints this space while the counter is below 0x0e, so fourteen spaces go out in a row. That is the alternative arm of the log preamble. The other arm prints the literal at 0006225c, "[%.02u:%.02u:%.02u.%.02u] ", which renders to exactly fourteen characters, so the two arms produce the same column width and the rest of the line stays aligned whether or not the entry carries a timestamp. AIL_internal_log_print_timestamp_prefix shows both arms in one function (timestamp at 0003d6b3, space loop at 0003d6cd, the JMP at 0003d6c7 skipping the loop when the timestamp was printed); the other 53 referencing functions -- AIL_set_preference, AIL_call_driver, AIL_API_read_INI, AIL_install_driver, the whole sample and sequence API surface -- each carry an inlined copy of the same preamble, which is why a two-byte literal collects 60 references. Immediately after the space loop the preamble runs a second loop from 1 that prints the one-character literal at 00062279 (byte 0xFA, the middle dot in CP437), the call-nesting indent.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a string literal wcc386 pooled into the CONST run of .object2, not a declared global; only pool ail code reaches it, so the text belongs to the sound library, but in rebuilt source it is the " " written inline in the log preamble and carries no symbol of its own]

=== 00062279 [PLATE]
The pooled string literal "\xfa" -- one character, the CP437 middle dot, and its terminator -- printed by the Miles AIL debug log as one indent mark per enclosing AIL call.

Read-only; nothing writes it. Every reference is fprintf(DAT_00069e7c, "\xfa"), where DAT_00069e7c is the log stream AIL_startup opened from the AIL_DEBUG path, and every one sits in the same loop: a counter that starts at 1 prints this character while it is below DAT_00069e6c, so the number of characters emitted is DAT_00069e6c - 1. DAT_00069e6c is the log's call-nesting depth -- each public entry point increments it on the way in (0003d94d in AIL_set_preference, 0003f6d7 in AIL_sample_volume) -- so a top-level call prints none and each level of nesting adds one, stepping the line right.

The loop is the second half of the log-line preamble; the first half fills the timestamp column, either with the literal at 0006225c, "[%.02u:%.02u:%.02u.%.02u] ", when the depth is 1, or with fourteen copies of the space at 00062277 when it is deeper, both of which are fourteen characters wide. AIL_internal_log_print_timestamp_prefix holds the shared copy that runs for the call line (space loop at 0003d6cd, this loop at 0003d6ee, returning 1 so the caller then prints its own "AIL_xxx(...)" text). The return line is not shared: each of the 53 other referencing entry points -- the sample, sequence, timbre, driver, timer and callback API surface, with AIL_API_read_INI carrying seven copies for its seven exits -- has an inlined duplicate of the same two loops in front of its result format, which is why a two-byte literal collects 60 references.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a string literal wcc386 pooled into the CONST run of .object2, not a declared global; only pool ail code reaches it, so the text belongs to the sound library, but in rebuilt source it is the character written inline in the log preamble and carries no symbol of its own]

=== 00062293 [PLATE]
The pooled string literal "w+t": the fopen mode that creates or truncates a file and opens it for update in text mode, with CR/LF translation.

Nothing writes it -- it is read-only literal-pool data in .object2, inside the Miles AIL literal slab that also holds "AIL_DEBUG", "AIL_SYS_DEBUG" at 00062285, the "3.02" version string and the 80-dash log separator at 00062297. It has exactly one use: AIL_startup opens the library's usage-script debug log with fopen(<AIL_DEBUG path>, "w+t") and keeps the stream in 00069e7c, having just set the flag at 00069e84 when the AIL_SYS_DEBUG variable is also present; the banner line, the start time and the separator are then written into that stream, and every later AIL log line goes to it. A NULL result leaves 00069e7c zero and AIL_startup simply skips the logging path, so the game runs with no log when AIL_DEBUG is unset or the file cannot be created.

The 'w' truncates any log from a previous run rather than appending, the '+' asks for read/write access the logger never actually reads back, and the explicit 't' makes __open_flags select text mode without consulting _fmode.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a compiler-emitted string literal image, not a global the source ever declared; naming.md forbids giving a string literal a data_ail_ name. The object it was emitted from is the vendor's ail_code.obj, so in the rebuild it comes back inside ailv3.lib -- it is the "w+t" written inline in the library's own fopen call and appears nowhere in the game's sources.]

=== 00063378 [PLATE]
The NUL-terminated string "fmt ", the RIFF chunk id of a WAVE format chunk.

Read-only, never written. Its only reference is at 00047b10 in AIL_internal_wav_chunk_dispatch, the routine that applies an in-memory WAV image to a sample handle. That function starts at wav_image+0x0c -- the first chunk header after the RIFF/size/WAVE preamble -- and loops: strnicmp(chunk_id, "fmt ", 4) at 00047b16, and on a mismatch advances to chunk + 8 + size + (size & 1), the RIFF word-alignment rule, and compares again (JMP back to 00047b0e). On a match ESI points at the "fmt " chunk header and the function reads the format fields relative to it: nChannels at ESI+0x0a, nSamplesPerSec at ESI+0x0c and wBitsPerSample at ESI+0x16. Those two chosen fields select the Miles format constant passed to AIL_set_sample_type at 00047b93 -- 1 channel/8 bits gives type 0 sign 0, 2/8 gives type 2 sign 0, 1/16 gives type 1 sign 1, 2/16 gives type 3 sign 1, i.e. DIG_F_MONO_8 / DIG_F_STEREO_8 / DIG_F_MONO_16 / DIG_F_STEREO_16 with DIG_PCM_SIGN set only for the 16-bit cases -- and any other combination leaves the sample type untouched. The sample rate then goes to AIL_set_sample_playback_rate. The same loop runs a second time from 00047baf against the sibling literal "data" at 0006337d to find the audio payload. The compare is length 4, exactly the four characters of a RIFF chunk id, so the terminator in the fifth byte takes no part and is only there because the compiler emitted a C string literal. The compare is also case insensitive, so "FMT " would be accepted. The chunk walk has no end-of-image bound, so a WAV image with no "fmt " chunk runs off the end of the buffer.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a literal image the compiler emitted for a source-level "fmt " inside the Miles sound library's WAV parser, not a named library global; the same treatment its neighbours binary_artifact_string_literal_ini_keyword_irq_63146 and s_Creative_00063382 already have]

=== 00063594 [PLATE]
The literal "TIMB", the XMIDI chunk identifier for a sequence's timbre list.

Read only, once, by AIL_internal_init_sequence_inner (0004a0f0), the body behind the public AIL_init_sequence (000407cf). After AIL_internal_xmidi_find_chunk (00048240) has located the requested FORM XMID, that function clears the three chunk-pointer fields of the sequence handle (S+8, S+0xc, S+0x10) and walks the FORM's chunk list from FORM+0xc to the end given by the FORM's big-endian length, stepping by each chunk's own big-endian length plus its 8-byte header. At every cursor it runs three unconditional length-4 compares in turn: against this literal at 0004a199, against "RBRN" at 0006359c (0004a1b4) and against "EVNT" at 000635a4 (0004a1cf). A zero result here stores the cursor in S+8, the pointer to the TIMB chunk; the compares are not chained with else, so the last matching chunk of each kind in the list wins. A sequence with no EVNT chunk (S+0x10 still zero after the walk) is rejected: the function copies "Invalid XMIDI sequence\n" from 0006357c into the AIL error-string buffer at 00069ef0 and returns 0. A missing TIMB chunk is not an error -- S+8 simply stays NULL and the timbre-installation step is skipped.

When S+8 is non-NULL, 0x200 bytes starting at the TIMB chunk header are copied into the timbre staging buffer at 0006a0fc, so the chunk's 8-byte IFF header lands at 0006a0fc and the timbre count that opens the chunk body lands at 0006a104. Each timbre is then handed to the loaded MIDI driver through the descriptor callback at drv+0x1a4, and entries the driver refuses are compacted out of the staging buffer and the count decremented.

All four bytes are compared and the comparison is case-sensitive; the chunk ids in the file are raw four-character IFF tags followed immediately by a big-endian length, with no terminator of their own. Never written; it lives in the read-only CONST image at 00060000-0006392f, in the same literal block as the Miles XMIDI diagnostics.

The compare is case-sensitive and covers exactly 4 bytes, so the fifth byte -- the literal's terminator -- never takes part in it. Never written; it lives in the read-only CONST image at 00060000-0006392f, in the same literal block as the Miles diagnostic strings.

=== 000636bc [PLATE]

=== 000636cc [PLATE]
The literal ".com", the first executable extension spawnve appends to a program name given without one.

Read only, at one site in spawnve (000556a9). When _splitpath2 reports the extension field of the path empty, spawnve takes strlen of the path built by _makepath, keeps the address of its terminator, and at 000558b8-000558c0 copies these five bytes over it with MOVSD+MOVSB -- an inlined strcpy, terminator included -- then calls L$2_spve_build_cmdline_and_spawn. If that comes back with errno == ENOENT (1) it overwrites the same five bytes with ".exe" from 000636d1 and retries; if that is ENOENT too it writes ".bat" from 000636c7 and, when file_exists confirms the file, runs it through the COMSPEC shell (getenv("COMSPEC"), default "COMMAND", switch built by __Slash_C) instead of spawning it directly. So the search order is .com, then .exe, then .bat, and only ENOENT continues to the next extension -- any other errno ends the search. The .com attempt is gated by a frame flag that this build sets to 0 at 000556be and never sets again, so it is always made. A path that arrived with an extension skips all of this: an extension equal to ".bat" under stricmp goes straight to the shell path, anything else is spawned as given.

The byte at 000636d0 is this literal's terminator, not a variable of its own. Four extension literals lie end to end here in the read-only CONST image at 00060000-0006392f: ".\\" at 000636c4 (the directory spawnve substitutes when the path has neither drive nor directory), ".bat" at 000636c7, this ".com", and ".exe" at 000636d1.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a string literal the compiler pooled into CONST inside the Watcom CRT spawnve object; in source it is the ".com" written inline in the strcpy, not a named global]

=== 000636ec [PLATE]
The four bytes 69 6e 66 00 -- the C string "inf", the text the Watcom float formatters print for an infinite double.

Nothing writes it; one instruction reads it. __Nan_Inf (00055a20) masks the high word of the double with 0x7ff0 and, when it equals 0x7ff0, has an IEEE-754 special value: it emits '-' (0x2d) first if the sign bit is set, then ORs the mantissa word groups together with the top word masked to 0x0f to see whether the fraction is zero. Zero fraction means an infinity and 00055a82 loads this address as a dword (MOV EDX,dword ptr [0x000636ec]); a non-zero fraction takes the other branch at 00055a8a and loads the "nan" literal at 000636f0 instead. Either way 00055a90 stores the dword straight into the caller's buffer (MOV dword ptr [EAX],EDX) and __Nan_Inf returns 1, so exactly four bytes -- three characters and the terminator -- land in the output. The two callers are the CLIB3S float formatters _FtoS (000551f3) and __cvt, which bail out through __Nan_Inf before any digit generation, so this is what reaches a %f / %e / %g conversion of an infinity. The text is fixed and lower case; there is no variable part and no sentinel.

The object is exactly four bytes because it is read as one dword, and it is dword-aligned: the preceding literal "COMMAND" (000636e2) ends at 000636e9 and the two zero bytes at 000636ea-000636eb are alignment padding, not part of either string. It sits in the CONST block of .object2 immediately before its twin "nan" (000636f0), the pair the nan_inf module owns.

Pool: binary_artifact  [a compiler-emitted string-literal image in the Watcom CRT's CONST block, not a declared library variable; the only code that names it is CRT __Nan_Inf]

=== 000636f0 [PLATE]
The lowercase 4-byte "nan" text, NUL terminator included, that __Nan_Inf emits for a not-a-number.

Read by exactly one instruction, at 00055a8a inside __Nan_Inf (00055a20). That function tests the double's exponent field for the all-ones pattern (AND EAX,0x7ff0 / CMP AX,0x7ff0) and returns 0 if it is an ordinary value; otherwise it writes '-' into the caller's buffer when the sign bit is set, ORs the four mantissa words together, and branches: mantissa non-zero loads this dword, mantissa zero loads L$N_nan_inf_inf_text at 000636ec. Either way the selected dword is stored with a single MOV dword ptr [EAX],EDX, so the trailing 00 goes into the buffer as part of the copy and is what terminates the formatted text. === 00063740 [PLATE]
Watcom C library character-classification table: one flag byte per character, indexed by (unsigned char)(c + 1) so that slot 0 belongs to EOF.

Read-only; nothing writes it at run time -- the initialiser in .object2 is the whole story. Every ctype.h macro reads it: __scnf and scan_white test _SPACE (0x02) to skip leading whitespace before a conversion, L$N_scnf_scan_int, FUN_0004d692 and FUN_0004d960 do the same before scanning an integer, string or float, L$1_scnf_parse_spec and FUN_0004d960 test _DIGIT (0x20) to accumulate the field width and the digits of a floating-point literal, and the sound library's INI reader (AIL_internal_API_read_INI_inner, AIL_internal_read_INI_parse_int) tests _SPACE to trim keys and values.

Entries for 0x80-0xff are all zero: no byte of the high half is printable, punctuation or a letter as far as this table is concerned.

Pool: crt  [_IsTable is a PUBDEF of the linked Watcom C library; the AIL INI parser reaching it is a visitor using isspace(), not an owner.]

Rebuild note:
_IsTable is supplied by the linked Watcom library -- declare it by including <ctype.h> and never emit a definition of it, or the rebuilt object collides with (or silently shadows) the library's copy. Its 0x80-0xff entries are all zero, so isprint/ispunct/isalpha are false for every Big5 byte; substituting a locale-aware table would change how the INI reader and the scanf family treat Chinese text.

=== 00063844 [PLATE]
Cumulative days before the first of each month in a common (non-leap) year: __diyr[m] is the number of days from 1 January to the first of month m, m running 0..12, so the entries are 0,31,59,90,120,151,181,212,243,273,304,334,365.

Read-only table in the Watcom CRT time module; the same object defines the leap-year twin __dilyr immediately after it at 0006385e. Nothing writes it at run time. mktime adds __diyr[month] when it folds a broken-down time into a day count, month being the remainder of the tm_mon normalisation by 12. __brktime takes the table's address as its working base, replaces it with __dilyr when the year is a leap year, and then walks it to find which month a day-of-year falls in. calc_yday and __isindst read the neighbouring pair __diyr[m] and __diyr[m+1]: the first is the day-of-year of the first of month m, the difference is the number of days in month m; both switch to __dilyr in the leap branch. Element 12 (365) exists only to close that difference for December. In calc_yday and __isindst the compiler fetches an entry as the high half of the dword at __diyr-2 followed by SAR 16, which is why 00063842 shows up as a referenced address -- the two bytes below the table are read into a register and shifted out unused.

Pool: crt  [reached only by mktime, __brktime, calc_yday and __isindst, and it matches PUBDEF __diyr at offset 0 of the time-utility object in CLIB3S.LIB / CLIB3R.LIB of Watcom 10.0a]

Rebuild note:
The table has 13 entries, not 12. calc_yday and __isindst compute the length of month m as __diyr[m+1] - __diyr[m], so writing the obvious twelve-month "days before month" table makes the December case read __dilyr[0] (0) and return a negative month length.

=== 0006385e [PLATE]
Days elapsed in a LEAP year before the first of each month: {0,31,60,91,121,152,182,213,244,274,305,335,366}, thirteen signed 16-bit entries. Read-only; nothing writes it.

Every reader first calls __leapyear (000523e5) on the year and picks this table when it returns non-zero, or __diyr at 00063844 -- the identical table for a common year, ending in 365 -- when it returns zero. mktime (00051e77) puts the chosen row base in EBP and adds MOVSX word ptr [EBP + tm_mon*2] into the running day count. __brktime (0005235f) keeps the row base in a stack slot, walks the month index upward while the remaining day-of-year is still at or past the next entry to recover tm_mon, then subtracts entry[tm_mon] to get tm_mday. calc_yday (0005244d) and __isindst (000525bf) take entry[m+1] - entry[m] to get the length of month m when resolving a daylight-saving rule.

Index range is 0..12: entries 0..11 are January..December, and entry 12 is 366, the length of the leap year -- it terminates __brktime's month search and supplies December's length to the differencing readers.

The readers reach element i with the Watcom idiom 'load the dword based at table-2 + 2*i, then SAR 0x10'; that is why 0006385c appears as an address in calc_yday and __isindst. It is a fabricated base, not an object -- the word it names is the last entry of __diyr.

Rebuild note:
The table is thirteen entries, not twelve. __brktime's month search and the entry[m+1]-entry[m] differencing in calc_yday and __isindst all read entry 12, so writing the obvious twelve-element month table reads off the end for December.

=== 00063878 [PLATE]

Compiler-emitted floating-point literal in CONST; nothing writes it. Read once, by _Scale10V at 00055b4d, which does FCOMP of the working value against it to detect a positive overflow. === 00063898 [PLATE]
The C library's HUGE_VAL: a const double holding IEEE-754 positive infinity (0x7FF0000000000000).

Never written at run time -- it is initialised data published by the library object hugeval.obj and only ever read. Its one reader in this image is strtod at 00055443, on the decimal-exponent overflow path: after calling __set_ERANGE at 0004bde5 to set errno, strtod tests the accumulated sign flag and either loads this value with FLD, negates it with FCHS and returns -HUGE_VAL, or copies the two dwords straight into the return slot for +HUGE_VAL. The underflow path returns zero instead and does not touch this. Watcom 10.0a's math.h declares it `extern const double __near _HugeValue` and defines HUGE_VAL as this symbol, so every HUGE_VAL in library or game source resolves here; nothing in the game reads it.

Pool: crt  [Byte-exact match with the CONST segment of hugeval.obj in Watcom 10.0a CLIB3S.LIB, whose sole PUBDEF is _HugeValue; the only referencing function is the CRT's strtod.]

=== 000638a0 [PLATE]
The power-of-ten ladder _Scale10V walks to build 10^n as a double.

Eight read-only 10-byte rows, each a 16-bit decimal exponent followed by an unaligned 8-byte double holding ten raised to it: 216/1e216, 108/1e108, 54/1e54, 27/1e27, 14/1e14, 8/1e8, 4/1e4 and 1/1e1. Nothing writes it. Its only user is _Scale10V (00055b40), the decimal-exponent scaler behind the printf/scanf floating-point conversions. It takes the absolute base at 00055b89, sets an accumulator to 1.0 at 00055bce, and walks the rows greedily: while the remaining exponent is at least the row's exponent it multiplies the accumulator by the row's value and subtracts that exponent (00055bdc-00055beb). A row is used at most once and then left behind by ADD EAX,0xa at 00055bf8 -- except the last: at 00055bf2 the walk tests whether the current row's exponent is 1 and, if it is, repeats that row instead of advancing, so the 1e1 row is what consumes the leftover 1 to 3 and is what stops the walk from running past the end of the table. The exponent argument's sign is re-examined afterwards at 00055bfd and decides whether the assembled 10^|n| is multiplied into or divided out of the value; an infinite result is clamped against the literals at 00063878 and 00063880 to the finite extremes at 00063888 and 00063890.

The anchors at 000638a2, 000638aa and 000638ac are the first two rows' fields, not variables of their own.

Pool: crt  [reached only by _Scale10V, which FD2 matched byte-for-byte to scale.obj in MATH387S; a file-static of that module with no public symbol, hence the L$N_ form]

Rebuild note:
The walk has no element count and no terminator but the exponent 1 in the final row. Writing the obvious for (i = 0; i < 8; i++) over the rows, or writing the ladder by halving (216/108/54/27/13/6/3/1, which looks right and is not what is here -- the real rows go 27, 14, 8, 4, 1), changes which rows are visited and therefore the order of the multiplications and the last-bit rounding of every conversion. If the last row's exponent is ever not exactly 1, the loop runs off the end of the table.

=== 000638f0 [PLATE]
The C runtime's XI startup-initialiser table: eight 6-byte Watcom rt_init records {uchar rtn_type; uchar priority; void (*rtn)(void);} covering 000638f0..0006391f.

Built by wlink concatenating the XI-segment contribution of each CLIB3S object that needs startup work, between the empty marker segments XIB and XIE; __InitRtns (0004dfa6) carries those two bounds as the immediates 0x638f0 and 0x63920. The cstrt386 startup body at 00043310 calls __InitRtns once with a priority ceiling of 0xff, before __CMain. The walker rescans the whole table on every pass: it skips any record whose rtn_type byte is already 2, keeps the last record whose priority is <= the running minimum (CMP byte ptr [ESI+1],AL / JA, so an equal priority replaces the incumbent), calls dword[rec+2] through EAX, then stores 2 into that record's rtn_type so it never runs twice; a null routine pointer is marked done without being called. Records in address order, priority then routine: 0x20 __delay_init (00043c82), 0x01 __sys_init_387_emulator via the thunk at 0003d50a, 0x02 __chk8087 (00044749), 0x20 the printf float-format hook installer at 0004cfc8, 0x20 __Init_Argv (0004e040), 0x20 FUN_00043612 (saves SS into L$N_stk386_saved_ss), 0x20 __InitFiles (00054893), 0x20 __setenvp (00054f86). Low priorities run first, so 1 and 2 are the FPU/emulator level and 0x20 the general library level; the resulting run order is 0003d50a, 00044749, then the 0x20 group in reverse address order __setenvp, __InitFiles, FUN_00043612, __Init_Argv, 0004cfc8, __delay_init. The matching shutdown table (YI) is the two records at 00063920..0006392b, walked by __FiniRtns.

Pool: crt  [the 48 bytes arrive as XI-segment data inside CLIB3S library objects and only __InitRtns ever reads them; no game and no AIL code touches the table]

Rebuild note:
Among records of equal priority __InitRtns runs the LAST one first, not the first, and it restarts the scan after every call; a rebuild that hand-writes this table and walks it forward reverses the whole 0x20 group, starting the C runtime with __delay_init instead of __setenvp. The table is also written at run time (MOV byte ptr [EBX],0x2 marks each record done), so it must not be declared const.

=== 00063920 [PLATE]
The C runtime's YI shutdown table: two 6-byte Watcom rt_init records {uchar rtn_type; uchar priority; void (*rtn)(void);} covering 00063920..0006392b, the mirror of the XI startup table at L$N_inirt386_xi_init_table.

Built by wlink concatenating the YI-segment contribution of each CLIB3S object that needs shutdown work, between the empty marker segments YIB and YIE; __FiniRtns (0004dff1) carries those two bounds as the immediates 0x63920 and 0x6392c. It is run on every exit path: the cstrt386 termination tail at 0004354d, reached from __exit (00043527) and from _exit, calls __FiniRtns(0, 0xff), and __do_exit_with_msg__ (0004352a) calls it before the INT 21h AH=4Ch terminate. The walker rescans the whole table on every pass: it skips any record whose rtn_type byte is already 2, keeps the last record whose priority is >= the running maximum in AL (0004e012 CMP AL,byte ptr [ESI+1] / JA, so an equal priority replaces the incumbent), loads dword[rec+2] and calls it, then stores 2 into that record's rtn_type so it never runs twice, and stops when a whole pass selects nothing. AL is reset from the first argument at the top of each pass, so the argument pair is a priority window, and both callers pass the full 0..0xff range. The two records in address order, priority then routine: 0x01 the 80x87 emulator shutdown through the tail-jump wrapper at 0003d50f (__sys_fini_387_emulator, 00044629), and 0x20 __full_io_exit (00054908), which flushes and closes the stdio streams. Because the highest priority runs first, the run order is __full_io_exit then the emulator shutdown -- the reverse of the order their XI counterparts run in at startup, which is the point of the priority byte.

Pool: crt  [the twelve bytes arrive as YI-segment data inside CLIB3S library objects, both routines behind them are CLIB3S shutdown entry points, and only __FiniRtns ever reads them; no game and no AIL code touches the table]

Rebuild note:
__FiniRtns selects the HIGHEST priority, not the lowest as __InitRtns does, and among equal priorities it runs the LAST record first, restarting its scan after every call. A rebuild that walks this table forward, or reuses the init walker's comparison, closes the stdio streams after tearing down the 80x87 emulator instead of before. The table is also written at run time (0004e036 stamps rtn_type to 2, which is the only thing that stops the second exit path from re-running a routine), so it must not be declared const.

=== 00063930 [PLATE]
Tile row (y) of every tile queued in the movement-range flood fill's frontier: two double-buffered 400-entry queues, [0] and [1], laid out back to back.

Written and read only by fdps_move_grid_flood_fill_range. It seeds slot 0 of buffer 0 with the start tile's row, then runs one wave per step: it walks the current buffer entry by entry, and every neighbour it accepts is appended to the other buffer, its row here and its column in the parallel array at 00063c50, with the two 16-bit entry counts kept on the caller's stack. The buffer selector flips by XOR 1 at the end of each wave and the fill ends when the other buffer's count comes back zero. Element values are tile rows, 0..height-1 of the movement grid reached through data_fdps_battle_move_grid_ptr; a stored zero is also the guard that stops the 'up' neighbour from stepping off the top edge. Index arithmetic is buffer*400 + entry, so buffer 0 occupies the first 400 bytes and buffer 1 the second; the 400-entry capacity is never checked.

This array is the first object in _BSS, so the address 00063930 also appears in L$1_cstrt386_start_body as the base of the startup REP STOSD that zeroes 00063930..0006a3bc. That is the segment start, not a use of this variable; the flood fill always writes an entry before reading it.

Pool: fdps  [the only code that uses the contents is fdps_move_grid_flood_fill_range; the CRT merely zeroes it as part of _BSS]

=== 00063c50 [PLATE]
Tile columns of the movement-range flood fill's frontier queue, double-buffered: 2 buffers of 400 one-byte entries, entry i of buffer b at [b * 400 + i].

Written and read only by fdps_move_grid_flood_fill_range, which pairs it entry for entry with the row queue at 00063930 (same 2 x 400 layout) and keeps the two 16-bit entry counts and the 0/1 buffer selector on its own stack. The fill seeds entry 0 of buffer 0 with the start tile's column, then processes one wave at a time: it walks the current buffer's entries, and every neighbour it accepts (up, right, down, left, in that order) has its column appended to the other buffer -- the same column for the vertical steps, column+1 for the step right, column-1 for the step left. The selector is flipped at the end of each wave and the fill stops when a wave leaves the other buffer's count at zero. Values are tile columns in the range 0..width-1 of the movement grid at data_fdps_battle_move_grid_ptr; only entries below the current buffer's count are live, and stale entries above it are never read. Nothing outside the fill reads this array -- the fill's result is the accumulated cost byte written back into the movement grid, which fdps_move_path_trace later walks.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_move_grid_flood_fill_range, a battle-logic function, and paired with the game's own movement grid]

=== 00063f74 [PLATE]
Unit index of the target that the map-AI's physical-attack scorer picked for the actor it is currently thinking for.

fdps_map_actor_score_best_attack is the only writer. Each time a (tile, target) candidate beats the running best it stores the target's unit index here, together with the score tier in DAT_00063f78 and the tile it would attack from in DAT_00063f80 (x) and DAT_00063f84 (y). The value indexes the 0x50-byte records based at data_fdps_map_unit_array_ptr, so it runs over 0 .. data_fdps_map_unit_count - 1; there is no sentinel for "no target", the scorer simply leaves the previous contents alone when it finds nothing (its early return with no weapon equipped does exactly that), and the fresh-or-stale question is answered by DAT_00063f78 instead, which every scorer zeroes on entry.

fdps_map_actor_take_best_action reads it as soon as the three scorers have run and hands it to fdps_get_unit_record, unconditionally and before any branch, to precompute the physical damage estimate (actor's attack stat at record +0x48 minus this target's defence stat at +0x4a). fdps_map_actor_move_and_attack reads it right through the melee exchange: fdps_map_cursor_move_to_unit, fdps_unit_face_target in both directions, fdps_check_can_counter_attack, fdps_battle_show_combat_gauges, fdps_unit_attack_target for the strike and the counter, fdps_combat_play_attack_exchange, fdps_run_death_scripts and finally fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up, which credits the experience to this unit. fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell also reads it, on the spell path, where it is not the spell's target -- see the rebuild note.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by game code: the four map-AI routines fdps_map_actor_score_best_attack, fdps_map_actor_take_best_action, fdps_map_actor_move_and_attack and fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell; no CRT or AIL reference]

Rebuild note:
fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell passes this physical-attack target index to fdps_run_death_scripts, where it is neither the caster nor the unit whose death script is running; on the fdps_map_actor_behavior_step path the physical scorer has not run for this actor at all, so the value is left over from an earlier one. It reaches the chapter event handler table at 000601c4 as the unit index of opcode-2 records. Passing the caster there instead -- the obvious reading, and what the matching call in FUN_00027c20 does -- hands chapter event handlers a different unit.

=== 00063f78 [PLATE]
Score of the best physical attack the map-AI actor being weighed could make this turn, as a coarse tier.

fdps_map_actor_score_best_attack owns it: it stores 0 here on entry, then each time a candidate (tile, target) pair beats the running best -- higher tier, or an equal tier with a better damage estimate -- it stores the winning tier here and the rest of the choice in the sibling globals data_fdps_battle_ai_best_physical_target_idx (00063f74) and the attack tile at 00063f80 (x) / 00063f84 (y). Only three values are ever written: 0 when no candidate was worth anything (also the value left behind by the early return taken when the actor has no weapon equipped), 8 for a blow whose damage estimate exceeds 2, and 0x12 (18) for a lethal blow, one whose estimate is strictly greater than the target's current HP. The damage estimate itself stays in a local and is never published here.

Two readers. fdps_map_actor_take_best_action compares it against the spell score at 00063f88 and the item score at 00063f8c: with all three below 6 the actor does nothing and the caller falls back to a move, otherwise a chain of five explicit comparisons picks attack, spell or item. fdps_map_actor_behavior_step reads it alone in AI modes 10 and 11: below 6 the actor tries to close on an opponent and rests if it cannot, at 6 or above it moves in and attacks. So 6 is the single threshold that separates "nothing worth doing" (tier 0) from "act" (tier 8 or 0x12).

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it -- fdps_map_actor_score_best_attack, fdps_map_actor_take_best_action and fdps_map_actor_behavior_step, all pool fdps]

Rebuild note:
What goes in here is the coarse tier 0 / 8 / 0x12, not the damage estimate the search actually ranks on. Storing the estimate -- the obvious thing, since it is the number being compared -- puts a figure in the tens or hundreds on the same scale as the spell and item scores of 8 and 18, and the AI then attacks in preference to everything else it could do.

=== 00063f84 [PLATE]

=== 00063f88 [PLATE]
The AI's best spell score for the actor currently being evaluated.

fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell owns this variable: it zeroes it on entry (0001342c) and raises it at 00013614 each time a (spell, tile) pair beats the running best, storing the winning spell id in DAT_00063f90 and the target tile in DAT_00063f9c (x) / DAT_00063fa0 (y). Nothing else writes it.

Readers treat it as one of the three action scores. fdps_map_actor_take_best_action compares it against data_fdps_battle_ai_best_physical_score (00063f78) and the item score (00063f8c) to pick which action the actor performs, and bails out entirely when all three are below 6. fdps_map_actor_behavior_step (00010693), fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase (000129f6) and fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell (00013cd9) all gate on the same threshold: 6 or above means the spell is worth casting, below 6 means do nothing. === 00063f8c [PLATE]
Best score the map-AI item search found for the acting unit, and the validity signal for the aim tile and bag slot that go with it.

fdps_map_actor_score_best_item (00013040) owns it: it clears the score to 0 on entry, then walks every filled bag slot of the acting unit and every aim tile that item could reach, calling fdps_score_targets_for_item for each combination. A total strictly greater than the score standing here replaces it, and the same branch writes the aim tile x to DAT_00063f98, the aim tile y to DAT_00063f94 and the bag slot to data_fdps_map_ai_best_item_bag_slot -- those three are never cleared on entry, so they only mean anything when this score says an item was actually found. The score is the sum of per-target weights from fdps_score_targets_for_item: 3 or 8 per hurt target for an HP restorative, tripled for an AI behaviour byte with bit 0x80 set, and 8 or 18 per target for a straight-line damage item; 0 for every item the AI does not weigh.

fdps_map_actor_behavior_step (000105e9) and fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase (000129ff) read it straight after the search and treat 6 or more, signed, as worth acting on. fdps_map_actor_take_best_action (00012c10) does the three-way choice: if this score, DAT_00063f88 and data_fdps_battle_ai_best_physical_score are all below 6 the unit does nothing; otherwise the largest of the three wins and decides whether the unit attacks, casts or uses an item.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it -- the AI scorer that writes it and the three turn-logic functions that read it]

=== 00063f90 [PLATE]
Spell id the map-AI picked for the actor it is currently deciding for.

The 0x12 threshold tested at 00012d1b splits the table: below 0x12 the record's first word is a plain HP figure and is comparable with a physical damage estimate; at 0x12 and above it is 0 or a negative attack-power multiplier and the actor's AI preference bit decides instead.

Unlike the score at 00063f88, which fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell zeroes on entry, this global is never cleared: after a search that found nothing it still holds the previous actor's choice. That is harmless because every reader gates on the score reaching 6 first, and a score that high implies this was written on the same run.

=== 00063f94 [PLATE]

fdps_map_actor_score_best_item writes it at 00013272 as one of four globals it updates together whenever an (item, aim tile) candidate beats the running best: the score at 00063f8c, the aim tile x at 00063f98, this aim tile y, and the chosen bag slot in data_fdps_map_ai_best_item_bag_slot at 00063f7c. === 00063f98 [PLATE]

Written by fdps_map_actor_score_best_item whenever a candidate beats the running best score: that block stores the score to 00063f8c, this x, the matching tile y to 00063f94 and the bag slot to 00063f7c. === 00063f9c [PLATE]
Map tile x (column) of the tile the map AI has chosen to centre its best spell on this turn.

Written only by fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell, which walks every spell the actor knows and can afford, floods the spell's cast range out of the actor's tile, and for each reachable candidate tile scores the units the spell would catch there. Whenever a (spell, tile) pair beats the running best it publishes the whole choice at once: the score to 00063f88, the spell id to 00063f90, and the tile here (x) and at 00063fa0 (y). Only the score at 00063f88 is cleared when a scoring pass starts; this variable keeps whatever the previous actor decided down every early-return path (actor knows no spells, spell-sealed, no affordable spell). That stale tile is unreachable because the score gate is applied by fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell and again by fdps_map_actor_behavior_step and fdps_map_actor_take_best_action before any spell is cast.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell and fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell, both game AI routines; it is one of the four spell-decision globals at 0x63f88-0x63fa0]

=== 00063fa0 [PLATE]
Map tile y (row) that the map AI decided to centre its chosen spell on.

Written only by fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell. That routine flood-fills the spell's cast range out of the actor's own tile, collects the reachable tiles as (x, y) byte pairs, and for each candidate tile asks fdps_collect_targets_in_range which units the spell would catch there and fdps_score_targets_for_spell what that is worth. Whenever a (spell, tile) pair beats the running best -- higher score, or an equal score with a larger spell damage figure -- it publishes the whole choice at once: the score to data_fdps_battle_ai_best_spell_score (00063f88), the spell id to 00063f90, the tile x to 00063f9c and the tile row here. Values are tile coordinates on the current battle map, taken from the marked-tile list, so they run over 0..map height and are never negative. This is the aim point of the area of effect, not a tile the actor moves to and not the tile of any one victim; the actor stays where it is and only the cursor travels.

Read only by fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell, and only after that routine's gate on data_fdps_battle_ai_best_spell_score >= 6 has passed: first with 00063f9c as the centre passed to fdps_collect_targets_in_range together with the spell record's reach byte +0x04, giving the unit list the cast is applied to, then as this value * 0x18 -- the tile size in pixels -- in fdps_map_cursor_move_to, which animates the map cursor onto the tile while the area overlay is showing. The scorer clears only the score on entry, so on any path that finds nothing this variable still holds the tile the previous actor chose; the score gate is what keeps a stale tile from ever being cast on.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the two game AI routines fdps_map_actor_score_best_spell and fdps_map_actor_cast_chosen_spell; no CRT or AIL reference]

=== 00063fb0 [PLATE]
Index of the unit the status window is showing, latched for the village-mode drawing path.

Written by fdps_draw_unit_status_panel, at its very first instruction, with the unit_index it was called with -- but only when data_fdps_village_mode_flag (00060070) is non-zero. Read by fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input under the same guard, where it overwrites that function's own unit_index argument for the rest of the frame. The value is then used as the entry index into the sprite table behind data_fdps_cel_sprite_cache_ptr (00060138), stride 0x30 per unit: entry + facing*0x0c + walk_frame*4 holds an offset relative to 00060138 which becomes the cel pointer for the animated unit sprite in the window.

Outside village mode nothing touches this global: the battle callers (fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window, fdps_unit_item_select_loop at 00025b20) pass the unit record's own sprite-cache byte at record+0x02 as unit_index instead, and both the write and the read are branched over. The range the value runs over is therefore the village roster's unit indices, the same numbering fdps_get_unit_record takes.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_draw_unit_status_panel and fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input reach it; it is game presentation state, no CRT or AIL code sees it]

Rebuild note:
The override is deliberate, not redundant. In village mode fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input discards the unit index its caller passed and uses this global instead, so rewriting the pair to pass the index as a parameter and dropping the global changes which sprite is animated -- including on the calls from 00025b20, which reach the frame loop with the value left behind by the last panel draw.

=== 00063fb4 [PLATE]
Pointer to the 320x200 (64000-byte) offscreen page that holds the village facility screen currently on display.

Written by the five village facility screens -- fdps_village_item_menu, fdps_run_church_screen, fdps_run_bar_shop, fdps_run_weapon_shop and fdps_run_secret_menu. Each does malloc(64000), publishes the result here, keeps its own local copy, blits the screen's backdrop CEL into it with fdps_cel_blit_sprite at pitch 0x140, and on exit frees the page through the local copy without clearing this global, which is therefore left pointing at freed memory between facility screens.

Read only on the town path, chosen by data_fdps_village_mode_flag: fdps_close_status_window memmoves the page into the caller's background buffer before the window close animation and memmoves it back to 0xa0000 afterwards, restoring the town screen; fdps_spell_list_window_wait_input copies it into its per-frame 320x200 frame buffer as the live background. Both also blit the page's inner 0x138 x 0xc0 rectangle from +0x504 (column 4, row 4 at stride 0x140) into a scene scratch buffer that is then freed without being read. On the field/battle path (flag clear) neither function touches this pointer; they composite the live map instead.

Zero at program start -- it lies in _BSS, which the CRT zeroes -- and never written back to zero afterwards.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it: five village screens write it, two game window helpers read it]

Rebuild note:
The page is a plain local in every function that allocates it, and is handed to the other village helpers as an ordinary parameter; only fdps_close_status_window and fdps_spell_list_window_wait_input find it through this global. Rewriting a facility screen with the buffer scoped to a local and the global assignment dropped -- the obvious tidy-up, since the local is what gets freed -- leaves those two window helpers reading a dangling pointer and painting garbage over the town screen.

=== 00063fb8 [PLATE]
Saved copy of data_fdps_ui_play_active_flag while the unit status window is open.

fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window writes it once, immediately after fdps_load_status_cel_image and before any drawing: it copies data_fdps_ui_play_active_flag (00060159) here and then zeroes that flag, which suppresses fdps_draw_cursor_info_panel for as long as the window is up. fdps_close_status_window reads it back into data_fdps_ui_play_active_flag as its very last statement, after the close animation and the screen repaint, so panel drawing resumes only from the caller's next frame. Values are the flag's own: 0 = gameplay panel drawing suppressed, non-zero = active. Nothing else in the image touches this address, so it is meaningful only between one open and its matching close; outside that window it holds the value left by the previous status window, or 0 from the CRT's _BSS clear before the first one.

Pool: fdps  [both referencing functions, fdps_battle_show_unit_status_window and fdps_close_status_window, are pool fdps; no CRT or AIL code reaches it]

=== 00063fbc [PLATE]
Value of the global timer tick counter (00069d64) at the last tick on which fdps_cycle_ui_palette actually rewrote the DAC.

Written and read only by fdps_cycle_ui_palette, which every modal menu, list and window loop calls once per iteration. That function first busy-waits on VGA input status port 0x3da for vertical retrace, then compares this latch against the tick counter 00069d64 that fdps_timer_tick_handler increments: equal means this tick has already been serviced and the function returns without touching the DAC, so the palette animation advances at most once per timer tick however fast the caller's loop spins. When they differ it stores the current tick here and rewrites DAC entries 8..15 from the three colour ramps, then steps data_fdps_ui_palette_cycle_phase. The value carries no meaning of its own -- only whether it equals the current tick -- so any tick number is valid and there is no sentinel. _BSS zeroes it at startup, which matches a tick counter that also starts at zero: the first call before the first timer tick services nothing.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cycle_ui_palette, a game UI routine, reaches it; no CRT or AIL code refers to this address]

Rebuild note:
The retrace wait must stay ahead of this test. Testing the latch first and returning early when the tick has not changed -- the obvious way to write "nothing to do" -- is what a rebuild would naturally do, and it would unpace every menu, list and window loop in the game, because those loops are throttled to the display refresh by the retrace wait that this guard sits behind, not by the guard itself.

=== 00063fc0 [PLATE]
The value of the global frame tick counter (DAT_00069d64) as of the last redraw of the unit status window, latched by fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input.

fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input (000170c0) polls fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat each pass; when no key is pending it compares the live tick at 00069d64 against this latch and does nothing until they differ, so the window repaints exactly once per tick. On a differing tick it calls fdps_cycle_ui_palette, rebuilds the window into scratch buffers, and only at the end of the body (0001750b) copies the current tick in here.

It is also the animation clock for the unit's idle sprite: the frame index is (latch % 16) / 4, remapped 3 -> 1 and clamped at 0, giving the ping-pong sequence 0,1,2,1 over 16 ticks. That index selects a dword from the per-class sprite offset block at data_fdps_cel_sprite_cache_ptr + class * 0x30. Note the frame comes from the value still in here, i.e. the tick of the PREVIOUS repaint, because the latch is not updated until the body finishes.

Zero-initialised by the CRT, which is a harmless starting phase: the first pass always sees a mismatch and repaints.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps code reaches it; it is a file-static of the status-window UI module, sitting with its three sibling tick latches at 00063fbc/00063fc4/00063fc8]

Rebuild note:
The idle-animation frame is derived from this latch BEFORE it is refreshed. Writing the natural `if (tick != last) { last = tick; ... frame = (last % 16) / 4; ... }` uses the new tick and shifts the idle animation one tick out of phase with the original; the original computes the frame from the old value and assigns the new one last.

=== 00063fc4 [PLATE]
Scancode that the previous call to fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat saw in the keyboard latch.

Written and read only by fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat. Each poll reads the raw scancode byte from the latch that fdps_keyboard_isr maintains (0xff when no key is down) and compares it with this variable. On a mismatch the key press is new: data_fdps_input_key_repeat_counter is reset to 0, this variable takes the new code, and the code is returned to the caller unchanged. On a match the key is still held and the repeat timing in data_fdps_input_key_repeat_counter / data_fdps_input_key_repeat_last_tick decides whether the poll yields the code or 0xff. Values are raw AT scancodes zero-extended to a dword; 0xff is stored while no key is down, so the idle state of this variable is 0xff rather than 0.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat, which is application input policy over the game's own keyboard latch; no CRT or AIL code touches it]

=== 00063fc8 [PLATE]
Value of the global timer tick counter (00069d64) at the last tick on which the keyboard auto-repeat filter acted on a held key.

Written and read only by fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat, which modal input loops poll once per frame. When the scancode read through fdps_keyboard_scancode_ptr differs from the previous poll's code in data_fdps_input_key_repeat_prev_scancode the key is new and this latch is left alone. When the code is the same the key is still down, and this latch decides whether the tick has already been serviced: equal to the tick counter that fdps_timer_tick_handler increments means the poll returns 0xff and changes nothing, so data_fdps_input_key_repeat_counter advances at most once per timer tick however fast the caller spins. When they differ the counter is incremented, the returned scancode is suppressed to 0xff unless the counter has reached 5 and is a multiple of 3 -- first repeat on tick 6, further repeats every 3 ticks -- and the current tick is stored here. The value carries no meaning of its own beyond whether it equals the current tick, so every tick number is valid and there is no sentinel. _BSS zeroes it at startup, which matches a tick counter that also starts at zero.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat, a game input routine; no CRT and no AIL code refers to this address]

Rebuild note:
The store belongs only on the held-key path that found the tick had advanced. Hoisting it to the top of the function, or also assigning it on the new-key branch, is the natural tidy-up and shifts the start of the repeat delay by one tick, because the original deliberately compares a newly pressed key's first held poll against a tick left over from an earlier key.

=== 00063fd0 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the class table loaded from PROMAP.DAT, a flat array of 10-byte per-class records.

fdps_load_data_tables writes it once at startup, as one of nine table pointers it fills by calling fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit with a literal filename; the slot stays NULL until then and no reader checks it. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers releases it with free() on shutdown, alongside the neighbouring table pointers at 00063fd4 and 00063fe0. Every read goes through fdps_get_class_record(index), which returns this base + index * 10 with no bounds check. Rows are addressed as the unit record's class byte (+0x20) plus one -- row 0 is a default row whose eight terrain costs are all 1, used by fdps_battle_ai_* callers that want unrestricted movement. Within a record, bytes +0..+7 are the movement cost of each terrain type with 0xff meaning impassable (fdps_move_grid_flood_fill_range consumes exactly those eight), and byte +8 is the class's critical rate in percent (read by fdps_battle_resolve_blow at 00019f80 and by 0001c520). Callers include fdps_battle_move_unit_toward, fdps_battle_unit_turn, fdps_map_cursor_select_loop and the map AI at 000126b0.

Pool: fdps  [all three referencing functions are game code, and the data is a game resource file]

Rebuild note:
The table is indexed by class code PLUS ONE, not by the class code: row 0 is a default all-costs-1 row and the real classes start at row 1. Writing the obvious table[class_id] shifts every class onto its neighbour's terrain costs and critical rate.

=== 00063fd4 [PLATE]
Base pointer of the enemy stat table loaded from EnemyDat.dat, a flat array of 10-byte records.

Read by fdps_get_enemy_record@00018b10, the only accessor, which returns this base plus enemy_index * 10 with no null check and no bounds check -- callers form enemy_index as the unit record's class byte at +0x7 minus 0x3c (FUN_00019f80, FUN_0001c520, FUN_00028460 for units on the map, FUN_000232b0 at deployment). === 00063fd8 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the character base-stat table, the contents of the VFS file FRIAPRDA.DAT.

fdps_load_data_tables fills it at startup by passing this slot as the out-parameter of fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit for "Friaprda.dat"; it is the first of the nine game data-table pointers that function fills at 0x63fd0..0x63ff0. fdps_get_character_base_record is the only reader that indexes it, returning base + char_id * 0x18, where char_id is the character's portrait id running 0..59 over the sixty records; there is no bounds check. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers passes the value to free() during shutdown and does not clear the slot afterwards. Each 24-byte record holds race +0x00, class +0x01, level +0x02, hp_base and mp_base as 16-bit words at the odd offsets +0x03 and +0x05, move +0x07, a four-byte initial spell mask +0x08, the starting item ids from +0x0c with 0xff ending the list, and ap_base +0x12, dp_base +0x14, dx_base +0x16. fdps_roster_add_character reads every one of those fields when it builds a unit record for a newly recruited character, scaling hp_base and mp_base by (level - 1) times the per-class growth figures.

Pool: fdps  [only game functions reference it, and the block it points at is one of the game's own .dat resources loaded through the game VFS]

Rebuild note:
The record is 0x18 bytes with 16-bit hp_base and mp_base at the odd offsets +0x03 and +0x05. Declaring the obvious C struct lets the compiler align those shorts and pushes the stride past 0x18, after which the char_id * 0x18 indexing lands on the wrong record; the struct has to be byte-packed or the fields read through byte offsets.

=== 00063fdc [PLATE]
Base pointer to the character promotion (class-change) table loaded from RankUp.dat.

Written once by fdps_load_data_tables, which passes this slot's address to fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit together with the member name "RankUp.dat"; the loader allocates the file image and stores its address here, so the value is a heap block owned by the game. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers releases it with free() during shutdown, alongside the neighbouring table pointers. The only reader is fdps_get_promotion_record, which returns base + char_id * 0xc: records are 12 bytes, the index is a roster character's base identity byte (unit record byte 0x8, range 0..8), and there is no bounds check in the accessor -- the callers at 0x000345a0, 0x00034c10 and 0x000352c0 guard it themselves. Each 12-byte record is four 3-byte promotion entries; byte 0 of an entry is the resulting form id (written to unit record byte 0x7 and used to build the "Stand%03d.saf" sprite name), byte 1 is the class code (written to unit record byte 0x20), byte 2 is never read. === 00063fe0 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the item-effect table read out of the VFS member ITEM.DAT: 251 records of 23 bytes, indexed by item id 0x00-0xFA.

Written once at startup by fdps_load_data_tables, which passes this slot's address and the filename "Item.dat" to fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit; the pointer stays live until fdps_free_global_resource_buffers hands it to free. The single reader is fdps_get_item_record, which returns base + item_id * 0x17 with no null check and no bounds check, so callers must supply an id already known to be in range. The item id is the same byte stored in a unit record's eight equipment slots at +0x0a and in shop and sell-list entries. Within a record, +0x00 is the item type, +0x01/+0x03/+0x05/+0x07 the ap/hit/dp/ev stat words, +0x0d the use effect, and +0x13 the shop price; only ids 0x00-0xE1 carry content, 0xE2-0xFA are all-zero records.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it -- fdps_load_data_tables, fdps_get_item_record and fdps_free_global_resource_buffers -- and it holds a game-owned .dat table]

Rebuild note:
fdps_get_item_record range-checks nothing, and the game depends on that: item id 0xFF is past the end of the 251 records, and the guide's "BUG item" whose price and effect change from run to run is exactly that read of whatever memory follows the table. Declaring this as an array of a 251-element record type, or adding the obvious id < 251 guard to the accessor, removes a player-visible behaviour.

=== 00063fe4 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the per-class equippable-item-type table loaded from PROEQU.DAT: 36 records of six item type codes each.

fdps_load_data_tables@00018930 writes it once at startup, as one of the nine table pointers it fills by calling fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit with a literal filename ("ProEqu.dat" at 0x61654); the slot is zero until then and no reader checks it for NULL. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers@00018a20 releases it with free() at teardown, between the ITEM.DAT pointer at 00063fe0 and the pointer at 00063ff0, and does not clear the slot afterwards. === 00063fe8 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the spell-learning table loaded from GETMGTAB.DAT, a flat array of 12-byte per-character learn records.

fdps_load_data_tables writes it once at startup as the eighth of the nine table pointers it fills, calling fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit with the filename literal "GetMgTab.dat" and the address of this slot; the loader allocates the buffer, stores the base here and aborts the program if the file is missing, so a non-NULL value means the whole file image is resident. The slot is zero until then and no reader tests it. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers releases it with free() on shutdown, next to the neighbouring table pointers at 00063ff0 and 00063fdc, and does not clear the slot afterwards.

Every read goes through fdps_get_spell_learn_record(learn_index), which returns this base + learn_index * 12 with no bounds check and no sentinel check. learn_index is byte +0x0a of the character's FRILEVUP.DAT growth record, and the value 0xff there means the character learns no spells -- rejecting it is the caller's job. The table holds 60 records. Each record is six 2-byte pairs, (level, spell id), in ascending level order; an unused pair is (0xff, 0xff), which never matches because a unit level never reaches 0xff. fdps_unit_award_exp_and_level_up is the only consumer: on each level gained it walks all six pairs and, for every pair whose level byte equals the unit's new level at unit record +0x21, draws the spell name (text entry spell_id + 0x1be) and calls fdps_set_flag_bit(unit_index, spell_id) to set that spell in the unit's learned-spell mask at unit record +0x1a.

Pool: fdps  [all three referencing functions are game code and the data is a game resource file]

Rebuild note:
The level-up loop grants every one of the six pairs whose level matches, not the first: a character can learn two spells at the same level, and writing the obvious search-and-break drops the second one. The table is also unbounded at the accessor -- fdps_get_spell_learn_record(0xff) computes base + 3060 and returns it happily, so the 0xff "learns no spells" test has to stay in the caller where the original put it.

=== 00063fec [PLATE]

=== 00063ff0 [PLATE]
Base pointer to the spell stat table loaded from MAGICDAT.DAT: 7-byte records indexed by spell id.

fdps_load_data_tables@00018930 writes it once at startup, as one of the nine table pointers it fills by calling fdps_vfs_load_file_or_exit with a literal filename ("MagicDat.dat" at 0006165f); the slot is zero until then and no reader tests it for NULL. fdps_free_global_resource_buffers@00018a20 releases it with free() at teardown, between the ProEqu.dat pointer at 00063fe4 and the GetMgTab.dat pointer at 00063fe8, and does not clear the slot afterwards. === 00064000 [PLATE]
Pointer to the scratch surface holding the four 125x5 fill strips that the combat animation's HP and MP gauges are painted from.

Allocated as malloc(0x9c4) = 2500 bytes at the start of a combat animation by fdps_combat_play_attack_exchange (00018e22) and by fdps_combat_play_spell_on_targets (0001a610), immediately after each loads FigBar.cel from MISC.VFS into the neighbouring pointer at 00064004. Both then compose the surface with four fdps_cel_blit_sprite calls, sprites 4..7 of that cel drawn at destination pitch 0x7d = 125, x 0, y = i * 5 for i = 0..3, so the surface is exactly four 125x5 strips laid one under another, 4 * 625 = 0x9c4 with no slack. Both free it when the animation ends (0001918c, 0001b8f4) and leave the pointer dangling until the next allocation. The only reader is fdps_draw_gauge_fill (00019263), which takes strip gauge_index as this pointer + gauge_index * 0x271 (625 = 125 * 5); gauge_index runs 0..3, where 0/1 are the HP and MP bars of one panel layout and 2/3 those of the mirrored layout, selected by fdps_draw_unit_hp_mp_gauges from unit record byte +0x06. Every consumer runs inside one of the two playback functions, so the pointer is only ever read while the allocation is live; outside a combat animation it holds whatever the last free left behind, and zero before the first one, since it sits in _BSS and nothing else writes it.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by three game functions -- the two combat animation drivers and the gauge painter -- and its contents come from a game VFS resource via fdps_cel_blit_sprite]

=== 00064004 [PLATE]
Pointer to the decoded FIGBAR.CEL sprite sheet holding the HP/MP gauge artwork used while a combat animation is playing.

Written in exactly two places, each at the top of a combat playback sequence: fdps_combat_play_attack_exchange (00018e10) and fdps_combat_play_spell_on_targets (0001a5fe), both from fdps_vfs_load_entry("MISC.VFS", "FigBar.cel"). The sheet carries 8 frames of 145x9. Frames 4..7 are immediately blitted, one per 5-pixel row, into the separate 0x9c4-byte buffer at 00064000 to build the 125x20 bar-fill strip (loops at 00018e3e and 0001a62c, stride 0x7d). Frames 0..3 stay in the sheet and are blitted straight out of it by fdps_draw_unit_hp_mp_gauges (000193a9, 000193cc), which picks frame pair 0/1 for the player-side panel in the upper right and 2/3 for the enemy-side panel in the lower left. Both writers free it again at the end of the sequence (0001917e, 0001b8e6), immediately before freeing 00064000, and neither clears the variable, so between combats it holds a stale non-null pointer; nothing reads it outside the load/free window. Zero before the first combat, since _BSS is cleared at startup.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it: fdps_combat_play_attack_exchange, fdps_combat_play_spell_on_targets and fdps_draw_unit_hp_mp_gauges, all pool fdps]

=== 00064010 [PLATE]
Hit/miss result of the last physical blow resolved on the map. 1 = miss, 0 = hit.

Written only by fdps_unit_resolve_attack_hit, and written twice: the prologue at 0001c53a stores 1 before any dice are rolled, so the default answer is 'miss', and 0001c8d2 stores 0 on the branch taken when rand()%100 < accuracy - evasion, i.e. the moment the blow is known to land. A miss therefore leaves the 1 standing, and the value is valid from the return of that routine until the next blow is resolved. Nothing in FDPS.LE reads it: these two stores are its only references. The same global in the predecessor engine (FD2's data_fd2_battle_last_hit_or_miss_flag) is read by the combat animation to substitute the miss 'whoosh' SFX and to suppress the defender's hit pose; FDPS keeps the writes but has no reader left, so the byte is vestigial engine state rather than something the on-map attack consults. It sits in _BSS, so it is 0 (= hit) before the first attack, which no code can observe.

Pool: fdps  [both references are in named game code and its only writer, fdps_unit_resolve_attack_hit, is pool_fdps; no CRT or AIL code reaches it]

=== 00064014 [PLATE]
Screen positions of the two combatants' HP gauges during the pre-attack gauge animation, as two {x, y} int pairs: pair 0 (elements 0 and 1) is the defender's bar, pair 1 (elements 2 and 3) the attacker's.

Written only by fdps_battle_show_combat_gauges, at the top of every attack it plays: it calls fdps_battle_compute_unit_gauge_position for the defender into pair 0, and for the attacker into pair 1 when fdps_check_can_counter_attack returns exactly 1; otherwise it stores -1 into element 2, the sentinel meaning no counter-attack is coming and the attacker's bar must not be drawn. The coordinates are view pixels, tile * 0x18 minus the view scroll origin plus the offset that keeps the 0x2d-pixel-wide bar off the unit and inside the 320x200 screen, so they may be negative; the 0x18-pixel border of the composite page is added by the reader, not stored here. Read back in the same function to form each bar's destination pointer as page + x + (y + 0x18) * 0x168 + 0x18, and re-tested against -1 before each of the three attacker-bar draws so that bar is skipped for the whole seven-frame run. The address of the array outlives the call: fdps_battle_show_combat_gauges returns it, and FUN_00012e50 hands pair 0 to fdps_unit_attack_target for the attack and pair 1 for the counter, so each blow drains the bar that was placed here. Values persist between attacks; nothing resets them.

Pool: fdps  [the only code that touches it is battle display code the game owns]

Rebuild note:
The array has to stay file-scope, not a local of fdps_battle_show_combat_gauges: the function returns its address and the caller reads pair 1 through that pointer after the call returns. Element 2 == -1 is the whole no-counter-attack signal; zeroing the pair instead draws the attacker's bar at (0,0).
