=== 00069d60 [PLATE]
The AIL (Miles Sound System) sequence handle allocated for MIDI music playback.

Written exactly once, by fdps_audio_init @ 0003052e: after AIL_install_MDI_INI returns a non-NULL MDI driver into data_fdps_audio_bgm_driver_handle (0x69d6c), fdps_audio_init sets the driver-present flag at 0x69d72 and calls AIL_allocate_sequence_handle(driver), storing the opaque handle here. The write is gated on the install having succeeded, so on a machine with no MIDI driver the slot keeps its _BSS zero (NULL) for the whole run.

Nothing reads it. No function in the image calls AIL_init_sequence, AIL_start_sequence, AIL_stop_sequence, AIL_set_sequence_volume or AIL_set_sequence_loop_count, so the sequence is allocated at startup and then left idle; FDPS drives background music from CD audio (see the CD audio globals) rather than through XMIDI. Compare FD2, where the same handle is the argument of every BGM playback call.

It sits in the game's audio state block: the eight sample handles at 0x69d30, this sequence handle at 0x69d60, the DIG driver handle at 0x69d68, the MDI driver handle at 0x69d6c, and the three presence flags at 0x69d70..0x69d72.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_audio_init, game glue over AIL, reaches it; it is game state holding a library handle, not a library global]

Rebuild note:
Nothing reads this global, so the obvious cleanup -- dropping a write-only variable -- would also drop the AIL_allocate_sequence_handle call that fills it. That call has side effects inside the MDI driver (it claims and initialises one of the driver's sequence slots), so both the call and the store must be kept.

=== 00069d64 [PLATE]
Free-running 25 Hz timer tick counter: the number of timer callbacks that have fired since the audio system was started.

fdps_timer_tick_handler is the only writer -- its whole body is INC dword ptr [0x00069d64] followed by a call to rand() -- and it is installed by fdps_audio_timer_install, which registers it with AIL_register_timer and then sets the rate with AIL_set_timer_frequency using the value fdps_audio_init was called with; main and fdps_restart_after_options both pass 0x19, so the counter advances 25 times a second and one tick is 40 ms. It is never cleared or reset: among 156 references exactly one writes, so the value is monotonic for the whole run and wraps only after years of uptime. Its absolute value is meaningless; every reader uses differences.

Roughly fifty game routines read it, all in the same shape -- a frame-paced busy-wait. The caller snapshots the counter into a local, draws a frame (typically fdps_blit_rect), then spins on CMP local,[0x00069d64] / JZ until the value changes and re-snapshots, so one loop iteration equals one tick. fdps_cycle_ui_palette, fdps_unit_status_window_wait_input, fdps_prompt_two_choice, fdps_battle_show_win_fail_window, fdps_combat_play_blow, fdps_combat_play_spell_on_targets, fdps_play_ending_credit_roll, fdps_play_vfs_animation, fdps_saf_play_over_background, fdps_animate_turn_banner and fdps_transition_zoom all pace their animation this way. A second group keeps its snapshot in a global instead of a local so the pacing survives across calls: data_fdps_ui_palette_last_cycle_tick, data_fdps_unit_status_window_last_tick, data_fdps_input_key_repeat_last_tick, data_fdps_scene_tile_anim_last_flip_tick and data_fdps_spell_list_window_last_tick are all snapshots of this counter. fdps_read_scancode_auto_repeat compares it against data_fdps_input_key_repeat_last_tick to admit at most one key event per tick and drive keyboard auto-repeat.

Pool: fdps  [only game code references it; the sole writer, fdps_timer_tick_handler, is game code that AIL merely calls back]

Rebuild note:
An interrupt callback writes this counter while the main thread spins on it, so the wait loops only terminate because the settled flag set compiles with -od and reloads the global every iteration. Declaring it as a plain unsigned int is faithful to the original build, but any object that reads it built with optimisation on -- a unit-test harness, a rebuilt module compiled without -od -- will hoist the load out of the loop and hang. Qualify it volatile in any such build.

=== 00069d68 [PLATE]
The AIL (Miles Sound System) DIG driver handle for digital sound effects.

Written once by fdps_audio_init@000304e0 with the return value of AIL_install_DIG_INI(); the install is optional, and a NULL return leaves data_fdps_audio_sfx_dig_driver_handle NULL and the whole digital-SFX half of the audio system switched off. On a non-NULL install the same function sets the byte flag at 00069d71 to 1 and loops eight times calling AIL_allocate_sample_handle(this handle), filling the eight-entry sample-handle array at 00069d30. Those two -- the flag and the sample handles -- are what the rest of the game reads; the handle itself is consumed only inside fdps_audio_init, and fdps_audio_shutdown@000305a0 tears the stack down through AIL_shutdown without ever passing this handle to an uninstall call. The value is opaque: only NULL versus non-NULL means anything to the game.

Pool: fdps  [game glue over AIL: only fdps_audio_init, a game function, touches it; AIL merely produced the value]

=== 00069d6c [PLATE]
The AIL (Miles Sound System) MDI driver handle for MIDI music.

Written exactly once, by fdps_audio_init@000304e0 at 0003050b, with the return value of AIL_install_MDI_INI(). The install is optional: on a machine with no MIDI driver configured it returns NULL, the slot keeps its _BSS zero, and the whole music half of the audio system stays switched off. On a non-NULL install the same function sets the byte flag at 00069d72 to 1 and calls AIL_allocate_sequence_handle(this handle), storing the result in data_fdps_audio_bgm_sequence_handle at 00069d60.

Those three instructions are the entire life of the value. Nothing outside fdps_audio_init reads it, and fdps_audio_shutdown@000305a0 tears the audio system down through AIL_shutdown without ever passing the handle to an uninstall call. The value is opaque to the game: only NULL versus non-NULL means anything here.

It sits in the game's audio state block, in the same layout as its DIG counterpart: the eight sample handles at 00069d30, the sequence handle at 00069d60, the DIG driver handle at 00069d68, this MDI driver handle at 00069d6c, and the three presence flags at 00069d70..00069d72.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_audio_init, game glue over AIL, reaches it; it is game state holding a library handle, not a library global]

=== 00069d70 [PLATE]
Boolean: whether digital sound effects are switched on.

fdps_audio_init sets it to 1 before probing the Miles drivers, so effects default to on; fdps_options_menu toggles it with XOR 1 as entry 1 of the four-setting menu and picks label id 0x0e when it is set, 0x32 when it is clear. fdps_sfx_play, fdps_audio_start_sample and fdps_audio_start_wav return without playing anything unless both this flag and the DIG-driver-installed flag data at 00069d71 are non-zero, so a player who switches effects off silences every sample and WAV while the CD music, gated separately by data_fdps_audio_bgm_enabled_flag, keeps playing. It is part of the saved settings: fdps_battle_system_submenu stores it at +0x30d4 of the in-battle save record and fdps_load_savegame reads it back, fdps_save_game_screen stores it at +0xa09 of the save-slot record and fdps_load_game_screen reads it back, in both cases immediately after the BGM flag.

Pool: fdps  [only game code reaches it; the Miles library never sees this flag, the game checks it before calling AIL]

=== 00069d71 [PLATE]
Non-zero when the AIL digital-sound (DIG) driver installed successfully, so sound effects can be played.

Written only by fdps_audio_init@000304e0: cleared to 0 before AIL is touched, then set to 1 at 00030546 on the branch where AIL_install_DIG_INI returned a non-NULL handle into data_fdps_audio_sfx_dig_driver_handle (00069d68); that same branch allocates the eight AIL sample handles into data_fdps_audio_sample_handle_table (00069d30). A failed install leaves it 0 for the rest of the run -- nothing else ever writes it, and it is not part of the saved game.

Read as the hardware half of the two-flag gate in front of every sound effect: fdps_sfx_play@000142d0, fdps_audio_start_sample@00030630 and fdps_audio_start_wav@00030a00 each require this flag AND data_fdps_audio_sfx_enabled_flag (00069d70, the player's sound-effects option) to be non-zero, and otherwise return -1 without calling AIL. fdps_sfx_play tests it a second time after bounds-checking the requested sample index. Only 0 and 1 are ever stored; only zero versus non-zero is tested. The music side has the parallel flag at 00069d72, set when AIL_install_MDI_INI succeeds.

Pool: fdps  [all four referencing functions are game code; AIL only supplied the value that decides it]

=== 00069d72 [PLATE]
Boolean: non-zero once the Miles AIL MDI (MIDI/BGM) driver has been installed successfully.

Written only by fdps_audio_init: cleared to 0 at the top of the function together with the digital-driver flag at 00069d71, then set to 1 immediately after AIL_install_MDI_INI returns a non-NULL driver handle (kept at 00069d6c), on the same path that allocates data_fdps_audio_bgm_sequence_handle (00069d60). It stays 0 when the machine has no MIDI music hardware configured in the AIL .INI. Only 0 and 1 are ever stored. In this build nothing reads it -- the code that needs to know whether music can play tests the driver handle at 00069d6c or the sequence handle at 00069d60 instead; the predecessor engine FD2 kept the same flag at 0x53EF0 and did gate BGM playback on it.

Pool: fdps  [written by fdps_audio_init, game code, and it sits among the other data_fdps_audio_* globals in _BSS; it merely records the outcome of an AIL call]

=== 00069d74 [PLATE]
Tick value of data_fdps_timer_tick_counter the last time fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll did any work; the per-tick gate for the CD background-music keep-alive.

Only fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll (00030c50) touches it. On entry it compares this word with the live timer tick at data_fdps_timer_tick_counter and returns immediately when they are equal, so however often the game loops poll the routine its body executes at most once per timer tick. When the tick has advanced, the body bumps data_fdps_audio_cd_repeat_tick_counter (00060170) and, every 0x4b (75) ticks, restarts the selected CD track through fdps_cd_play_track if a track is selected (data_fdps_audio_cd_current_music_index != -1), CD audio is enabled and fdps_cd_audio_is_idle reports playback stopped. The last instruction before returning copies the live tick into this variable, arming the gate for the next tick. Values are raw timer ticks, unsigned and free-running; there is no sentinel - the CRT leaves it at 0, which merely means the first poll after startup is skipped until the timer moves off 0.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cd_music_repeat_poll, a game-loop routine with no library match, reaches it]

=== 00069d80 [PLATE]
Pointer to the chapter's village shop stock table, the SHOP%02d.DAT member of "Field.vfs" held in a malloc'd buffer.

fdps_load_field_chapter_resources writes it on every chapter (re)load: it formats "Shop%02d.dat" from data_fdps_chapter_current_chapter_id -- the internal 0..29 number, with no +1, unlike the fdetxt text file loaded two lines earlier -- and stores what fdps_vfs_load_entry returns. fdps_run_village_phase frees it when the village phase ends and leaves the pointer dangling rather than clearing it; the next chapter load overwrites it. fdps_shop_collect_stock_items is the only reader of the contents: the row base is this pointer + shop_index * 0xc and it reads twelve zero-extended bytes from there. Rows are 0 the item shop, 1 the weapon shop, 2 the secret shop, and the shipped members are 36 bytes, exactly those three rows. Each byte is an item id in the item table's numbering (the ids fdps_get_item_record takes); 0xff means an empty slot and is skipped wherever it sits, it is not a terminator.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by game menu and chapter-load code; it holds a game resource loaded by name out of a game archive]

Rebuild note:
0xff is an empty-slot marker, not an end-of-row sentinel -- it occurs between two stocked entries (SHOP05.DAT row 1 is 03 04 ff 1f 20 30 31 65 ff 74 75 83). A reader written the obvious way, stopping at the first 0xff instead of scanning all twelve bytes, drops most of that shop's stock.

=== 00069d84 [PLATE]
Pointer to the ShopWin.Cel sheet, the window frame every village-mode panel is drawn into.

fdps_run_village_phase writes it at 0003130f with fdps_vfs_load_entry("MISC.VFS", "ShopWin.Cel"), on the branch that also sets data_fdps_village_mode_flag, and frees it at 0003149e when the village phase ends; it holds a malloc'd CEL sheet only for the life of that phase and is not cleared afterwards. Readers pass it to fdps_cel_blit_sprite as the sheet, always sprite 0 at (0,0), to lay the panel frame down before filling it: fdps_shop_select_item, fdps_shop_render_buy_target_frame, fdps_village_select_member and fdps_church_select_promote_candidate compose into a 312-wide offscreen page (pitch 0x138), fdps_village_animate_window_zoom blits it at the moving corner of the zoom-in at pitch 0x140, and fdps_draw_text's page-break code uses it at (0x18, 0x8d) with pitch 0x168 as the village message window, the counterpart of data_fdps_message_window_sheet_ptr (Message.cel) on the battle map.

Pool: fdps  [only game functions reach it; it is a game resource loaded through fdps_vfs_load_entry]

=== 00069d90 [PLATE]
Pending chapter-event handler index for the unit action currently in progress, 0xff meaning "no event".

Seeded with 0xff by each dispatcher immediately before a unit acts -- fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase (twice, once per unit-action branch), fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase, fdps_battle_unit_turn and fdps_battle_system_menu -- and written by fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event, the only producer: when the tile a unit stepped onto or ended its turn on carries a scripted event whose trigger byte matches the reported occasion, that entry's handler byte is stored here. The same dispatchers read it back once the action is finished and, if it is no longer 0xff, call (*data_fdps_chapter_event_handler_table[slot])(unit_index) -- LEA EDX,[EDX*0x4+0x0] then CALL dword ptr [EDX + 0x601c4]. fdps_map_set_pending_tile_event also reads it, only to leave it unchanged when its gates fail.

Values are handler ordinals into the 50-slot table at 000601c4, so 0..49, taken verbatim from byte [0] of the tile's 2-byte entry in the loaded chapter script image ("map%02d.dat", base in the global at 0006013c). 0xff is the sentinel for both "this tile carries no handler" and "no event is pending"; it is a data-file value, not a computed one, and nothing range-checks the non-sentinel values before they are scaled by 4 and called.

Pool: fdps  [only game battle and map code reaches it, and it indexes a table of game chapter-event handlers]

Rebuild note:
The slot lives in _BSS, so its startup value is 0 -- a valid handler ordinal (chapter 3's wave-deploy handler), not "no event"; the 0xff sentinel exists only because every dispatcher writes it before the unit acts. Equally, the sentinel is 0xff and the compares are against the dword constant 0xff, so declaring this int and using the idiomatic -1 for "none" makes the != test succeed and dispatches through table[-1].

=== 00069da0 [PLATE]
The chapter-event / battle-end code: 0 the battle continues, 1 defeat (Game Over), 2 the chapter is cleared.

Cleared to 0 by main@00029220 before the first chapter and again after every outcome it has handled, and by fdps_chapter_state_reset at the start of each chapter. It is raised from two directions. The generic end-condition check fdps_battle_check_default_end_conditions runs only while the code is still 0: it presets 2, knocks it back to 0 if any enemy-side unit is still standing, and stores 1 if a mandatory unit has been retired. Chapter scripts raise it directly -- fdps_chapter_event_set_game_over and fdps_chapter_03_event_turn_limit_game_over store 1, the boss-defeat events of chapters 15, 22 and 23 store 2, fdps_run_death_scripts stores 2 for opcode 4 and 1 for opcode 5, and each fdps_chapter_NN_post_action handler applies that chapter's own rule. Chapters 19 and 24 also read it back, requiring 2 before offering their optional duel, and put it back to 0 when the duel is accepted so the battle carries on.

Everyone else only tests it against 0 and stops: fdps_battle_enemy_turn_phase, fdps_battle_npc_turn_phase, fdps_battle_advance_turn and fdps_battle_player_phase_loop break out of their sweeps the moment it is non-zero, so a chapter script that ends the battle takes effect on the very next unit boundary. main then reads it once per pass: 1 calls fdps_show_game_over and returns to fdps_title_screen, 2 dispatches data_fdps_chapter_end_handler_table[chapter] and fdps_run_village_phase, and any other value simply restarts the loop.

Pool: fdps  [only game-logic functions reach it -- battle phases, chapter event scripts and main]

Rebuild note:
Whether a store is guarded by "only while the code is still 0" is a property of each writing site, not of this variable. Most chapter post-action handlers write it unconditionally, so on a turn where two conditions fire the last writer wins; hoisting the guard into a shared setter, which is the obvious tidy-up, silently changes which ending several chapters give.

=== 00069da4 [PLATE]
Flat linear pointer to the 512-byte DOS conventional-memory block that holds the MSCDEX IOCTL control block.

fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers writes it once at startup (called from fdps_cdrom_detect): it asks DPMI INT 31h function 0100h for 0x20 paragraphs, takes the returned real-mode segment out of the int386x output REGS at data_fdps_cd_dpmi_out_regs (00069dac) and stores segment << 4 here, while storing the same segment << 16 at 00069da8 as a pre-packed seg:0000 far pointer. The two globals are therefore two views of ONE block: 00069da8 is the address the MSCDEX driver sees, this is the address the game dereferences. DOS/4GW identity-maps the first megabyte, so segment << 4 is directly usable as a flat pointer.

Every CD-ROM IOCTL wrapper reads it as the memcpy destination for the control block it is about to send and as the memcpy source for the reply the driver wrote back: fdps_cd_read_head_sector (6 bytes), fdps_cd_read_audio_channel_info and fdps_cd_set_audio_channel_control (9), fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and fdps_cdrom_read_track_info (7), fdps_cdrom_read_upc and fdps_cd_read_q_channel (11), fdps_cdrom_read_device_status (5), fdps_cd_read_media_change_status (2), fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command (1). The largest control block seen is 11 bytes, well inside the 512-byte allocation. The companion buffer at 00069de8 holds the 0x1a/0x1e-byte device request header itself, not the control block.

Value 0 means the buffers have not been allocated yet; _BSS gives that state for free and the allocation is never re-run.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps functions reach it; it is part of the game's own CD-ROM state block at 00069da4-00069e54, and no vendor module owns fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers]

Rebuild note:
This must stay a pointer into DOS conventional memory obtained from DPMI 0100h, and the same block whose seg:0000 form is stored at 00069da8 -- pointing it at a malloc'd or static buffer compiles and runs but leaves the MSCDEX driver reading and writing real-mode memory the game never looks at, so every IOCTL silently returns stale data.

=== 00069da8 [PLATE]
Real-mode far pointer -- segment in the high word, offset always zero -- of the DOS low-memory block that carries the IOCTL control block of every MSCDEX device request the game issues.

fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers writes it once, at 0003bb65, from the second of its two DPMI function 0x100 (allocate DOS memory block, 0x20 paragraphs = 512 bytes) calls: the real-mode segment DPMI returns in the int386x output block at 00069dac is zero-extended and shifted left 0x10, giving seg:0000 packed into a dword. Three instructions later the same segment, shifted left 4, goes to 00069da4 as the flat protected-mode address of those same 512 bytes. The two are one block seen two ways and are not interchangeable. The function checks nothing: if DPMI 0x100 fails, the error code DPMI leaves in AX is packed and stored as if it were a segment, and neither block is ever released -- there is no DPMI 0x101 call anywhere in the program.

Eleven functions read it and all do the same thing: fdps_cd_read_head_sector, fdps_cd_read_audio_channel_info, fdps_cd_set_audio_channel_control, fdps_cdrom_read_upc, fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command, fdps_cd_read_q_channel, fdps_cd_read_media_change_status and fdps_cd_set_door_lock build a DOS device request header on their stack frame and store this dword whole into its transfer-address field at offset 0x0e, with the transfer byte count at offset 0x12 (2 to 0x0b depending on the IOCTL) and the command byte at offset 0x02 always 3 for IOCTL input or 0xc for IOCTL output. The header itself is then memcpy'd into the OTHER DOS block -- flat address at 00069de8, its segment kept as a word at 00069e54 -- and fdps_cd_device_request hands MSCDEX ES:BX pointing at it via DPMI 0x300, INT 2F AX=1510. The IOCTL payload travels through the flat view at 00069da4: the caller memcpy's the request bytes there before fdps_cd_device_request and copies the reply back out of it afterwards.

It is zero until fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers runs, which fdps_cdrom_detect does before it issues its first request (fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info), so no request is ever built on a zero transfer address.

Pool: fdps  [all twelve referencing functions are the game's own MSCDEX wrappers, none of which matches a library object]

Rebuild note:
This dword and the one at 00069da4 are two encodings of the same DOS block and the code depends on which goes where: the request header's transfer-address field takes this packed real-mode seg:0000 form, while the memcpy into and out of the buffer takes the flat form. Collapsing them into one pointer variable -- the obvious thing to write -- makes MSCDEX decode the flat value as segment:offset and transfer at a different physical address entirely, so the reply never reaches the buffer the caller then reads.

=== 00069dac [PLATE]
Output union REGS for the CD-ROM subsystem's software-interrupt calls: the register values coming back from INT 2Fh and INT 31h.

The game never initialises it; the CRT wrappers int386 and int386x copy the CPU registers into it when the interrupt returns, and the game reads fields out of it afterwards. Its input counterpart is the REGS block at 00069dc8 and the segment registers are at 00069df0. fdps_cdrom_detect issues INT 2Fh AX=1500h (MSCDEX installation check) and then reads ebx at +0x04 as the number of CD-ROM drives (zero means no redirector is loaded and detection returns 0) and cl at +0x08 as the index of the first CD-ROM drive letter. fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers issues INT 31h AX=0100h (DPMI allocate DOS memory block, BX=0x20 paragraphs) twice and each time reads ax at +0x00 as the real-mode segment of the new 512-byte block: the first block's segment goes to 00069e54 and its linear address (segment << 4) to 00069de8, the second block's seg:0000 far pointer (segment << 16) to 00069da8 and its linear address to 00069da4. fdps_cd_device_request passes it as the output block for its INT 31h real-mode call and ignores the contents. Layout is Watcom's union REGS: eax +0x00, ebx +0x04, ecx +0x08, edx +0x0c, esi +0x10, edi +0x14, cflag +0x18. The carry flag at +0x18 is never tested, so a failed DPMI allocation goes unnoticed and the garbage segment is used as an address.

Pool: fdps  [only the game's own CD-ROM functions reference it; int386/int386x merely receive a pointer to it, which does not make it CRT state]

Rebuild note:
These 28 bytes are ONE union REGS, not seven independent scalars. int386/int386x write the whole block, so the drive count at +0x04 and the drive-letter index at +0x08 are only correct while they remain fields of a single object at a single address; emitting them as separate globals lets the linker place them anywhere and the interrupt result then overwrites whichever unrelated global lands at those offsets. This is exactly FD2 playtest bug B2 (rebuild_info/build_test/playtest_bugs.md).

=== 00069dc8 [PLATE]
Input register block handed to int386/int386x by the CD-ROM code: one 28-byte Watcom `union REGS`.

Every write to it sets up the registers for the INT call that follows on the next few instructions; nothing ever reads it back, because results come out of the companion output block at 00069dac (whose cflag, at 00069dc4, is what fdps_cd_device_request tests for failure). Members are laid out as Watcom's DWORDREGS -- eax +0, ebx +4, ecx +8, edx +0xc, esi +0x10, edi +0x14, cflag +0x18 -- and the code reaches them through the w. and h. aliases. fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers puts w.ax = 0x0100 and w.bx = 0x20 and calls int386x on INT 31h twice: DPMI "allocate DOS memory block", 0x20 paragraphs = 512 bytes, with the segment registers at 00069df0. fdps_cd_device_request puts w.ax = 0x0300 (DPMI simulate real-mode interrupt), h.bl = 0x2f (the interrupt to simulate, INT 2Fh), h.bh = 0, w.cx = 0 (no stack words to copy) and x.edi = 0x00069e22, the address of the real-mode call structure, with es set to ds. fdps_cdrom_detect puts h.al = 0, h.ah = 0x15, w.bx = 0 and calls int386 on INT 2Fh: the MSCDEX installation check, which answers in out.w.bx = drive count and out.h.cl = first drive letter. Members no call site sets keep whatever the previous call left in them -- only the segment-register block and the real-mode call structure are cleared before use, never this one.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cd_* and fdps_cdrom_* reach it; int386x is merely the CRT entry it is passed to, the storage is the game's]

Rebuild note:
These 28 bytes are one object. Ghidra shows five separate anchors inside them (00069dc8, 00069dc9, 00069dcc, 00069dcd, 00069dd0, 00069ddc) because the code touches individual register fields, and declaring those as separate globals lets the linker reorder or pad them apart, after which int386x reads the wrong registers -- FD2 shipped exactly that bug and it cost a dead keyboard (playtest bug B, one 28-byte union REGS split into scalars). Emit it as a single `union REGS` and reach the fields through .w / .h, not as `x.eax`: the original writes 16 and 8 bit stores that leave the upper halves stale, and a dword store would clear them.

=== 00069de4 [PLATE]
Exclusive end of the CD-DA play range: the HSG logical sector one past the last sector to be played.

Written only by fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, which runs after fdps_cdrom_read_track_info has queried a track. If that track is the disc's last one it takes the lead-out address from DAT_00069e0b; otherwise the routine queries track + 1 and takes that track's start address from DAT_00069e01, so the value is always the first sector NOT part of the selected track. Read only by fdps_cd_play_track and fdps_cd_play_track_range, each immediately after the resolve call, and passed as the second argument of fdps_cd_play_audio_range(start_sector, end_sector) together with data_fdps_cd_play_range_start_sector at 00069dec. That routine puts start_sector in the MSCDEX Play Audio packet at +0x0e and end_sector - start_sector at +0x12 as the sector count, with addressing mode 0 (HSG) at +0x0d, so the value is a plain unsigned logical sector number and the range is half-open. fdps_cd_play_track_range also returns end minus start as the length of the run it started. Zero at startup (_BSS) and meaningless until the first resolve call.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom or Miles AIL code touches it]

Rebuild note:
fdps_cd_resolve_track_range rewrites this global and 00069dec on every call, so a caller that wants a range spanning two tracks must read the start sector after the first resolve and before the second. Issuing both resolve calls and then reading the pair -- the obvious way to write it -- yields the second track's start sector and plays the wrong range.

=== 00069de8 [PLATE]
Flat linear pointer to the 512-byte DOS conventional-memory block that carries the MSCDEX device request header of every CD-ROM request the game issues.

fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers writes it once at startup, at 0003bb3d. The function sets DPMI function 0x100 (allocate DOS memory block) and 0x20 paragraphs into the int386x input REGS at data_fdps_cd_int_regs_in (00069dc8), calls int386x(0x31, ...), then takes the real-mode segment DPMI returned in the output REGS at data_fdps_cdrom_int_out_regs (00069dac), stores it as a word at 00069e54 and stores segment << 4 here. DOS/4GW identity-maps the first megabyte, so segment << 4 is directly usable as a flat protected-mode pointer. 00069e54 and this pointer are two views of ONE block: 00069e54 is the address MSCDEX is given, this is the address the game dereferences. The second DPMI allocation in the same function produces the separate IOCTL control-block buffer, flat at data_fdps_cd_ioctl_buffer (00069da4) and packed real-mode at data_fdps_cd_ioctl_buffer_real_mode_ptr (00069da8).

Fifteen wrappers read it and all in the same shape: build a DOS device request header on the stack, memcpy it in here, call fdps_cd_device_request, then memcpy the header back out to pick up the status word the driver wrote at header offset 3 (latched into 00069e20). The header lengths are 0x1e for fdps_cd_read_head_sector; 0x1a for fdps_cd_read_audio_channel_info, fdps_cdrom_read_upc, fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, fdps_cd_read_media_change_status and fdps_cd_read_q_channel; 0x18 for fdps_cd_set_audio_channel_control, fdps_cd_seek, fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command and fdps_cd_set_door_lock; 0x16 for fdps_cd_play_audio_range; 0xd for fdps_cd_stop_audio -- all far inside the 512-byte allocation. The IOCTL commands additionally put the real-mode far pointer of the OTHER block into the header transfer-address field at offset 0x0e, so the payload travels through 00069da4 / 00069da8 and only the header travels through here.

fdps_cd_device_request itself never touches this pointer: it copies the segment word from 00069e54 into the ES field of the DPMI real-mode call block at 00069e44 and leaves BX zero at 00069e32, then issues INT 2Fh AX=1510h through DPMI function 0x300. The header therefore has to sit at offset 0 of the block.

Value 0 means the buffers have not been allocated yet; _BSS gives that state for free. fdps_cdrom_detect calls fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers before the first request, and neither block is ever re-allocated or released -- there is no DPMI 0x101 call anywhere in the program.

Pool: fdps  [all fifteen referencing functions are the game's own MSCDEX wrappers; no vendor module owns fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers]

Rebuild note:
The block this points at must be DPMI-allocated DOS conventional memory, and this pointer must stay the flat segment<<4 view of the very block whose real-mode segment sits at 00069e54 -- MSCDEX is told where the request header is by that segment with BX=0, never by this pointer. Writing the obvious thing (a static array, a malloc'd buffer, or handing this flat pointer to the driver) compiles and runs, but the driver then reads its request header from an unrelated physical address and writes its status where the game never looks, so every CD-ROM request appears to succeed while returning whatever was already in the buffer.

=== 00069dec [PLATE]
Inclusive start of the CD-DA play range: the HSG logical sector of the first sector to be played.

Written only by fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, on entry, by copying DAT_00069e01 -- the track start address left behind by the preceding fdps_cdrom_read_track_info call. Read only by fdps_cd_play_track and fdps_cd_play_track_range, each right after a resolve, and passed as the first argument of fdps_cd_play_audio_range(start_sector, end_sector) together with data_fdps_cd_play_range_end_sector at 00069de4. That routine builds the MSCDEX Play Audio request: addressing mode 0 (HSG) at +0x0d, this value at +0x0e, and end_sector - start_sector at +0x12 as the sector count, so the range is half-open and the value is a plain unsigned logical sector number. fdps_cd_play_track_range latches this global into ESI before it resolves its second track, and returns end minus start as the length of the run it started. Zero at startup (_BSS) and meaningless until the first resolve call.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT or Miles AIL code touches it]

Rebuild note:
fdps_cd_resolve_track_range overwrites this global and 00069de4 on every call, so fdps_cd_play_track_range must copy the start sector out before it resolves the second track. Resolving both tracks first and then reading the pair -- the obvious way to write it -- leaves the second track's start sector here and plays the wrong range.

=== 00069df0 [PLATE]
Segment-register block handed to int386x by the CD-ROM code: one 12-byte Watcom `struct SREGS`, the companion of the input REGS at 00069dc8 and the output REGS at 00069dac.

Both users clear it with memset(&sregs,0,0xc) on entry and neither ever reads it back; int386x loads the selectors out of it before the software interrupt and stores the returned ones into it. Layout is Watcom's 386 SREGS -- es +0x00, cs +0x02, ss +0x04, ds +0x06, fs +0x08, gs +0x0a -- and es is the only member the game ever assigns. fdps_cd_device_request sets it at 0003bbfe with MOV word ptr [0x00069df0],DX where DX was loaded from DS, so ES addresses the game's own data segment for its INT 31h AX=0300h call (DPMI simulate real-mode interrupt), whose contract is ES:EDI -> real-mode call structure; the EDI half goes into the in_regs edi slot at 00069ddc as 0x00069e22, the 50-byte real-mode call structure. fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers passes the block still all zero for both of its INT 31h AX=0100h calls (DPMI allocate DOS memory block), which take no segment register. Zero at startup as _BSS, but nothing depends on that: both call sites memset it first.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers and fdps_cd_device_request reach it; int386x is merely the CRT entry it is handed to, the storage is the game's]

Rebuild note:
The original hands int386x an SREGS that is zero except for es = ds. The textbook idiom, and the one Watcom's own manual shows before int386x, is segread(&sregs), which fills all six members from the current registers; writing that here changes the selector ES carries into the DPMI 0300h call from the data segment to whatever ES happens to hold, and DPMI then reads the real-mode call structure from the wrong base. Keep the memset-then-set-es sequence, and keep the twelve bytes as one object: split into separate globals the linker may pad them apart and int386x reads the wrong slots.

=== 00069dfc [PLATE]
Number of CD-ROM drive letters MSCDEX reports, as returned by the installation check.

Written in exactly one place: fdps_cdrom_detect (0003c636) builds the MSCDEX installation check INT 2Fh AX=1500h in the input union REGS at 00069dc8, calls int386 with the output block at 00069dac, and if the returned BX is non-zero copies that word here and the returned CL -- the index of the first CD-ROM drive letter, 0 = A: -- to the byte at 00069dfe. A returned BX of zero means no CD-ROM redirector is loaded; in that case fdps_cdrom_detect returns 0 and leaves this global at its startup value of zero, so a zero here means either 'no CD-ROM' or 'detection never ran'.

Nothing in the program reads it. The partner byte at 00069dfe is the one that gets used: fdps_cd_device_request writes it into the drive field of the MSCDEX device request header at 00069e3a, so every CD access goes to the FIRST CD-ROM drive letter regardless of how many this count says exist.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* / fdps_cdrom_* MSCDEX layer; union REGS is a CRT type but this is the game's own storage]

=== 00069dfe [PLATE]
Drive-letter index of the CD-ROM drive the game talks to, 0 = A:, 1 = B: and so on.

Written once by fdps_cdrom_detect, from the low byte of the ECX returned by the MSCDEX installation check (INT 2F AX=1500, issued through int386 with data_fdps_cd_int_regs_in / data_fdps_cdrom_int_out_regs): that call returns BX = how many CD-ROM drive letters exist and CX = the letter of the first of them. fdps_cdrom_detect returns 0 without touching this byte when BX is zero, and main (00029220) then prints the CD-ROM error messages and exits, so no CD code runs with the value unset. The drive count from BX is kept separately at 00069dfc and is never used to pick a drive -- however many drives MSCDEX reports, the game always addresses the first one.

Read only by fdps_cd_device_request, which zero-extends it into the ECX field (00069e3a) of the real-mode call structure at 00069e22 before issuing MSCDEX send-device-request (AX=1510) via DPMI INT 31 AX=0300; MSCDEX reads CX there as the drive to send the request header to. Every CD operation in the game -- fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, CD audio playback -- goes through that one call, so this byte selects the drive for all of them.

Pool: fdps  [only fdps_cdrom_detect and fdps_cd_device_request reference it; the MSCDEX interface is hand-built in game code, not a CRT or AIL global]

=== 00069dff [PLATE]
CD-ROM track number that the currently published track-info globals describe.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, which stores the low 16 bits of its `track` argument here after an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input "Read Audio Track Info" request, next to that track's start sector in data_fdps_cd_track_info_start_sector (00069e01) and its 0xd0-masked control byte at 00069e05. The write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, since the status word is never tested. Values run from the disc's lowest track (00069e06) to its highest (00069e07), both published by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info; zero means no track-info request has been made yet, because the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup.

Read by fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, which takes no parameters and uses this word as the track whose disc-address range it is resolving, and by fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, which saves it on entry so that after querying the neighbouring track it can call fdps_cdrom_read_track_info once more and leave the track-info trio describing the track the caller had selected. Both readers sign-extend it.

Pool: fdps  [only the game's own CD-ROM layer touches it; the three referencing functions are all pool fdps and build MSCDEX device requests by hand]

=== 00069e01 [PLATE]
Start position of the CD-ROM audio track last queried, as an HSG logical sector number.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, at the end of every call: it takes the packed Red Book start address out of the MSCDEX Read Audio Track Info reply (control block offset 2) and runs it through fdps_cd_msf_to_sector, which subtracts the 150-frame two-second lead-in, so the stored value is a plain logical sector number and not an MSF triple. It is published together with the track number in DAT_00069dff and the masked track control byte in DAT_00069e05, and it is overwritten whether or not the driver accepted the request -- the reply status word is recorded in DAT_00069e20 but never tested.

Read in two places, each right after its own query. fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors takes this value as the track's start, queries track + 1 (or falls back to the lead-out sector in DAT_00069e0b when the track is the disc's last, per the highest track number in DAT_00069e07), takes this global again as the end, and returns the difference as a length in CD frames at 75 frames per second -- the lead-in offset cancels in the subtraction. fdps_cd_resolve_track_range copies this value into data_fdps_cd_play_range_start_sector at 00069dec and, after querying the following track, into data_fdps_cd_play_range_end_sector at 00069de4, giving the half-open sector range that fdps_cd_play_audio_range sends as a Play Audio request. Both routines finish by re-querying the track that was selected on entry, so this global, DAT_00069dff and DAT_00069e05 are left describing the same track as before; no reader depends on that restore, it is state hygiene. Zero at startup (_BSS) and meaningless until the first fdps_cdrom_read_track_info call.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* / fdps_cdrom_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT or Miles AIL code touches it]

Rebuild note:
Every fdps_cdrom_read_track_info call overwrites this global, so a reader that needs two tracks' start sectors must latch the first one into a local before it queries the second. Writing fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors or fdps_cd_resolve_track_range the obvious way -- query both tracks, then read data_fdps_cd_track_start_sector -- yields the second track's start sector for both ends and gives a length of zero or an empty play range.

=== 00069e05 [PLATE]
Control field of the CD-ROM track that the currently published track-info globals describe, masked with 0xd0.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input "Read Audio Track Info" (control code 0x0b) device request for its `track` argument and stores byte 6 of the returned transfer buffer -- the track's control/ADR byte -- here after ANDing it with 0xd0. The mask drops the ADR nibble and the copy-permit bit and keeps three control bits: 0x40 data track, 0x80 four-channel audio, 0x10 pre-emphasis. The same call also publishes the track number in data_fdps_cd_track_info_track_number (00069dff) and the track's start sector at 00069e01, so all three always describe the same track. The write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, since the status word is never tested; the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup, so before the first request the byte reads 0, which means plain stereo audio.

Read only by fdps_cd_track_is_audio, which queries the track it is given and then returns (masked control != 0x40) -- that is, every track that is not a plain data track counts as audio, and it is the value of this byte alone that decides whether the game will play a track as CD music.

Pool: fdps  [both referencing functions are pool fdps and build the MSCDEX device request by hand; nothing in the CRT or the sound library reaches this address]

Rebuild note:
The audio test is an equality against the 0xd0-masked byte, not a bit test. Writing the obvious `(control & 0x40) == 0` for "is audio" -- or masking with 0xf0 instead of 0xd0 -- changes the answer for any track whose control field also carries pre-emphasis (0x10), four-channel (0x80) or copy-permit (0x20): the original reports those as audio even when the data bit is set, and reports a copy-permitted data track as data.

=== 00069e06 [PLATE]
Lowest (first) track number on the CD currently in the drive.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-input device request carrying control-block code 0x0A (read disk info) through fdps_cd_device_request and then hands out the reply: control-block byte 1 lands here, byte 2 in 00069e07 (the highest track number), and the lead-out track's MSF address in 00069e08/00069e09/00069e0a, with its sector equivalent in 00069e0b; the whole 6-byte tail of the reply is also kept verbatim at 00069e16 and the request header's status word at 00069e20. The value is a plain unsigned track number, 1 on an ordinary disc, not BCD.

No code reads this byte. The track walkers -- fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf, fdps_cd_play_whole_disc -- bound themselves against the highest track number and the lead-out address only, and take the first track as given.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own CD-ROM driver code, fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info]

=== 00069e07 [PLATE]
Number of the highest (last) track on the CD-ROM currently in the drive.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request with subcommand byte 0x0A (Read Disk Info) and distributes the seven-byte reply: the lowest track number to DAT_00069e06, this byte (reply byte 2) as the highest track number, the lead-out address unpacked into minutes/seconds/frames at DAT_00069e08/09/0a, the same address converted to a sector count in DAT_00069e0b, the raw six-byte payload copied to DAT_00069e16, and the device request's status word to DAT_00069e20. The write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, because that status word is never tested here. Valid values run from the lowest track number in DAT_00069e06 up to 99; zero means no disc summary has been read yet, since the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup.

Read in three places, always to answer "is this track the last one on the disc". fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors refreshes the summary itself and then compares the requested track against this byte unsigned: below it, the track's length is the next track's start sector minus its own; equal to it, the end point is the lead-out sector in DAT_00069e0b instead. fdps_cd_resolve_track_range makes the same decision the other way round -- when this byte is less than the queried track plus one it publishes the lead-out sector as the exclusive end of the play range -- but it does NOT refresh the summary first, so it uses whatever the last fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info call left here. fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf copies the byte straight out through its highest-track output pointer, next to the lowest track number and the lead-out MSF, for callers that want the whole disc summary.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* / fdps_cdrom_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT and no Miles AIL code touches it]

Rebuild note:
This byte is latched disc state with a lifetime longer than any one call. fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, and through it fdps_cd_play_track and fdps_cd_play_track_range, read it without querying the drive, relying on an earlier fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info (fdps_cdrom_detect runs one at startup). Rewriting fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info to hand the disc summary back to its caller instead of publishing it here, or dropping the startup detect call, leaves this byte zero; every track then compares as the disc's last, so the play range ends at the equally-zero lead-out sector DAT_00069e0b and nothing plays.

=== 00069e08 [PLATE]
Minutes field of the lead-out track's Red Book address on the CD currently in the drive.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request with subcommand byte 0x0A (Read Disk Info) through fdps_cd_device_request and then hands out the seven-byte reply: the lowest track number to data_fdps_cd_lowest_track_number (00069e06), the highest to data_fdps_cd_highest_track_number (00069e07), and the packed lead-out address in reply bytes 3..6 to fdps_cd_unpack_msf, which splits 0x00MMSSFF into this byte (minutes), DAT_00069e09 (seconds, 0..59) and DAT_00069e0a (frames, 0..74, one frame being 1/75 second). The same packed address also goes to fdps_cd_msf_to_sector, whose logical sector count lands in DAT_00069e0b; the raw six-byte reply tail is kept verbatim at DAT_00069e16 and the request header's status word at DAT_00069e20. Values run 0..99. The write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, since the status word is never tested here; the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup, so before the first request the byte reads 0.

No code in the image reads this byte. Everything downstream works from the sector count instead: fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors and fdps_cd_resolve_track_range take the lead-out end point from DAT_00069e0b, fdps_cd_play_whole_disc plays sector 0 for DAT_00069e0b sectors, and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf recomputes its own minute/second/frame triple from DAT_00069e0b - 0x96 rather than reading these three bytes.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own hand-built MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT and no Miles AIL code touches it]

Rebuild note:
This byte is the drive's raw lead-out address, which counts the 150-frame (two second) lead-in before track 1; the disc-playing-time triple that fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf hands its callers is computed separately from DAT_00069e0b with those 150 frames subtracted. Rewriting fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf to return these three bytes -- the obvious tidy-up, since they are otherwise unread -- makes every reported playing time two seconds too long.

=== 00069e09 [PLATE]
Seconds field of the lead-out address of the CD-ROM currently in the drive, in Red Book minute/second/frame form. Values run 0 to 59.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input request with subcommand byte 0x0A (Read Disk Info) and distributes the seven-byte reply: the lowest track number to data_fdps_cd_lowest_track_number, the highest to data_fdps_cd_highest_track_number, the raw six-byte payload to data_fdps_cd_disk_info_reply, the request header's status word to data_fdps_cd_last_request_status, and the packed lead-out address both split into minutes/seconds/frames across data_fdps_cd_leadout_msf_minute, this byte and data_fdps_cd_leadout_frame by fdps_cd_unpack_msf, and converted to a logical sector count in data_fdps_cd_leadout_sector by fdps_cd_msf_to_sector. Zero also means no disc summary has been read yet, since the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup and the write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request -- the status word is never tested here.

Nothing in the image reads it. The unpacked minute/second/frame triple exists alongside the sector count in data_fdps_cd_leadout_sector, and it is the sector count that every consumer uses: fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors as the end point for the disc's last track, fdps_cd_resolve_track_range as the exclusive end of a play range, fdps_cd_play_whole_disc as the length handed to fdps_cd_play_audio_range, and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf, which re-derives its own minute/second/frame output from that sector count rather than from these bytes.

Those two paths do not agree, and the gap is 300 frames, not the 150 one would guess. This byte holds the drive's raw lead-out address, which counts the two-second (150-frame) Red Book lead-in. fdps_cd_msf_to_sector already takes that lead-in off once when it fills data_fdps_cd_leadout_sector (it ends on + -0x96), and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf subtracts 0x96 a second time before dividing by 0x4b and 0x3c. Its published triple therefore sits four seconds below the triple stored here.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* / fdps_cdrom_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT and no Miles AIL code touches it]

=== 00069e0a [PLATE]
Frames field of the lead-out track address of the CD currently in the drive (0-74, at the Red Book rate of 75 frames per second).

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, which issues an MSCDEX IOCTL-Input device request with control-block subcommand 0x0A (Read Disk Info) through fdps_cd_device_request and then hands out the reply: control-block byte 1 to data_fdps_cd_lowest_track_number, byte 2 to data_fdps_cd_highest_track_number, and bytes 3..6 -- the lead-out address packed as 0x00MMSSFF -- to fdps_cd_unpack_msf, which drops the minutes into DAT_00069e08, the seconds into DAT_00069e09 and the frames here. The same packed value goes through fdps_cd_msf_to_sector into the lead-out sector number at DAT_00069e0b, the raw six-byte payload is kept verbatim at DAT_00069e16, and the request header's status word at DAT_00069e20. The write happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, because that status word is never tested here. Zero means no disc summary has been read yet, since the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup.

No code reads this byte. Everything downstream that needs the end of the disc -- fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, fdps_cd_play_whole_disc -- uses the sector form in DAT_00069e0b instead, and fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf publishes the minutes/seconds/frames triple to callers that ask for the disc summary in Red Book form.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_* / fdps_cdrom_* MSCDEX wrappers; no Watcom CRT and no Miles AIL code touches it]

=== 00069e0b [PLATE]
The disc's lead-out address as a logical sector number: how many sectors of audio the CD in the drive holds.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, at the end of every MSCDEX Read Disk Info IOCTL: the reply's packed MSF lead-out address goes through fdps_cd_msf_to_sector, which converts minute/second/frame to (m*4500 + s*75 + f) and then subtracts 0x96, the 150-frame two-second lead-in Red Book addressing counts before track 1. So the value stored here is already an LBA with the lead-in removed, on the same scale as data_fdps_cd_track_start_sector and the play-range globals. Zero until the first successful disc-info query, since _BSS is zeroed at startup.

Read as the end of the disc by three routines, each of which must have a fresh disc-info query behind it: fdps_cd_resolve_track_range copies it into data_fdps_cd_play_range_end_sector when the selected track is the highest track on the disc; fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors uses it as the end point when measuring the last track, so the track length comes out as leadout minus that track's start sector; fdps_cd_play_whole_disc hands (0, this) to fdps_cd_play_audio_range, making the Play Audio request cover every sector from the start of the disc to the lead-out. fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf converts it back to a minute/second/frame triple to report the disc's total playing time.

Pool: fdps  [only the game's own CD-ROM layer touches it -- all five referencing functions are pool fdps, and it is filled from a request block the game assembles itself]

Rebuild note:
fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf subtracts 0x96 from this value a second time before splitting it into minutes/seconds/frames, even though fdps_cd_msf_to_sector already removed the 150-frame lead-in on the way in. The reported playing time is therefore two seconds short of the disc's actual length. Write that routine the obvious way -- one lead-in subtraction -- and it stops matching the original.

=== 00069e0f [PLATE]
The disc's media catalog number (UPC/EAN), 7 bytes of packed BCD as returned by the CD-ROM driver.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_upc, which builds an MSCDEX IOCTL Input request with control-block subcommand 0x0e (Read UPC Code), sends it through fdps_cd_device_request, and copies the control block's 7-byte UPC/EAN field (control-block offset 2) here. The copy is unconditional: the request's status word is latched into data at 00069e20 but never tested, so these 7 bytes are rewritten on every call whether or not the driver accepted the request. When the driver answers with CONTROL/ADR = 0 the disc carries no catalog number and the field is zeroed before the copy, so all-zero is the "no catalog number" value. The bytes are packed BCD digits, not text, and are not NUL terminated. No other code in the image reads this global; it is a recorded driver answer, not an input to any check -- the disc-presence check the game actually enforces is elsewhere.

Pool: fdps  [its only reference sits in fdps_cdrom_read_upc, a game function that shares the CD state block at 00069da4/00069da8/00069de8/00069e20 with the neighbouring fdps_cd_* globals; no Watcom or AIL library symbol covers it]

Rebuild note:
Declaring these 7 bytes as a char array and handing them to any str* routine or a %s runs off the end -- there is no terminator, and the following bytes are the next CD-state globals. It is also written before it is ever read (it never is), so a rewrite that only fills it on a successful request still matches the original, but one that skips the write entirely loses the all-zero-means-no-catalog-number distinction if the field is ever consumed later.

=== 00069e16 [PLATE]
Verbatim copy of the payload of the last MSCDEX Read Disk Info reply: lowest track number, highest track number, and the packed Red Book address of the lead-out track.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, and on every call. That function builds a 26-byte DOS device request header (command 3, IOCTL Input, transfer count 7) plus a 7-byte control block whose subcommand byte is 0x0A, stages both through the DOS-addressable buffers data_fdps_cd_request_header_buffer and data_fdps_cd_ioctl_buffer, calls fdps_cd_device_request, copies both blocks back, and then memcpy's the control block's six payload bytes -- everything after the subcommand byte -- to this address. The layout is therefore byte 0 = lowest track number, byte 1 = highest track number, bytes 2..5 = the lead-out track's address in the driver's packed frame/second/minute/zero form. The same six source bytes are also handed out field by field in the instructions that follow: byte 0 to DAT_00069e06, byte 1 to DAT_00069e07, the packed address unpacked into minutes/seconds/frames at DAT_00069e08/09/0a and converted to a logical sector count in DAT_00069e0b. The copy happens whether or not the driver accepted the request, because the request-header status word recorded in DAT_00069e20 is never tested here; the CRT zeroes _BSS at startup, so all six bytes read 0 until the first call, which fdps_cdrom_detect makes during start-up.

Nothing in the image reads these bytes. Every consumer of the disc summary -- fdps_cd_get_track_length_sectors, fdps_cd_resolve_track_range, fdps_cd_get_disk_info_msf, fdps_cd_play_whole_disc -- goes to the unpacked scalars at DAT_00069e06, DAT_00069e07 and DAT_00069e0b instead. This block is the undistributed original kept alongside them, in the same manner as the write-only UPC copy at DAT_00069e0f and the write-only device-status dword at DAT_00069e1c.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info; no Watcom CRT and no Miles AIL code touches it]

=== 00069e1c [PLATE]
The device status bit field MSCDEX last returned for the CD-ROM drive.

Written only by fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, at the end of every call: that routine sends an MSCDEX device request with command code 3 (IOCTL Input) carrying a 5-byte control block whose code byte is 6 (Device Status), and stores the four bytes the driver leaves at control-block offset 1 here. The bits are MSCDEX's documented device status -- bit 0 door open, bit 1 door unlocked, and above them the drive capability bits (cooked-only reading, read/write, audio track playback, interleaving, prefetching, audio channel manipulation, HSG and Red Book addressing).

Nothing in the image reads it. fdps_cd_audio_is_idle, the only caller of fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, calls it and tail-jumps to fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy, which tests the BUSY bit (0x0200) of the request header status word in data at 00069e20; the device status dword parked here is never consumed. It is a debugging or leftover output of the wrapper, kept because the request has to be issued for its status word.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, a game MSCDEX wrapper, and it sits among the game's other CD state globals at 00069da4-00069e21]

=== 00069e20 [PLATE]
The DOS device-driver request-header status word returned by the most recent CD-ROM driver call.

Every routine that issues a request through fdps_cd_device_request latches header offset 3 here on its way out: fdps_cd_read_head_sector, fdps_cd_set_audio_channel_control, fdps_cdrom_read_upc, fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, fdps_cd_stop_audio, fdps_cd_ioctl_output_command and fdps_cd_read_media_change_status. Most of them return something else entirely (a sector, a byte, nothing), so this global is the only place a caller can see whether the driver accepted the request. Two readers consume it. fdps_cd_status_is_not_busy masks it to bit 9 alone -- 0x0200, the request header BUSY bit -- and returns 1 when that bit is clear, which is how the audio layer decides that playback has finished. fdps_cdrom_detect compares the whole word against 0x810c after fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info and returns 2 when it matches; 0x810c is error (bit 15) plus done (bit 8) plus error code 0x0c, the driver's way of saying the request failed, which the caller reads as "redirector present but no usable disc". Any other value leaves the detect result at 1. Bits 0..7 are the driver error code and are only meaningful when bit 15 is set; the low byte is deliberately discarded by the BUSY test.

Pool: fdps  [all ten references sit in the game's own CD layer and share the request buffers at 00069da4/00069de8; no Watcom or AIL library symbol covers it]

Rebuild note:
Declare it unsigned. As a signed short the detect test has to be written == -0x7ef4 (which is what Ghidra prints today) and the natural == 0x810c never matches, while >> 8 becomes an arithmetic shift on exactly the error responses that set bit 15.

=== 00069e22 [PLATE]
The DPMI real mode call structure the CD-ROM layer uses to reach MSCDEX: the register image DPMI function 0300h loads before it simulates INT 2Fh AX=1510h, Send Device Request.

Written only by fdps_cd_device_request, and rebuilt from scratch on every call. That function memsets all fifty bytes to zero, then fills four fields: EAX (+0x1c) = 0x1510, the MSCDEX Send Device Request function; ECX (+0x18) = the CD-ROM drive index, zero-extended from data_fdps_cdrom_drive_letter_index; EBX (+0x10) = 0 and ES (+0x22) = the real-mode segment of the DOS-addressable block held at DAT_00069e54, so that ES:BX addresses the DOS device request header the caller has staged through data_fdps_cd_request_header_buffer. Everything else stays zero, including the flags word at +0x20 and SS:SP at +0x30/+0x2e, which is how DPMI is told to supply the real-mode stack itself. The structure's address then goes into the edi slot of data_fdps_cd_int_regs_in (DAT_00069ddc) while data_fdps_cd_int_sregs gets es = ds, giving DPMI the ES:EDI pointer it requires, and int386x is called on INT 31h with ax = 0x0300 and bl = 0x2f. The layout is the DPMI one -- EDI +0x00, ESI +0x04, EBP +0x08, reserved +0x0c, EBX +0x10, EDX +0x14, ECX +0x18, EAX +0x1c, then the nine words flags +0x20, ES +0x22, DS +0x24, FS +0x26, GS +0x28, IP +0x2a, CS +0x2c, SP +0x2e, SS +0x30.

Nothing ever reads the structure back. DPMI writes the real-mode register results into it on return, but fdps_cd_device_request judges the call only by the carry flag of the output register block (DAT_00069dc4) and prints "DEVICE REQUEST FAILED!!!" if it is set; the driver's own answer comes back inside the request header in DOS memory, which each caller copies out for itself. Every MSCDEX operation in the game passes through here -- fdps_cd_read_head_sector, fdps_cd_set_audio_channel_control, fdps_cdrom_read_upc, fdps_cdrom_read_disk_info, fdps_cdrom_read_track_info, fdps_cdrom_read_device_status, fdps_cd_stop_audio and the play calls all build a request header and then call fdps_cd_device_request. The CRT zeroes _BSS at startup, but nothing depends on that: the memset runs first on every call.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by the game's own fdps_cd_device_request; int386x is merely the CRT entry the pointer to it is handed to, the storage is the game's]

Rebuild note:
The memset of all fifty bytes before each call is load-bearing, not hygiene. DPMI 0300h reads SS:SP (+0x30/+0x2e) out of this structure and supplies a real-mode stack of its own only when both are zero, and it loads the flags word at +0x20 into the simulated interrupt's FLAGS. Filling in just the four fields the call needs -- the obvious rewrite once the object is a named struct, and the obvious economy once you notice _BSS is already zero -- leaves the previous call's returned SS:SP and FLAGS in place from the second call onwards, and MSCDEX is then entered on a stack DPMI did not allocate.

=== 00069e54 [PLATE]
Real-mode segment of the DOS conventional-memory block that carries the MSCDEX device request header; also the flag that says those buffers have been allocated.

Written once, at 0003bb2a in fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers: the function asks DPMI for a 0x20-paragraph DOS block (AX=0x100, BX=0x20 into the input REGS at data_fdps_cd_int_regs_in, then int386x(0x31,...)) and copies the returned segment out of the ax field of data_fdps_cdrom_int_out_regs as a word. The very next instructions store segment << 4 into data_fdps_cd_request_header_buffer, so this word and that pointer are two views of ONE block: this is the address MSCDEX is given, that is the address the game dereferences.

fdps_cd_device_request reads it at 0003bbc9 and stores it into the ES slot (offset 0x22) of the DPMI real-mode call register block at 00069e22, with the EBX slot left at 0, so ES:BX points at the request header when the extender issues INT 2Fh AX=1510h through DPMI function 0x300. It is the only route by which the driver learns where the header is.

fdps_cdrom_detect reads it at 0003c68e as a guard: CMP word ptr [0x00069e54],0x0 / JNZ, and only calls fdps_cd_alloc_dos_buffers when it is still zero. Zero therefore means 'the two DOS blocks have not been allocated yet', a state supplied by the CRT zeroing _BSS at startup and never restored afterwards - nothing frees the blocks and there is no DPMI 0x101 call in the program. Any other value is a live real-mode segment below 0xA000.

Pool: fdps  [all three referencing functions are the game's own CD-ROM code; int386x merely returns the value through a REGS block the game owns]

Rebuild note:
This word must stay the real-mode SEGMENT of the request-header block and must stay the thing fdps_cdrom_detect tests for zero. Writing the obvious C - deriving it from the flat pointer, or adding a separate 'buffers allocated' boolean and initialising this from the pointer - breaks it two ways: MSCDEX is handed ES from here and would read its request header at the wrong physical address, and the allocate-once guard depends on this exact word being zero before anything writes it, which only the CRT's _BSS clear provides.

=== 00069e56 [PLATE]
The program's single MSCDEX Audio Q-Channel Info control block: the request byte sent to the CD-ROM driver and the 11-byte reply describing where CD-DA playback currently stands.

fdps_cd_read_audio_position is the only user. It passes this block to fdps_cd_read_q_channel, which writes control code 0x0c into byte 0, copies all 11 bytes into the DOS transfer buffer at [data_fdps_cd_ioctl_buffer], issues an IOCTL-input device request through fdps_cd_device_request (real-mode INT 2Fh AX=1510h), and copies the driver's reply back over the block. fdps_cd_read_audio_position then reads four bytes of the reply out by absolute address and stores them through its caller's pointers: +2 (00069e58) is TNO, the track playing now; +4 (00069e5a) is MIN and +5 (00069e5b) SEC and +6 (00069e5c) FRAME, the running time reached inside that track, with SEC 0-59 and FRAME 0-74. The MSCDEX layout continues +1 CONTROL/ADR, +3 POINT/INDEX, +7 zero and +8..+10 the absolute MIN/SEC/FRAME position on the disc; the program never reads those. Only byte 0 is ever written by the game -- bytes 1..10 go out to the driver holding whatever the previous reply left there, zero on the first call because the CRT clears _BSS.

Pool: fdps  [reached only by fdps_cd_read_q_channel and fdps_cd_read_audio_position, both project C driving MSCDEX; no CRT or AIL code touches it]
